# Changelog

All notable changes to Netcanon are documented here.
Format follows [Keep a Changelog](https://keepachangelog.com/en/1.1.0/).

> **Note on pre-launch commit SHAs.**  Older entries below cite
> commits by short SHA (`(commit X)`).  Pre-launch the project went
> through a `git filter-repo` history rewrite to scrub PII (see the
> Phase 1 entry).  That rewrite changed every commit's SHA, so most
> short-SHA citations in entries written before Phase 1 won't
> resolve via `git show <sha>` against current history.  The
> *narrative* around each SHA is the load-bearing context; the SHA
> is decorative.  Entries written after Phase 1 (the entries closest
> to the top of `[Unreleased]`) cite current SHAs that resolve.

See also: [`README.md`](README.md) for project orientation;
[`ARCHITECTURE.md`](ARCHITECTURE.md) for the four-layer design that
much of the work below evolves.

**Date convention:** entries below use the maintainer's local
authoring date (UTC-7 / Pacific).  Git tag commits may land on the
following UTC day; cross-check `git log <tag>` for the exact UTC
timestamp if your timezone matters for an audit.

---

## [Unreleased]

### Security

- **The Docker image no longer carries pip.**  The base image's pip
  (26.2.1) vendors a certifi CA bundle that trusts emSign roots whose
  intermediate CA keys were compromised (GHSA-6q48-6c7w-9gw2,
  CRITICAL), and the gating image scan failed every pull request on
  it.  netcanon never used that copy -- the server makes no outbound
  HTTPS request through pip -- but it was in the image.  The runtime
  stage now uninstalls pip once netcanon is installed, so no copy pip
  vendors can ship.  If you install packages into the container
  yourself, `python -m ensurepip` restores a pip, and with it the
  copy it bundles; build an image of your own on top instead.

- **A value of several lines was written as lines of the config, and
  the text after a line break was a command on the target.**  Every
  renderer puts a value into its line as it stands.  An interface
  description that held a line break and then `username intruder
  privilege 15 nopassword` -- which the OPNsense and IOS-XE NETCONF
  parsers keep from an element's text (`&#10;`), and the FortiOS parser
  from a value printed between quotes over several lines -- came out
  with that line on its own onto 12 of the 13 public codecs, many of
  the jobs saying `completed`.  And the FortiOS parser read each line
  of such a value as a statement: a replacement message whose HTML
  held a line `end` and then `config system admin` made an account
  with no password on the IOS-XE and EOS targets, in jobs that said
  `completed`.  No value is now written on more than one line, and
  FortiOS reads a quoted value whole (Fixed, below).  If you translated
  an OPNsense, IOS-XE NETCONF or FortiGate config with 0.7.7 or
  earlier, look in the old output for lines the source config did not
  have before it reaches a device.

- **A control character a value held was written into every output,
  where a terminal acts on it rather than shows it.**  A parser that
  reads its config as text keeps a control character a value holds,
  and every renderer wrote the value as it stood: an IOS-XE
  description holding `ESC [1A ESC [2K` -- up a line, and erase it --
  came out so onto every line-based target, and an operator reading
  the output on a terminal did not see the line above it (an account
  written there from another part of the config, say).  No target is
  now given one: the pipeline (and the sanitiser) writes each run of
  them -- every character Unicode calls a control character, but a
  tab and the line breaks -- as a space and says where in the job's
  warnings, as it does a line break, and `CodecBase.render` refuses a
  tree that still holds one.  A space and not nothing: a secret with
  a character taken out would be another secret, written with no
  review line.  The RouterOS parser now reads `\a`, `\b` and a
  control character's byte (`\1B`) as the character, and the same
  rule mends it.  Guarded by
  `tests/unit/migration/test_a_value_holds_no_control_character.py`.
  If you reviewed an output of 0.7.7 or earlier on a terminal, read it
  again with `cat -v` or an editor that shows control characters.

- **A secret that holds a line break or a control character is left
  out, never mended.**  The two rules above write each run as a
  space, which is right for a description and wrong for a secret:
  AOS-S, FortiOS, Junos, RouterOS and OPNsense write an SNMP
  community with white space between quotes, so a community that held
  a line break came out as a community nobody set, and with the
  character taken out instead it would be another one too.  Such a
  secret is left out first, with what it composes: an SNMP community
  with every trap host that would carry it, a local user or an SNMPv3
  user whole, a RADIUS key or an FHRP authentication alone (the
  server and the group kept).  The job says each place, never the
  value, and is `partial`.  The places are one table (`SECRETS` in
  `netcanon/migration/_one_line.py`), which a test holds to every
  field of the schema named as a secret.  Guarded by
  `tests/unit/migration/test_a_value_holds_no_control_character.py`.

- **A value of the config was written into a RouterOS output as
  script, and a description could run a command on the router that
  imported it.**  RouterOS reads an imported `.rsc` as a script:
  outside a string white space parts two words, `;` ends the command,
  and `$`, `[ ]` and `( )` substitute a variable or run a command or
  an expression -- and inside a string `$[...]` and `$(...)` run as
  well.  The RouterOS renderer escaped only `\` and `"` in a string
  and wrote most values bare, so a description `$[/system
  reset-configuration]` from any source came out as that command on
  the router that imported the output, in a job that said
  `completed`, and a value with a `;` in it -- a RADIUS secret, an
  SNMP community, a user's name, a DHCP domain -- ended its command
  there, and what followed was read as the next one.  A value is now
  written as it stands only when it is made of letters, digits and
  `- . _ / : , %` (what an export leaves bare), and as a string
  otherwise, with `\`, `"` and `$` escaped, as an export escapes `$`
  (Fixed, below).  If you translated a config onto RouterOS with 0.7.7
  or earlier, read the old output for `$`, `;`, `[` and `(` outside a
  quoted string, and for `$` inside one, before it reaches a router.

- **A RADIUS key that IOS-XE, EOS or AOS-S had stored in a form of its
  own was written into the target's config as the secret itself, and
  the server authenticated nobody.**  IOS-XE `key 7 <blob>` and `key 6
  <blob>` came out on AOS-S, FortiOS, OPNsense and RouterOS as the
  secret `7 <blob>` (and `key 0 <secret>` as the secret `0 <secret>`);
  the one-line `radius-server host ... key 7 <blob>` came out on IOS-XE
  itself as `key <blob>`, the blob as the secret; EOS `key 7 <blob>`,
  the form EOS prints, came out as the secret `7` on every target, EOS
  included (and `key 0 <secret>` as the secret `0`); and AOS-S
  `encrypted-key "<blob>"` came out as the secret `<blob>` on every
  target, AOS-S included.  Each such config commits, the server it
  names rejects every request, and every job said `completed`.  Each
  parser now holds a stored form behind its platform's envelope, which
  only that platform's renderer writes back (Fixed, below).  If you
  translated an IOS-XE, EOS or AOS-S config with a RADIUS key with
  0.7.7 or earlier, look in the old output for a key written as `7
  <blob>`, `0 <secret>`, `7` or `0` alone, or an AOS-S blob, and
  re-enter the secret.

- **A credential that held white space was written as two words, and
  the second was read as a keyword.**  Every line-grammar renderer put
  a password, an SNMP community, an SNMPv3 user's name, group or
  passphrase, and a VRRP/HSRP key into its line as it stood.  A
  community `public rw` from a source that quotes values (FortiOS,
  RouterOS, Junos, VyOS, AOS-S) or holds them as element text
  (OPNsense, IOS-XE over NETCONF) came out on NX-OS as `snmp-server
  community public rw` -- a READ-WRITE community `public` -- and on EOS
  as a community whose second word is read as an ACL name; a password
  `secret scrypt` on NX-OS sets the password `secret`.  On AOS-S, which
  quotes and documents no escape, a `"` in a value ended it there.
  Such a value is now left out and said (Fixed, below).  No committed
  input holds one; a config translated with 0.7.7 or earlier from a
  source whose credentials hold white space or a quote is worth reading
  for the lines it wrote.

- **A name written into an OPNsense or VyOS review comment could end the
  comment, and what followed it was configuration.**  Where a target
  cannot take an account's password, the account is left out and a
  review comment names it, as the source holds the name.  OPNsense
  writes that comment as `<!-- ... -->` and VyOS as `/* ... */`, and
  neither renderer kept the name from ending it: a source account
  named `x--><user>...</user><!--` became, on OPNsense, an account the
  source never had, holding whatever elements the name spelled out (a
  password hash among them), and `a*/system{...}/*` left `system{...}` on a
  VyOS line as nodes.  A name that only held `--`, which XML allows
  nowhere in a comment (`svc--backup`), failed the OPNsense render
  with an error that said nothing of the name.  Every review comment
  is now built by one helper (`netcanon/migration/_comments.py`),
  which writes `*/` as `* /` and puts a space after a hyphen that
  another follows; a comment that ends at the end of its line is left
  as it was.  Guarded by
  `tests/unit/migration/test_a_value_stays_in_its_comment.py`, which
  reads the OPNsense output with an XML parser and the VyOS output by
  its comment grammar, and reads the source for any other place that
  builds a block comment around a value.  The VyOS SNMPv3 review
  comment, and the one VyOS writes where it leaves out a credential
  that is not one value, are built by the same helper.

- **A local user whose password could not be carried was written onto
  FortiOS and RouterOS with no password at all.**  When a target cannot
  take a source's password hash, the account is to be left out with a
  review line.  FortiOS, RouterOS and OPNsense wrote the review line
  and then the account without its password: `edit "<name>"` with its
  access profile (`super_admin` for a privilege-15 user), `/user add
  group=full name=<name>`, a `<user>` element.  RouterOS documents that
  a user added with no password has a blank one, and a FortiOS admin
  with no `set password` is the same.  Over the committed captures, 93
  accounts in 66 captures onto FortiOS, 99 in 70 onto RouterOS, and 60
  in 43 onto OPNsense (where an account with no `<password>` element has no hash to check
  a password against, so it is not known to log in), in
  jobs that reported a review line and nothing else.  The account is
  now left out whole, as on every other target, and the review line
  stands in its place (Fixed, below).  If you translated a config with
  local users onto FortiOS or RouterOS with 0.7.7 or earlier, look in
  the old output for an account under a `review:` line before it
  reaches a device.

- **An EOS banner's lines were read as configuration, and a banner line
  became an administrator account with no secret on the target.**  A
  printed EOS config whose `banner motd` or `banner login` held a line
  `username <name> privilege 15 nopassword` came out with that account
  onto 12 of the 13 public codecs -- `username <name> privilege 15
  nopassword` on EOS and IOS-XE, a `super-user` with no authentication
  on Junos -- and the jobs onto seven of them said `completed`.  The
  EOS parser now reads every body that runs to an `EOF` line as text
  (Fixed, below).  If you translated an EOS config with a banner with
  0.7.7 or earlier, look in the old output for accounts the switch
  does not have before it reaches a device.

- **A banner's lines were read as configuration by the IOS-XE CLI,
  NX-OS, AOS-CX, OS10 and AOS-S parsers, and a banner line became an
  account with privilege 15 on the target.**  A config of any of the
  five whose banner held a line, in the platform's own grammar, for an
  account with privilege 15 (`username <name> privilege 15 ...` on
  IOS-XE, `role network-admin` on NX-OS, `group administrators` on
  AOS-CX, `role sysadmin` on OS10, `password manager user-name ...` on
  AOS-S) came out with that account onto all but one of the public
  codecs, and with the banner's VLAN, interface address and route,
  many of the jobs saying `completed`.  No committed banner holds such
  a line.  Each of the five now reads a banner as text, ended where
  its vendor ends it (Fixed, below), and refuses a banner it cannot
  tell from the configuration: one whose line ends in a form feed or
  another character a device does not end a line at (EOS's own pass
  too), and, on IOS-XE, AOS-S and OS10, one whose text held the end
  the device printed after it -- either of which, read, made a banner
  an account again.  If you translated a config of any of them that
  has a banner with 0.7.7 or earlier, look in the old output for
  accounts the device does not have before it reaches a device.

- **An IOS XR banner's lines were read as configuration, and a banner
  line became an account on the target.**  A printed IOS XR config
  whose banner held a line `username <name>` with ` group root-lr`
  under it came out with that account onto 12 of the 13 public codecs
  -- with privilege 15 on nine of them, and on Junos, NX-OS and AOS-CX
  under the role `root-lr`, which they do not have -- and with the
  banner's interface address onto all 13; the jobs onto five of the
  twelve said `completed`.  No committed IOS XR capture has a banner.
  The parser now reads a banner as text, ended where Cisco ends it
  (Fixed, below).  If you translated an IOS XR config with a banner
  with 0.7.7 or earlier, look in the old output for accounts the
  router does not have before it reaches a device.

- **Reading a pasted config could take time that grew with the square of
  it.**  Five shapes, each in shipped code.  Patterns that began
  `^\s` and were applied to the whole text walked, from every line start,
  to the end of the run of blank lines they were in: a 64 KB body of lines
  of spaces held `/detect` for about a minute.  A lazy value in front of
  trailing white space re-read the line for every character it took: a
  run of spaces inside a Dell OS10 route line, or after an IOS-XR `ntp`
  line.  A search for a trailing number, or for a RouterOS key, started
  again inside the run it had just crossed.  And RouterOS line
  continuations were joined by adding to one string: parsing 3 MB of
  lines that each end in a backslash took two and a half minutes.  And
  a handler that runs once per line looked through everything the
  earlier lines had made — the routing instance of a `vrf` line, the
  static routes so far, every interface for each `trunk` line — so a
  config with nothing odd in it cost the square of the number of its
  stanzas: six thousand RouterOS DHCP networks and their pools took 37
  seconds, sixteen thousand Junos static routes 7.  A pattern at
  work does not let the server's other threads run, so each delayed every
  other request.  All are mended — in the `probe()` of nine codecs, in
  the parsers and renderers, in the Tier-3 detection every `parse` runs,
  in the switchport-to-VLAN projection the switch codecs share, and in
  the probe and prompt patterns of the shipped device definitions.
  Detection, every probe and every parsed tree are unchanged on every
  config in the repository and the development corpora, and every
  committed capture replays identically through the plan endpoints.  What
  changed in meaning is the defect or a text no device prints: a pattern
  for an indented keyword no longer matches it at the left margin after a
  blank line; a device-definition probe no longer takes a value that is
  only white space; the RouterOS export banner has to be on one line; a
  prompt pattern's user or host part cannot contain the separator after
  it.  A new test searches for the next one: it builds texts from each
  regex the product holds and times every codec's `probe` and `parse` on
  a capture with a run put into it (`tests/unit/test_untrusted_text_cost.py`).
  The last shape has a search of its own, run by hand
  (`tools/stanza_cost_search.py`), and a pinned text for each handler it
  found.  It is a search, not a proof; the two things it left known and
  not mended are the next entry's.  Put a request timeout and a memory
  limit in front of a server that takes text from people it does not
  trust.

- **A small config could still take seconds, or hundreds of megabytes,
  to read.**  Three more shapes, none of which changes an output.
  *A list of one record that a line adds to after looking for its value
  there* — the addresses of one interface, the members of one LAG, the
  route targets of one VRF — cost the square of the lines the record was
  given: 32,000 addresses on one Junos IRB unit (2 MB) took 12 seconds,
  8,000 secondary addresses on one AOS-CX SVI (0.3 MB) 28, 32,000
  RouterOS NTP servers 24, and 640 lines in one AOS-S VLAN (13 KB) 4.
  Each is about a second or less; the look is by key (`Uniques`, in
  `netcanon/migration/codecs/_helpers.py`), in every parser that had it.
  *A scan of another list for every item*, after the parse: rendering
  400 VLANs, port-channels and member ports to OPNsense took 12 seconds
  and takes 0.06; the port-name translator's collision warning, the
  model-aware plan's account of dropped ports, the NX-OS route-target
  lines and the VyOS SNMPv3 users each build an index once.  And *what
  the switchport projection made and dropped*: for a trunk whose list is
  wide it made a VLAN record and a membership for every id, and the six
  port-centric codecs dropped all but the declared ones on their next
  line.  50 Arista trunks that allow `2-4000` (5 KB) took 0.4 seconds and
  180 MB to parse, and take 0.01 seconds and 1 MB; 48 NX-OS trunks that
  state `1-99,101-4094`, translated to Junos, 0.4 seconds and 176 MB,
  now 0.04 and 1.  The projection takes the set its caller keeps
  (`project_switchport_to_vlan(intent, keep=...)`) and makes nothing
  else; an id that is not a VLAN id in a wide list (`1-200,5000`) still
  fails the parse, as it did.  Lists of VLAN ids are built from one
  shared tuple of ints (8 bytes an id on a port, where it was 38), and a
  membership costs 45 bytes while it is stamped, where it cost 800: a
  thousand trunks that carry every VLAN on a thousand declared VLANs
  (118 KB), translated to AOS-S, are 0.7 seconds and 72 MB, where 500 of
  each were 0.7 seconds and 293 MB.  Nothing moved: every committed
  capture parses, renders bare and translates onto all thirteen codecs
  to the same digests as before, the cross-mesh results and the
  reconciliation are unchanged, and the projection is compared in the
  suite with the one it replaces, on built switches, with and without
  the set.  New tests pin a text for each place
  (`tests/unit/test_untrusted_text_cost.py`), read the source for a list
  that is looked through before it is added to, and count what a VLAN id
  and a membership cost in bytes
  (`tests/unit/migration/test_projection_makes_what_is_kept.py`).
  What that left -- what a config expands to (800 ranges on one AOS-S
  line are 800,000 names and 295 MB), the product of two honest counts,
  and no limit on the time or the memory a request takes -- is the next
  entry's.

- **What a config makes is counted, and a request has a time limit.**
  A range is a few bytes that parse to thousands of entries, `all` is
  4,094, and every trunk that allows every VLAN is a member of every
  VLAN, so neither the size of a request nor the cap on its text bounded
  the memory it took: one AOS-S line of 800 port ranges (11 KB) was 295
  MB to parse, and 50,000 interface stanzas of one line each (0.9 MB)
  were 240 MB.  The product now counts what a request makes, at each
  place a few bytes become many entries and BEFORE the entries are made,
  again on every finished parse, and the length of every output
  (`netcanon/migration/limits.py`): VLAN ids that lists and ranges name
  (and the 4,094 of a trunk that states no allowed list, on the four
  platforms where that is every VLAN),
  port memberships, ports that only a range or a list names, interfaces,
  what a Junos `interface-range` copies onto its members, the words
  block-form Junos is written out as, and characters of output.  Past a
  limit the request is **refused in a sentence** that names what was
  large, how large, and the limit: the AOS-S line at its ninth range, in
  a hundredth of a second and under two megabytes; a thousand trunks
  that carry every VLAN on a thousand VLANs is the default limit
  exactly, and one trunk more is refused before the first membership is
  stamped.  A request also has one **deadline**, which every parser
  looks at in every loop over the lines of a config.  What this does not
  bound is said in SECURITY.md and is not small: requests in flight
  under every set of limits but `small` (below), the size of an answer
  (188 MB at the default limits, to a target that reports every
  membership as unsupported), records no limit counts (static routes,
  addresses), and a renderer, which the deadline does not stop -- a
  request whose time runs out in one comes back as any other.  So the
  advice stands: a server that takes text from people it does not trust
  wants a memory limit that stops the worker, a limit on connections,
  and unless it runs `small` a limit on requests in flight, in front of
  it.  Nothing within the limits
  moved: every committed capture parses, renders and translates onto all
  thirteen codecs as before.  What an ordinary request costs did not
  move by anything that could be measured: through the application, the
  111 committed captures a codec reads, each translated to two targets,
  the best of five and three alternating runs, took 1.63 to 1.70
  seconds in all before the limits and 1.63 to 1.69 with them.

### Added

- **The Cisco Catalyst 9300 can be declared as a source or target
  device.**  Two model families: `C9300` (the 24/48-port T, P, U, H
  and S models, the C9300-24UX, -48UXM and -48UN) and
  `C9300-higher-scale` (C9300-24UB, -48UB, -24UXB, which Cisco's data
  sheet says stack only with each other, so a stack that mixes the two
  is refused).  A stack of up to eight; each switch has one bay for
  the C9300-NM-4G, -4M, -8X, -2Q or -2Y.  Names come from a new
  `catalyst` naming rule -- type, switch, module, port -- with the
  type stated per group of ports from Cisco's interface lists
  (`prefix:`), never derived from a speed: a C9300-48UXM is
  `TwoGigabitEthernet1/0/1-36` then `TenGigabitEthernet1/0/37-48`.
  Every name is graded `vendor-doc`; no capture claim is made, since a
  C9300 config lists the interfaces of every network module the bay
  can take and so no capture's names equal one deployment's ports.
  The stack's one management interface, `GigabitEthernet0/0`, is a
  new kind of entry, a port of the whole deployment
  (`deployment_ports:`): it belongs to no member and pairs with the
  other side's management port -- a flat profile's management port
  now belongs to no member either, so the two pair.
- **A Catalyst's source switches are read from its config.**  A
  Catalyst `show running-config` has a `switch N provision <type>`
  line for each switch of its stack (a switch that is alone too), and
  `detect-deployment` -- and with it the source picker of the
  Interface rename modal -- now reads them: the members by switch
  number, in the family's `stack` mode, each line quoted as evidence.
  The notes say that the line is what the stack is provisioned for,
  and that no line states a network module, so each switch's bay is
  proposed empty; a C9300 config, which holds the interfaces of every
  module the bay takes, is then `consistent: false` and lists them.
  Lines in a banner or a stanza are not read;
  a line that sets out to state a switch and cannot be read is
  counted; XML (the NETCONF codec) is said not to be read.  The
  detector is `codecs/cisco_iosxe_cli/deployment_detect.py`, under
  the `cisco_iosxe` vendor id both IOS-XE codecs share.
- **The Cisco Catalyst 9200 and 9200L can be declared as a source or
  target device.**  Three model families, because Cisco stacks none of
  them with another: `C9200` (the 24/48-port T, P and PL models and
  the C9200-24PXG and -48PXG; StackWise-160), `C9200-PB` (C9200-24PB
  and -48PB, which Cisco's stacking guide says "can only be stacked
  with each other") and `C9200L` (the fixed-uplink models;
  StackWise-80).  A stack of up to eight.  A C9200 has one bay, for
  the C9200-NM-4G or -4X on the 1G models and the -4X or -2Y on the
  PXG models; the C9200-NM-2Q is not modelled, since no Cisco document
  read gives the names of its ports.  A C9200L's uplinks are fixed and
  named as module 1 (`TenGigabitEthernet1/1/1-4` on a C9200L-24P-4X).
  A PXG model's Multigigabit ports are `TenGigabitEthernet`, numbered
  on from its gigabit ports (`GigabitEthernet1/0/1-16`, then
  `TenGigabitEthernet1/0/17-24`).  The C9200L-48PXG-4X has twelve
  Multigigabit ports; Cisco's command reference numbers
  TenGigabitEthernet ports 37 to 48 but says a 48-port switch's
  Multigigabit ports are 41-48, so that they are ports 37-48 is
  inferred and the part is graded `inferred`.  No configuration of any of them was seen: no
  capture claim is made, and whether a C9200 config holds the
  interfaces of a module that is not fitted, as a C9300's does, is not
  established.  `detect-deployment` proposes their stacks from the
  `switch N provision` lines, as for the C9300.
- **The Cisco Catalyst 3850 can be declared as a source or target
  device.**  One model family, `C3850`: the 24/48-port T, P, F and U
  models, the Multigigabit WS-C3850-24XU and -12X48U, and the SFP and
  SFP+ models WS-C3850-12S, -24S, -12XS and -24XS, in a StackWise-480
  stack of up to nine.  One bay, for what Cisco's data sheet lists per
  model among the C3850-NM-4-1G, -2-10G, -4-10G and -8-10G.  Named as
  a C9300 is: a WS-C3850-24XS with a C3850-NM-8-10G in switch 2 is
  `TenGigabitEthernet2/0/1-24` and `TenGigabitEthernet2/1/1-8`.  Two
  parts are graded `inferred`, each with its reason: the
  WS-C3850-12X48U's twelve Multigigabit ports, which Cisco numbers
  nowhere, are taken as ports 37-48 from the command reference's
  TenGigabitEthernet range and the configuration guide's example; and
  the C3850-NM-2-10G, whose two 1G and two 1G/10G slots no Cisco
  document read names, is `GigabitEthernet1/1/1-2` and then
  `TenGigabitEthernet1/1/3-4`.  Not modelled: the C3850-NM-2-40G (no
  Catalyst 3850 document read names a 40-Gigabit interface) and the
  WS-C3850-48XS, which does not stack.  What the stack's caveat says
  is not checked: Cisco's eight-switch limit for a stack that holds a
  WS-C3850-24XS, -24XU or -12X48U, and its license levels.  No
  configuration of a 3850 was seen.  `detect-deployment` reads
  `switch N provision ws-c3850-48p` as it reads a C9300's line.
- **The Cisco Catalyst 3650 can be declared as a source or target
  device.**  One model family, `C3650`: the T, P and F models with four
  1G uplinks (S), two 1G and two 10G (D) or four 10G (Q), the
  WS-C3650-24PDM and -48FQM among them, and the Multigigabit
  WS-C3650-12X48UQ and -12X48UR, in a StackWise-160 stack of up to
  nine.  The uplinks are fixed and named as module 1, as a C9200L's
  are: a WS-C3650-48PQ as switch 2 has `TenGigabitEthernet2/1/1-4`.
  Graded `inferred`, each with its reason: the names of a D model's
  uplinks, `GigabitEthernet1/1/1-2` and then
  `TenGigabitEthernet1/1/3-4`, which Cisco labels G1-G4 (the two on the
  right also TE3 and TE4) and names in no interface list; and the
  twelve Multigigabit ports of the 12X48UQ and -12X48UR, taken as 37-48
  as the 3850's are.  Not modelled: the WS-C3650-8X24PD and -8X24UQ (no
  document read says which eight of their 24 ports are Multigigabit),
  the -12X48FD (the hardware guide and the data sheet disagree on its
  uplinks) and the -12X48UZ (no 3650 document read names a 40-Gigabit
  interface).  A model is named without its license suffix (-L, -S or
  -E), and the license level is not checked.  No configuration of a
  3650 was seen.  `detect-deployment`
  reads a 3650's `switch N provision` line as it reads a C9300's.
- **`NETCANON_CONFIG_LIMITS`** -- `standard` (the default), `large`,
  `unlimited`, or `small` -- chooses how much one config may expand to
  and how long one request may take.  One setting with a name on both
  platforms: the environment variable for the server, the Docker image
  and pip; **Preferences... -> Config size limit** in the desktop
  application (`DesktopPreferences.config_limits`); `netcanon sanitize
  --limits` on the command line.  A value that is none of the four
  stops the server at startup, and the server logs the limits in force
  when it starts.  The numbers are in `docs/CAPABILITIES.md` § H, and a
  test holds every number a document prints to the code's.
- **A refusal is a result on every surface.**  The seven endpoints that
  return a job answer 200 with a `failed` job whose `error` begins
  `refused:` and whose new `refusal` field carries the limit, how many
  were asked for and the limit's number -- with both devices declared
  too.  `POST /api/v1/sanitize` answers 413; `detect-deployment` still
  proposes the device and says in a note why it did not check the
  proposal against the port names; the command line exits 2.  The
  migrate page paints the sentence in its red banner and does not
  follow it with "Did you mean another vendor?", which is for a config
  that could not be read; the sanitise page keeps the sentence on the
  page (`sanitize-refusal`), where other failures are a toast that is
  gone in four seconds.  What a refusal quotes from the config goes to
  the client and never to a log.  (Under `small` two answers come from
  the server before any of these handlers runs, and are the same on
  all of them: 503 for a request it has no place for, and 408 for one
  whose body did not arrive in its time -- the next entries.)
- **Under `small`, a server works on one request at a time.**  Every
  limit is for one request, and requests at once add up: two of the
  largest requests `small` admits, at once, ended a 256 MiB instance
  that either of them fitted in -- and the sanitise page itself sent
  two at once.  The limits now also say how many requests that read
  config text a server WORKS on at once: one under `small`, and no limit
  under `standard`, `large` and `unlimited` (one user at a desktop has
  nobody to wait behind, and the operator of a server chooses the set).
  A second request waits its turn, inside its own deadline; at most two
  wait; and one whose deadline passes in the line is refused like any
  other -- a `failed` job whose `refusal.limit` is `at_once`, a note
  from `detect-deployment`, and **503 with `Retry-After`** from the
  sanitiser and `detect` (not 413: nothing was too large, and the same
  request can be sent again) -- in a sentence that says the server was
  busy and to send it again.  The turn is held until the request's
  answer has gone out, is given back on every way out, and is taken
  back at the request's deadline from a client that does not read its
  answer.  `/health`, the pages and every endpoint that reads no config
  text never wait behind it; the command line never waits.
- **Under `small`, a request is counted when its headers arrive.**  A
  body is memory before its request can ask for a turn, and bodies that
  arrived together added up however few of the requests were let work:
  twenty of the largest at once ended a 256 MiB instance that had
  refused seventeen of them.  The server now counts a request that
  would read config text -- by its method and path, in its outermost
  middleware -- BEFORE it reads the body.  There are three places (one
  at work and two waiting); one more request is answered **503 with
  `Retry-After`** at once, in the busy sentence, its body unread --
  the same answer on every endpoint that reads config text, the seven
  that return a job included.  A request's deadline runs from its
  arrival, so the time its body takes to come is time it has spent,
  and a body that has not arrived by then is answered **408** and its
  connection closed.
- **Under `small`, an answer nobody reads is abandoned at its request's
  deadline.**  The turn lent to an answer was taken back then, and the
  answer stayed for as long as its client kept the connection: four of
  the largest, each sent as the last one's time ran out, ended an
  instance with no two requests ever at work together.  At the
  deadline an answer that has not gone out is now let go: no more of
  it is sent, what was held for it is freed, the connection is closed,
  and the server's log says so in byte counts.  So **under `small` an
  answer has the request's 20 seconds to be read in**: a client that
  reads, however slowly, is not cut inside them, and the largest
  answer `small` admits, read at a megabyte a second, is not finished
  in them.  An answer is handed to the server 64 KiB at a time, since
  a server takes all it is handed into its buffer at once.  And
  `netcanon serve` -- the Docker image's entry point -- starts the
  server on a socket on which the system itself ends a connection
  whose client has taken nothing for that long (`TCP_USER_TIMEOUT`, on
  Linux; nothing elsewhere): a server can only close a connection once
  what it wrote has been taken.  A server started another way
  (`uvicorn netcanon.main:app`) does not have that part.
- **Busy is said as busy.**  A request that waited most of its time
  for its turn and then ran out of time was refused as slow: `seconds`
  as its limit, "a Netcanon you run yourself allows 120", 413 from the
  sanitiser.  A refusal for time that follows a wait now says how long
  the request waited for its turn and to send it again, has `at_once`
  as its limit, and is answered 503 with `Retry-After` where the busy
  refusal is.  A request that did not wait is refused for its time as
  before.
- **What the above was measured to do**, in a container with an
  instance's limits started by the image's own entry point, each
  request sent again and again until the instance's peak stopped
  rising or sixty times (`docs/demo-plan/07-budget.md` has every row,
  the rounds, and what each client got).  None of these ends the
  instance: three of the largest translations at once (189 MB of its
  268 the first time, 233 after 30 rounds); bursts of twelve, sixteen,
  twenty and thirty of them (232 to 237 MB, three translated and the
  rest answered 503 unread); three sanitise requests at once and then
  ten translations, alternating 28 times (230 MB); thirty clients
  that send a translation and leave; forty of the largest answers one
  after the other, none of them read; a reader at a megabyte a second.
  The image before each of these was measured the same day: three
  translations at once ended one without turns in the first round,
  and with turns the fourth burst of twenty, the sixth round of the
  alternating requests, the second thirty that left and the fourth
  unread answer each ended one.  What is still true: the peaks are
  high, an instance does not come back down, and nothing limits how
  many connections a client opens.

### Changed

- **AOS-S output has no `interface` stanza that says `enable` and
  nothing else** for a port that a VLAN's `untagged` / `tagged` list
  or a `trunk` line of the same output names.  The device prints a
  stanza only for a port with a setting of its own, and the output
  now does the same: a port that is disabled, named or addressed has
  its stanza, and so has a port no other line names.  Whether a line
  names a port is asked of the parser's own reader, on the line as
  it is written, and the line counts only if every port on it comes
  back as itself: a `trunk` line with a member whose name has a
  space in it is read by nobody, and a list writes `01` as `1`, so
  the ports of such a line keep their stanzas.  So does a port under
  a name the switch does not use (`Ethernet1`).  Every port
  reads back as it did -- the parser gives a listed port the record
  an empty stanza makes (the first entry under Fixed).  Over the
  committed captures, an output onto AOS-S from another vendor loses
  such stanzas in 14 jobs and gains or loses nothing else; an AOS-S
  config onto AOS-S gains none, and loses the stanzas that were
  empty in the source or held only a line Netcanon does not model.
  The output is a whole configuration: read into a switch that
  already has one, a port left out keeps what that switch had for
  it.  Reading its own lists back, the render counts what their
  ranges name as a parse does: an AOS-S output whose ranges name
  more different ports than the `ports` limit (2,048 under `small`)
  is refused where it is written.  Over the committed captures the
  most one output's ranges name is 51.
- **What else moves for an AOS-S source**, with the first entry under
  Fixed.  The validation report lists the paths of every port, not
  only of those with a stanza: a port's VLAN membership is listed as
  unsupported on a target that has no form for it, and the type
  Netcanon infers for a port (`/interfaces/interface/config/type`)
  as lossy where it is -- which takes four jobs of the committed
  captures from severity `ok` to `warn`; no job's status moves.
  `source_ports` -- and with it the rename table, where no source
  device is declared -- lists the ports that have a stanza as their
  stanzas come, then the others in the order an operator counts
  them; it followed the order the VLANs first named them (1, 48-52,
  35-47, 2... on a committed 2930F capture, which is 1 to 52 now).
  A port named only in a list counts toward the `interfaces`
  limit where the config is read (it was counted only by a target
  that made a record for it), and the VLANs it is tagged in toward
  `vlan_ids`; in every shipped set of limits a config that passes
  `memberships` passes that.  Two ports that end on one target name
  are two stanzas of that name, and the warning says `the target
  will render duplicate/fused interface stanzas`.  And the port a
  **FortiOS or OPNsense VLAN interface** is put on moves: those
  renderers choose a parent port for each VLAN among the ports the
  tree holds, and it now holds the listed ones.  Over the committed
  AOS-S captures, 32 VLAN interfaces onto each: on FortiOS 16 are on
  a port that is a member of the VLAN in the source (3 before), 9 on
  a port that is not (15), and 3 have no `set interface` line (10);
  on OPNsense 15 are on a member (2), 10 on a port that is not (17),
  and 7 on a name no source port has (13).  Not every move is to a
  member: four FortiOS VLAN interfaces that had no parent line are
  on a port that is not in the VLAN, and three OPNsense ones went
  from `lan` to such a port.  Nothing on the job says a parent was
  chosen, and how one is chosen is as it was.
- **The public demo runs `small`** (`NETCANON_CONFIG_LIMITS` in the
  instance environment), sized in a container with an instance's own
  limits: the request built to reach every limit at once is translated
  with the instance at 169 MB of its 268 the first time and 215 after
  34 times, and the three texts that took
  hundreds of megabytes are refused in milliseconds.  Under `small` a
  refusal says whose limit it is and what a Netcanon you run yourself
  allows; it names no setting.  Requests at once take turns there, a
  burst is turned away before it is read and an answer nobody reads is
  let go (see "Added"); what is still true of an instance is in
  `docs/demo-plan/07-budget.md`.
  `deploy/VERIFY.md` proof 14 shows by behaviour that a running image
  has the limits -- one built before them ignores the variable and says
  nothing -- proof 15 that requests at once take turns, proof 16 that
  a burst is turned away unread, and proof 17 that an answer nobody
  reads is let go.
- **The sanitise page sends its two requests in turn.**  One submit is
  the audit and the output, each a whole parse and render of the same
  config; they were sent at once, and are now sent one after the other,
  the audit first, and the output is not asked for when the audit was
  refused.  A server that was busy for as long as a request may wait
  answers 503, and the page keeps that sentence where it keeps a
  refusal for size.
- **A job's answer is written a piece at a time.**  The seven endpoints
  that return a job handed the job to the framework, which made the
  answer in five passes over it; a job's validation report has a path
  for every membership, so the answer to the largest job `small` admits
  is 38 MB and making it took more memory than the translation.  The
  job is now written straight to JSON, a field or a run of a long list
  at a time, under every set of limits.  The bytes and the
  `Content-Length` are the same, compared job by job with the
  framework's own (`tests/integration/test_job_answer.py`); an ordinary
  job is one body, as ever, and costs what it did as near as could be
  measured.
- **The sanitiser redacts the tree it parsed, and no longer a copy of
  it.**  `sanitize_text` parsed a config, copied the whole tree and
  redacted the copy, which made it the heaviest request a server takes.
  The tree is its own and nothing else holds it, so it is redacted
  where it stands (`sanitize_intent(..., in_place=True)`; called with
  no argument that function still returns a copy).  The output and the
  audit are the same, on every committed capture.  Measured in a 256
  MiB container on the largest config `small` admits, sent again and
  again: 231 MB before, 188 now; three such requests at once went
  from the edge of the container to 198 MB.
- **`netcanon serve` starts the server itself.**  It did what
  `uvicorn.run` does for one worker and now does it step by step, so
  that under limits that say how many requests work at once the
  socket it listens on can be bound first (see "Added").  Under every
  other set of limits the server binds its own socket, as it did; a
  server that fails to start still exits with status 3.  The desktop
  application's embedded server is started the same way.
- **Under a set of limits that makes requests take turns, a request
  first hands freed memory back to the system** (`malloc_trim`, on Linux
  with glibc; nothing elsewhere).  The C library keeps what a thread
  freed for that thread, and a server runs its requests on whichever
  thread is idle.
- **A VyOS set line nested more than 64 levels deep is a parse
  failure.**  Past about a thousand levels it was an unexpected error
  (the walk that writes the nested blocks ran out of stack).  A real
  path is a dozen words.
- **`netcanon sanitize`** takes `--limits`, and refuses a config past
  them with exit status 2.  Under `small` the sentence is the command
  line's own ("This run used the 'small' config size limit ... pass
  --limits standard"), where it spoke of a server.

### Fixed

- **What goes with a dropped name is said, where no devices are
  declared.**  The port translator removes, with a name it drops, a
  static route out of it, a DHCP pool on it, a VRRP track entry of
  it, a VXLAN source interface that is it and its place in a LAG
  (`_strip_dropped_ports`).  The job listed the name and none of
  that: with both devices declared the plan said it, from a reading
  of its own; with none -- what every plan endpoint runs by default
  -- nothing did, and the output, which no longer holds it, could
  not.  The Cisco Live EVPN leaf's `Loopback2` is its VTEP source;
  onto Junos it has no place, and the VTEP was left with no source
  in a job that said why `Loopback2` went and nothing of the
  overlay.  Over the committed captures onto every public codec,
  with no port map, such drops took VTEP sources, routes, DHCP pools
  and every member of LAGs, unsaid.  The translator now records what
  it removes, where it removes it and by the tests that remove it
  (`PortRenameResult.taken`), for an operator's drop as for its own,
  and `run_plan_with_checked_names` writes a warning line for each
  kind in the plan's own words (`port_mapping.what_went_lines`, the
  plan's lines unchanged): `port_rename: the VXLAN source interface
  was dropped (Loopback2), so the VTEP is left without the source it
  was bound to — give it one`.  A line and not a status: a name the
  translator dropped holds the job already, and one an entry dropped
  was the operator's to decide.  Guarded by
  `tests/unit/migration/test_what_goes_with_a_dropped_name.py`: the
  record held to what is gone from the tree, by identity, on every
  committed capture onto every public codec (how many jobs record
  something pinned by source codec); the lines from configs of each
  kind; once, and not twice where devices are declared; each check
  handed the defect it is for.  The guard that holds the no-devices
  job to `run_plan_with_overrides`'s now takes the lines into
  account, last.  (#544 follow-up.)
- **A run of more digits than a number is read from is refused in
  words, not failed as a fault.**  Python converts a string of digits
  to a number only up to a limit (`sys.get_int_max_str_digits()`,
  4,300 digits by default), and every parser reads numbers from the
  runs of digits its patterns take.  A config that held a run of 4,400
  digits failed the parse of seven of the public codecs (on one
  capture of each), at some two dozen places, as `unexpected error in
  stage parsing: Exceeds the limit (4300 digits) for integer string
  conversion ... use sys.set_int_max_str_digits() to increase the
  limit` -- words about
  the server, and advice no operator can take; an entry of a port map
  whose target held such a run failed seven of the targets the same
  way at render.  Nothing was written wrong.  `CodecBase.parse` now
  refuses such a text before any parser reads it -- `parse failed:
  <codec>: line <n> holds a run of more than 4,300 digits, more than a
  number is read from, so the text is not read`, naming the line and
  quoting nothing -- and `CodecBase.render` a tree whose value holds
  one, naming the field (`render failed: <codec>: a value of the tree
  (interfaces[].name) holds ...`), on every target: one rule at the
  two boundaries every caller crosses
  (`netcanon/migration/_long_numbers.py`).  The limit is read when the
  check is made, so a server that sets another is held to its own; no
  committed input holds a run anywhere near it.  Guarded by
  `tests/unit/migration/test_a_number_too_long_to_read.py`: every line
  of a capture of each public codec that holds a number, made too
  long; a port an entry names so onto every target; and each check
  taken out, to show the texts reach the failure it is for.
- **An IOS XR sub-interface whose encapsulation is no 802.1Q tag is
  left out, and said.**  `encapsulation untagged` defines "the
  matching criteria to map untagged frames on an interface" (Cisco,
  "Interface and Hardware Component Command Reference for Cisco 8000
  Series Routers", VLAN Subinterface Commands), and `encapsulation
  default` matches "any tagged or untagged traffic that has not been
  matched by another subinterface" (Cisco, "Understand IOS XR L2VPN
  Services and Features").  The parser read neither, and kept the
  sub-interface -- an `l2transport` attachment circuit, as a rule --
  as one of no tag: VyOS wrote `vif <its number>`, and every other
  target a sub-interface of no tag, in jobs that said `completed`.
  The tree has no form for either, so such a sub-interface is left
  out with the row of a tag statement not read whole (`... -- not one
  802.1Q tag and at most one inner tag, so the sub-interface is not
  translated`), as `encapsulation dot1ad` is.  It is the rule of the
  sub-interface that states no tag (below), for a line that states
  something else; a port's own `encapsulation` (a serial line's `ppp`)
  is read as before.  Guarded by
  `tests/unit/migration/test_an_encapsulation_that_is_no_tag.py`.
- **An IOS XR or EOS sub-interface that states no tag is left out, and
  said.**  "An 802.1Q VLAN subinterface must have a configured VLAN ID
  to send and receive traffic; without a VLAN ID, the subinterface
  remains in the down state" (Cisco, "IOS XR Interface and Hardware
  Component Command Reference", `dot1q vlan`), and on EOS "a VLAN must
  be configured on the subinterface" for it to be operational
  (Arista, EOS User Manual, "Ethernet Ports").  The two parsers kept
  such a sub-interface, with no tag: VyOS wrote it as `vif <its
  number>`, the number taken for a tag, and RouterOS, FortiOS and
  OPNsense put its address on an interface the output defines
  nowhere, in jobs that said `completed`.  A sub-interface of a port
  or a bundle that states no `encapsulation` is now left out, under a
  row of its own, `untagged: interface <name> (...)`: a statement the
  source held and did not run, which the migrate page lists beside
  the sections with a sentence of its own and does not count, and a
  text of nothing else is not `completed`.  IOS XR's older tag
  statement, `dot1q vlan <id> [<inner>]`, is read as a tag (it was
  none).  A sub-interface of a serial line is read as before; an
  IOS-XE or NX-OS sub-interface with no tag as well (Known
  limitations).
  Guarded by `tests/unit/migration/test_a_sub_interface_with_no_tag.py`.
- **A RouterOS VLAN interface that states no `vlan-id=` is VLAN 1.**
  "vlan-id (integer: 1..4094; Default: 1)" (MikroTik, "VLAN"), and an
  export prints no default ("By default, the export command writes
  only user-edited configuration, RouterOS defaults are omitted",
  MikroTik, "Configuration Management"), so `/interface vlan add
  interface=ether2 name=mgmt` is VLAN 1 on `ether2`.  The parser
  passed such a line over: the VLAN interface was in no output, its
  addresses were written on its name, which the output defined
  nowhere, and a RouterOS config translated to RouterOS said
  `completed`.  It is now read as VLAN 1, as the verbose form
  (`vlan-id=1`) is; a `vlan-id=` with no number after it is no VLAN
  id, left out with a row as `vlan-id=0` is.  No committed capture
  holds such a line.  Guarded by
  `tests/unit/migration/codecs/mikrotik_routeros/test_a_vlan_id_left_out_is_1.py`.
- **A Junos unit the tree has no form for is left out, and said.**  A
  unit is not always a routed sub-interface.  Under `encapsulation
  flexible-ethernet-services` a port takes units of several kinds
  ("allows the ethernet-switching family to be configured on any
  logical interface unit number instead of only unit 0", Juniper,
  Flexible Ethernet Services); a `vlan-bridge` unit is a bridge
  domain's, a `vlan-ccc` unit a cross-connect's ("you can configure
  the `ccc` family only", Juniper, `encapsulation (Logical
  Interface)`), a `vlan-vpls` unit a VPLS circuit's, a `family
  bridge` unit 0 a bridge domain's port.  The parser read each as a
  routed sub-interface with its tag (`TenGigabitEthernet0/0/1.100`,
  `encapsulation dot1Q 100`, on IOS-XE), or as an empty one, and the
  VLANs of an L2 sub-unit had no member, in jobs that said
  `completed` with nothing to report; and a port's own
  `encapsulation` was not read at all, so a Junos config translated
  to Junos lost it unsaid.  A unit that states a family other than
  `inet`, `inet6`, `iso` and `mpls` (`ethernet-switching` above unit 0
  among them; a family word nobody knows as well), or an
  `encapsulation` and no inet family, is now left out with a row of
  the Tier-3 banner; unit 0 of such a kind leaves its port with what
  the port's own lines state, and a routing instance that names such
  a unit binds nothing.  A routed unit that states an `encapsulation`
  (`ethernet` on a logical tunnel, whose units then "behave as
  Ethernet interfaces", Juniper, Configuring Logical Tunnel
  Interfaces) is kept, and its encapsulation is said in another row
  with every port's.  No
  committed capture holds such a unit or such a statement.  A
  `native-vlan-id` whose unit is left out is said, as one that names
  no unit was (its row now reads "no unit of that one vlan-id is in
  the output").  Guarded by
  `tests/unit/migration/codecs/juniper_junos/test_a_unit_the_tree_does_not_hold.py`.
- **A sub-interface Junos cannot number goes by its tag.**  Juniper's
  `unit` statement gives "Range: 0 through 16,384".  A sub-interface
  of another vendor went to Junos after its port with its own number:
  IOS-XE `GigabitEthernet0/0/1.20000` with `encapsulation dot1Q 200`
  was `set interfaces ge-0/0/1 unit 20000 vlan-id 200`, a unit Junos
  does not number, in a job that said `completed` with nothing to
  report.  A unit numbered above the target's bound
  (`CodecBase.largest_unit`, stated for Junos alone) now goes where
  its port goes named by its 802.1Q tag -- `unit 200 vlan-id 200` --
  as a tagged unit 0 does; one with no tag is not sent after its port,
  and the job is `partial` and lists it (`untranslated_ports`, or with
  devices declared `unresolved_ports`).  A unit of two tags is named
  by its INNER tag, as a sub-interface whose config states its port
  already was: the outer tag can be every unit's of a port, as on the
  IOS-XE carrier capture, which numbers six such units
  outer-then-inner (`GigabitEthernet2/0/4.223415`, `encapsulation
  dot1Q 2234 second-dot1q 15`) -- they had been `unit 223415` and the
  like, and are `unit 15` to `unit 1020` now.  A Junos tagged unit 0
  of two tags goes onto another vendor by its inner tag the same way
  (`ge-0/0/1.0` of `outer 100 inner 10` is `Ethernet1.10`); VyOS,
  whose `vif` is its tag, keeps the outer.  A tag that is another
  unit's number of the same port is one name, listed in
  `fused_ports`.  Between two configs of one codec a unit keeps its
  number, and an entry in `port_rename_map` decides as before.  The
  translator and the model path's reading of the run ask one question
  (`port_names.goes_by_its_tag`, `port_names.unit_tags`).
  Guarded by `tests/unit/migration/test_a_unit_the_target_cannot_number.py`.
- **A Junos unit 0 that carries a tag is a sub-interface.**  Under
  `vlan-tagging` a unit 0 can be given a `vlan-id` like any other
  unit (Juniper's router examples tag unit 0; the EX and QFX
  references say a tag "cannot be configured on logical interface
  unit 0").  The parser read unit 0's lines onto the device, as it
  does where unit 0 carries no tag and is the interface itself: the
  unit's tag and addresses were the port's own on every target --
  `encapsulation dot1Q 54` and the unit's address on the main
  interface -- its description took the device's place, and a
  routing instance that named `ge-0/0/1.0` bound the port, in jobs
  that said `completed`.  The unit is now a record of its own,
  `ge-0/0/1.0`, beside the device, which keeps what its own lines
  state (description, media MTU, `disable`) -- on a device where
  Juniper puts `vlan-tagging` (a port, a channel of one, an `ae` or
  `reth`).  A tagged unit 0 of any other name is read onto its
  device, as before: that is how another vendor's VLAN interface (a
  FortiGate `VL_100`) is written to Junos, and is read back.  Across
  vendors it goes
  after its port named by its TAG (`Ethernet1.54`), as `.0` is the
  port itself on every other platform; between two Junos configs it
  stays unit 0, and an `ae` or `reth` unit 0 is written under its
  device (`set interfaces ae2 unit 0 vlan-id 54`), where it had been
  a name Junos refuses.  A routing instance and a route that name
  `ge-0/0/1.0` name the unit and follow it.  A unit 0 tagged 54
  beside a unit 54 of the same port is one name on another vendor,
  and the job is `partial` and lists both.  With devices declared,
  such a unit is read as having followed its port by its tag, and
  so is any unit onto a target that names a sub-interface by its tag
  (VyOS), where it had been a name nobody decided.  A tagged unit 0
  with `family ethernet-switching` has no form in the tree: it is
  left out, its device kept, and a row of the Tier-3 banner says so
  -- between two Junos configs too, where it had been written back
  with an `interface-mode access` the source did not state.  A
  hand-written sub-interface numbered 0 from another platform
  (`interface Gi0/0/1.0` with `encapsulation dot1Q 5`) goes by its
  tag the same way; one with no tag is left to the classifier, as
  before.
- **A sub-interface's tag is a VLAN id.**  A frame of VID 0 carries
  a priority and no VLAN, and VID 4095 is reserved (IEEE 802.1Q):
  the tree's tag is a VLAN id, 1 to 4094.  The IOS-XE, IOS XR, EOS
  and Junos parsers left a sub-interface with any other tag out,
  with a row; four parsers did not.  VyOS read `vif 0` as a
  sub-interface of tag 0, and NX-OS `encapsulation dot1q 0` the
  same, and each was written so onto every target that writes a
  tag -- from NX-OS in jobs that said `completed`.  RouterOS
  refused the whole config for one `vlan-id=0`.  FortiOS made no
  VLAN of a `set vlanid 0` and kept its interface, its address on
  an interface of no tag.  Each now leaves such a sub-interface out, with its
  addresses (a route or a DHCP server that names it keeps the
  name), and a row of the Tier-3 banner names it; a RouterOS or
  FortiOS VLAN interface on it goes with it.  The NX-OS parser
  reads `encapsulation dot1q` whole: a line that is not one VLAN
  id is left out the same way, where its first number was the tag.
- **A RouterOS VLAN on a VLAN is two tags, and a FortiOS one is said.**
  "In RouterOS, Q-in-Q can be configured by adding one VLAN interface
  over another" (MikroTik, "VLAN"): `add interface=ether1 name=vlan1
  vlan-id=11` and `add interface=vlan1 name=vlan2 vlan-id=12` send
  both tags on `ether1`.  The parser read the second as a VLAN
  interface of one tag on the first, and so did the FortiOS parser a
  VLAN interface whose `set interface` is a VLAN interface: an SVI of
  the inner tag and a VLAN no port carried on every target that has
  the two, in jobs that said `completed` (with a port map; without
  one the operator's name held the job).  A RouterOS VLAN interface
  on a sub-interface of a port or a bond is now a sub-interface of
  that port with two 802.1Q tags, the first's outside, and reaches
  IOS-XE, IOS XR, EOS and Junos with both; across vendors it is named
  by its INNER tag (`ether1` -> `GigabitEthernet0/1.12`), its outer
  sub-interface by its own.  RouterOS writes a source's sub-interface
  of two tags back the same way, on the VLAN interface of its port
  with its outer tag -- made where the tree has none, `<port>.<outer>`
  (another name where the output has that one), under a comment that
  says so -- and reads it back (`/interfaces/interface/dot1q-inner-vlan`
  is supported).  What the tree has no form for is left out, with
  its addresses (a route or a DHCP pool that names it keeps the
  name), and a row of the Tier-3 banner names a few and counts the
  rest: a RouterOS VLAN interface that says
  `use-service-tag=yes` ("IEEE 802.1ad compatible Service Tag") on a
  port, a bond or a VLAN interface; one on a VLAN interface that is
  not one 802.1Q tag on a port or a bond (a bridge's VLAN interface,
  a third tag); a FortiOS VLAN interface that says `set vlan-protocol
  8021ad`; and a FortiOS VLAN interface on a VLAN interface.  Fortinet
  documents Q-in-Q with an 802.1ad outer tag ("QinQ", FortiOS
  Administration Guide), and whether FortiOS sends two 802.1Q tags
  for one on an `8021q` VLAN interface is not established.
- **A Junos trunk's native VLAN in the grammar before ELS is read.**
  EX switches before ELS state a trunk's native VLAN under the unit,
  `unit 0 family ethernet-switching native-vlan-id <id>` ("Configure
  the VLAN identifier to associate with untagged packets received on
  the interface"), beside its `vlan members`: not a member, the VLAN
  is carried untagged both ways; a member as well, it is received
  untagged and sent tagged (Juniper KB17419, for non-ELS EX
  switches).  The parser read `port-mode trunk` and nothing of the
  statement, so the trunk's untagged VLAN was lost onto every target,
  Junos included, in jobs that said nothing.  A native VLAN off the
  members is now the trunk's native VLAN, put into its list (the
  list is what a trunk carries), and written in each target's form
  -- onto Junos in the ELS grammar, as before.  What the tree has no
  form for is said in a row of the Tier-3 banner, one row for each
  reason, naming a few: a native VLAN that is a member as well (the
  VLAN stays on the list, tagged), one on a port that is not a trunk,
  one beside a `native-vlan-id` on the interface itself, and one
  that is not a VLAN id.  No real capture has the statement (the one
  in that grammar states no native VLAN); the synthetic Junos kitchen
  sink's trunk has one, and now declares the VLAN it names
  (`default`, VLAN 1), as a switch does.  Guarded by
  shapes `p1` and `p2` of
  `tests/unit/migration/test_the_list_holds_the_native_vlan.py`, whose
  reader of Junos text now reads the statement beside the members,
  onto every target both ways, and by
  `tests/unit/migration/codecs/juniper_junos/test_the_older_grammar_native_vlan.py`
  for the rows.

- **A routed port's untagged frames go to the sub-interface that
  says so.**  Junos `native-vlan-id <tag>` on a device whose units
  carry tags names the unit of that `vlan-id` as the one that takes
  the frames that arrive with no tag ("The logical interface on which
  untagged packets are to be received must be configured with the
  same native VLAN ID"), and IOS-XE says the same on the
  sub-interface, `encapsulation dot1Q <tag> native` ("the default
  handler of untagged packets coming to the port").  The tree held
  the Junos statement as the device's `trunk_native_vlan`, a
  switchport's field, and IOS-XE took its own out of the text with a
  row.  So a Junos router's native sub-interface was written onto
  IOS-XE as `switchport trunk native vlan` on a routed port, and was
  left out by EOS and NX-OS, in jobs that said `completed`.  The tree
  now states it on the sub-interface (`dot1q_native`); both parsers
  read it and both renderers write it, each in its own form (Junos
  with `flexible-vlan-tagging`).  Every other target reports
  `/interfaces/interface/dot1q-native` unsupported and the job is
  `partial`.  A Junos `native-vlan-id` that names no unit of one tag,
  and a second IOS-XE native sub-interface on one port, are said in a
  row.  A VLAN map that renumbers the tag keeps the sub-interface
  native; one that drops the tag drops the native with it.  Known
  limitation: what such a sub-interface SENDS without a tag is not
  established on either platform (the vendor reference says so).
  Guarded by `tests/unit/migration/test_a_native_sub_interface.py`,
  which reads each output as text, by a reader per grammar written in
  the test, and finds the sub-interface by its address.

- **Onto FortiOS, a VLAN rides on the port that carries it.**  The
  renderer chose one parent for every VLAN interface of an output --
  the first LAG for a VLAN, and for an interface of a VLAN (an SVI)
  a port scored for a private address -- and never asked which port
  the source carries the VLAN on.  The NX-OS kitchen sink's VLANs 10
  and 20 came out on a routed port that carries no VLAN, and VLAN 30
  on a port-channel that does not carry it, in jobs that said
  nothing; over the committed captures, nearly a third of the
  VLAN interfaces whose VLAN some port carries were on a port that
  does not.  FortiOS now takes the parent from the rule OPNsense
  already had, shared between them (`vlan_carriers` in
  `codecs/_helpers.py`): a LAG one of whose ports carries the VLAN,
  then a port that names it, then a trunk of every VLAN.  A VLAN
  nothing carries is on the port chosen as before.  A VLAN whose
  carriers the target has no name for (an OS10 breakout lane onto
  FortiOS) is on that port too, in a job that is already `partial`
  for the names it dropped.  Guarded by
  `tests/unit/migration/codecs/fortigate_cli/test_a_vlan_rides_a_port.py`,
  which reads the carriers from the source's own tree.

- **A RouterOS bridge or an IOS-XE `VirtualPortGroup` is no other
  vendor's loopback.**  The port translator reads both as a
  `virtual` interface, a kind only its own vendor has, and AOS-CX,
  NX-OS and OS10 wrote one of another vendor as a loopback ("the
  closest analogue"), IOS-XE a RouterOS bridge as
  `VirtualPortGroup0`.  The bridge of a RouterOS router's own
  default configuration holds the LAN's gateway
  (`192.168.88.1/24`): onto those four it was on an interface with
  no port, so the LAN's hosts reached nothing, in jobs that said
  `completed`.  Each such name now says whose it is, and only its
  own platform writes it (the IOS-XE CLI and NETCONF codecs keep a
  `VirtualPortGroup` between them); onto every other platform it is
  dropped with what was on it and listed in `unresolved_ports`, and
  the job is `partial`, as the other eight targets already did.
  Give it an entry of `port_rename_map` -- the target's name for
  the LAN's interface -- to keep its address.  Guarded by
  `tests/unit/migration/test_a_virtual_interface_is_its_vendors_own.py`.

- **A RouterOS string is read by MikroTik's table of escapes.**  The
  parser read a backslash and the character after it as that
  character, whatever it was, so a description an export writes
  `Caf\C3\A9` reached every target as `CafC3A9`, `\_` (a space) as
  `_` and `\n` as `n`, in jobs that said nothing.  It now reads each
  escape on MikroTik's "Scripting" page: `\_` is a space, `\t` a tab,
  `\n`, `\r`, `\v` and `\f` line breaks -- which the pipeline writes
  as a space and says, as it does any value's -- and a run of hex
  escapes (capitals, as the page says) the text its bytes are in
  UTF-8.  RouterOS keeps a string as bytes and the export does not
  say their encoding, so a run that is not UTF-8 (a comment typed in
  Windows-1251) is kept as the export wrote it, escapes and all,
  rather than read in a guessed one.  `\a`, `\b` and a control
  character's byte (`\1B`) are read as the character, which the
  pipeline writes as a space and says (Security, above).  Guarded by
  `tests/unit/migration/codecs/mikrotik_routeros/test_an_escape_is_read.py`,
  which holds each row of the page's table, typed by hand, its own
  example, and runs of bytes of each kind to the parser, and an
  export through the pipeline onto every public codec.

- **A RouterOS VLAN interface on a port was not a sub-interface onto
  another vendor.**  `/interface vlan add interface=ether3
  name=gn-mgmt vlan-id=11` was read as a VLAN interface and a VLAN of
  its tag, and the port it rides on was not kept in the tree: onto
  IOS-XE, NX-OS, EOS or Junos it came out as VLAN 11 and its VLAN
  interface (`interface Vlan11`, `irb.11`), which no port carries,
  and a name such as `gn-mgmt`, which no classifier reads, was
  written into the other vendor's config as it stood, holding the
  job `partial`.  That was also how RouterOS's own output for
  another vendor's sub-interface was read back.  RouterOS writes a
  VLAN interface on a port and on a bridge with the same line, so
  the parser now tells them apart by the parent: on a port -- one a
  line of `/interface ethernet` names, renamed or not, or else one
  whose name says it is a port -- or on a LAG, it is a sub-interface
  of it, typed as its parent, with its tag and no VLAN; on a bridge,
  or on anything else (`wlan1`), it is a VLAN interface and a VLAN,
  as before.  Across vendors a sub-interface goes where its port
  goes, named by its tag whatever its own name looks like (`gn-mgmt`
  on `ether3` onto EOS is `interface Ethernet3.11` with
  `encapsulation dot1q vlan 11`); between two RouterOS configs it
  keeps its name; and it is dropped with a port that is dropped, in
  one warning.  With devices declared it is read as following its
  port, where it was a name nobody decided.  Onto AOS-S, AOS-CX,
  OS10 and IOS-XE NETCONF, which have no form for a sub-interface's
  tag, such a job is now `partial`, the validation report listing
  the tag, where it said `completed` over a VLAN interface.
  `/interfaces/interface/dot1q-vlan` is supported on RouterOS, where
  it was lossy, and `/vlans/vlan/id` is lossy, where it was
  supported: a VLAN another platform carries on a port or a LAG is
  written as an `/interface vlan` on it and read back as a
  sub-interface of the port, with no VLAN record.  A sub-interface
  of a port the operator renamed
  (`ether4` named `wan`) goes after the name, which no classifier
  reads, and the job lists both.  Guarded by
  `tests/unit/migration/codecs/mikrotik_routeros/test_a_vlan_on_a_port_is_a_sub_interface.py`
  (each kind of parent, read as typed by hand, and the outputs read
  as text), `tests/unit/migration/test_a_sub_interface_onto_routeros.py`
  (another vendor's sub-interface read back as one), and RouterOS as
  a source onto every codec in
  `tests/unit/migration/test_units_follow_their_port.py`.
- **A FortiOS VLAN interface on a port or an aggregate was not a
  sub-interface onto another vendor.**  `edit "VL_100"` / `set
  vlanid 100` / `set interface "LAG_INTERNAL"` was read as a VLAN
  interface and a VLAN of its tag: onto IOS-XE, NX-OS, EOS or Junos
  it came out as VLAN 100 and its VLAN interface (`interface
  Vlan100`, `irb.100`), which nothing on the aggregate carries, and
  a name such as `gn-mgmt`, which no classifier reads, was written
  into the other vendor's config as it stood, holding the job
  `partial`.  Both committed FortiGate captures that have VLAN
  interfaces have them on an aggregate.  FortiOS writes a VLAN
  interface on a port and on a switch interface with the same
  lines, so the parser now tells them apart by the parent: on a
  port -- one whose own edit says `set type physical`, or, where it
  states no type or has no edit, one whose name says it is a port
  -- or on an aggregate that is not a FortiLink one, it is a
  sub-interface of it, typed as its parent, with its tag and no
  VLAN, its alias the sub-interface's description; on a FortiLink
  aggregate, a hardware or software switch (`internal`, `lan`),
  the interface named `fortilink`, or anything else, it is a VLAN
  interface and a VLAN, as before (one on another VLAN interface is
  left out: "A RouterOS VLAN on a VLAN is two tags", above).
  Across vendors a sub-interface goes where its parent goes, named
  by its tag; between two FortiOS configs it keeps its name.  An
  aggregate's name is the operator's own, which no classifier
  reads, so the job lists it and the sub-interfaces on it until an
  entry names it, and they go with that entry
  (`{"LAG_INTERNAL": "Port-Channel1"}` onto EOS is `interface
  Port-Channel1.100`).  Onto AOS-S, AOS-CX, OS10 and IOS-XE NETCONF
  such a job is `partial` for the tag, as for RouterOS above.
  `/interfaces/interface/dot1q-vlan` is supported on FortiOS, where
  it was lossy: another vendor's sub-interface written onto FortiOS
  is read back as one where its port has a name a FortiGate gives a
  port.  The output writes no `set type` for a port, so on a port
  named otherwise (another vendor's name, which the bare pipeline
  leaves as it is, or `port-0-1-2` for NX-OS `Ethernet1/2`) it is
  read back as a VLAN interface and a VLAN.  The same holds for a
  VLAN another platform carries on a port or a LAG, written as a
  VLAN interface on it: on a port with a FortiGate's name it is
  read back as a sub-interface of the port, with no VLAN record,
  and `/vlans/vlan/id` is lossy, where it was supported.  Guarded by
  `tests/unit/migration/codecs/fortigate_cli/test_a_vlan_on_a_port_is_a_sub_interface.py`
  (each kind of parent, read as typed by hand, and the outputs read
  as text) and `tests/unit/migration/test_a_sub_interface_onto_fortios.py`
  (which outputs are read back as a sub-interface, typed by hand).
- **An OPNsense VLAN device on a port or a LAGG was not a
  sub-interface onto another vendor.**  `<vlan><if>ixl0</if>
  <tag>10</tag><vlanif>vlan0.10</vlanif>` was read as a VLAN
  interface and a VLAN of its tag: onto IOS-XE, NX-OS, EOS or Junos
  it came out as VLAN 10 and its VLAN interface (`interface Vlan10`,
  `irb.10`), which nothing on the port carries.  The committed
  OPNsense capture has five such devices, all on one port.  The
  parser now reads the parent: on a bridge (one `<bridges>` names,
  or one named `bridge` and digits), another VLAN device, a zone's
  key (`lan`, `opt3`: never a device's name, and what the renderer
  writes for a VLAN in a config with no port), or a name that says
  it is a VLAN interface, a loopback or a tunnel, it is a VLAN
  interface and a VLAN, as before; on any other parent -- a
  port, or a LAGG where `<laggs>` names it -- it is a sub-interface
  of it, typed as its parent, with its tag and no VLAN.  Zones are
  not typed and the classifier does not read every driver's name
  (`igc0`), so such a parent is a port whatever its name.  The
  sub-interface's description is its zone's, or the device's
  `<descr>` where the zone has none; a `<descr>` beside a zone's own
  is said in a row, as on every device of the capture.  Across
  vendors it goes where its parent goes, named by its tag; between
  two OPNsense configs it keeps its name.  A parent no classifier
  reads is listed until an entry names it.  Onto AOS-S, AOS-CX,
  OS10 and IOS-XE NETCONF such a job is `partial` for the tag, as
  for RouterOS above.  `/interfaces/interface/dot1q-vlan` is
  supported on OPNsense, where it was lossy: another vendor's
  sub-interface written onto OPNsense is read back as one, and so is
  a VLAN another platform carries on a port or a LAG, written as a
  VLAN device on it, with no VLAN record: `/vlans/vlan/id` and
  `/vlans/vlan/description` are lossy, where they were supported.
  A device
  no zone assigns is written with its `<descr>` and still no zone, so
  another vendor's sub-interface that holds a description and
  nothing else is the device alone with that `<descr>`, where it was
  a zone that assigned and enabled the device.  Over the committed
  captures the OPNsense capture's five devices are tagged units of
  their port onto IOS-XR and VyOS, where each was a name the target
  had none for, and one more job onto VyOS passes the validation
  report, which the port-name check holds `partial` for `igc0`, so
  that check now makes 220 of 590 jobs `partial`.  Guarded by
  `tests/unit/migration/codecs/opnsense/test_a_vlan_on_a_port_is_a_sub_interface.py`
  (each kind of parent, the capture, and the outputs read as text)
  and `tests/unit/migration/test_a_sub_interface_onto_opnsense.py`
  (another vendor's sub-interface read back as one).
- **A job no longer offers "declare both devices" where no device
  can be declared.**  The sentence of a job whose port names are not
  settled offered the pairing wherever a hardware port was among
  the names, also where no model family and no target profile is of
  the source's vendor or the target's (NX-OS, IOS-XR, OS10 and VyOS
  as shipped): advice nobody could take, which the rename modal did
  not give.  The API now asks the same registries the modal asks
  (`a_device_is_described`), and where either side has none the
  sentence ends with the entries that settle the names.  Nothing
  else about such a job changes: its status and its three lists are
  as they were.  Guarded by
  `TestPortNamesWithNoDevices` in
  `tests/integration/test_migration_models_api.py` (an IOS-XR
  capture onto AOS-S, on every plan endpoint, and which vendors have
  a device, typed by hand) and `TestWhatTheJobSays` in
  `tests/unit/migration/test_run_plan_checked_names.py`.
- **Junos: a set line's bracket list is read, a statement a value.**
  The CLI takes `set ... vlan members [ DATA VOICE ]` (and `display
  set` prints it one value a line); the block form's list was
  written out so, and a set line's was read as it stood, with `[`
  for its value.  A port given its VLANs that way was in none -- a
  trunk carrying nothing, on every target -- a name server was `[`,
  and so on for every leaf that takes a list, in jobs that said
  nothing.  Several of the repository's own Junos reference pages
  write the form.  The values are counted in words before the
  statements are made, each being the line's path again, as the
  block form's are; a refusal names "words of set commands written
  out from a bracket list".  No committed capture writes a set line
  with a list.  Guarded by
  `tests/unit/migration/codecs/juniper_junos/test_a_set_line_bracket_list.py`,
  which holds each list to the same config written one value a line,
  tree for tree.
- **Junos: a port that states no mode is an access port.**  A port
  whose `family ethernet-switching` has `vlan members` and no
  `interface-mode` (or `port-mode`) line was read as a trunk, on the
  word of a comment that the commit validator treats it so; Juniper
  documents the opposite -- with no port mode configured, "all
  interfaces on the switch are in access mode".  An access port of
  VLAN 10 came out as a trunk of VLAN 10 on every target, in a job
  that said `completed`.  It is now an access port of its first VLAN.
  An access port whose `vlan members` name more than one VLAN (or
  `all`) -- stated or not, which was left to its first VLAN in
  silence before -- is said in one row of `dropped_tier3_sections`
  for all such ports, which names a few and counts the rest.  No
  committed capture has such a port.  Guarded by
  `tests/unit/migration/codecs/juniper_junos/test_a_port_with_no_mode_is_access.py`.
- **Junos: a VLAN's description is read and written.**  The parser
  read nothing of `set vlans <name> description <text>` and the
  renderer wrote no such line, so a Junos VLAN's description was gone
  on every target, in jobs that did not say so, and one from another
  platform -- an AOS-CX `description` beside a `name` of the VLAN's
  own -- was gone on Junos, which has a line for it.  The parser keeps
  a description by the VLAN's name until the whole config is read (a
  set-form config may state it ahead of `vlan-id`), and the renderer
  writes it beside the name.  A description that is written as the
  VLAN's name, because the name was only an interface's (an OPNsense
  `<descr>`, a RouterOS `comment=`), is not written a second time.
  Junos now declares `/vlans/vlan/description` supported; onto a
  target with no VLAN description (EOS, IOS-XE, NX-OS, AOS-S, OS10) the
  job lists it as lossy.  Every AOS-CX capture with a VLAN description
  now keeps it on Junos.  Several reference notes said EOS and AOS-S
  wrote a Junos VLAN description as a comment; neither does, and the
  notes say so.

- **A value is written on one line, on every target, and the job says
  where** (Security, above).  The pipeline writes each run of line
  breaks in a value -- any character `str.splitlines` ends a line at,
  not only a line feed -- as one space, after the transforms (an
  operator's map puts values into the tree too), and says each place
  in the job's warnings: `interfaces[em0].description held a line
  break: it is written on one line, ...`.  The sanitiser does the same
  before it renders.  And `CodecBase.render` refuses a tree that still
