  the text has no indentation, that the parser tells a stanza's lines
  by their indentation and so cannot tell where a stanza of it ends,
  the number of the first line that opens a stanza with the line
  after it at the margin, and asks for `show running-config` as the
  switch prints it.  It quotes nothing of the text, and says nothing
  of what the switch would do.  Detection still proposes EOS for each
  capture in that form.  A text in which only some lines lost their
  indentation is read by its indentation.  Indentation is a space or
  a tab: a text indented with no-break spaces (a paste out of a web
  page), which the stanza readers took for lines at the margin and
  read as far less, is refused the same way.  The check is the one
  IOS XR's refusal uses, now shared (`first_flat_stanza` in
  `netcanon/migration/codecs/_scanner.py`), with each parser's own
  headers and sentence; under it a comment line, indented or not, is
  passed over and is never indentation, `exit` (like `!` and `end`) is
  no line of a stanza's body, and indentation is a space or a tab.
  IOS XR now reads a text so too: one whose only indented lines were
  comments was read, and is now refused; one indented with no-break
  spaces was read, its `ntp` servers lost (that reader takes only a
  space or a tab: of the committed IOS XR configs so indented, the
  one with an `ntp` block read otherwise than as committed, the rest
  alike), and is now refused; a flat one whose stanzas
  have no body, each closed by `exit`, was refused, and is now read.
  No committed capture of any codec, as committed, dedented or
  without its `!` lines, moves under IOS XR.  Make a translation made
  from such a text with 0.7.7 or earlier again from `show
  running-config`.

- **EOS `router bgp` was read by EOS's own widths, and an empty line
  ended a stanza.**  The `router bgp` reader counted spaces only, and
  took a `vlan <id>` block at exactly three of them and a block's
  lines at six or more: re-indented with tabs, or with two spaces a
  level, 4 of the 6 committed EOS configs (the 5 captures and the
  synthetic one) lost MAC-VRFs, route distinguishers or route targets
  (with four spaces, 3 of them).  A `!` of any depth closed the `vrf`
  or `vlan` block it was in, so a VRF's own line after one of its
  address-families was lost; a comment in column 0 ended the section;
  and a `vrf` line at any depth opened a routing instance.  An empty
  line ended the open interface, VLAN or `router bgp`: with its line
  ends doubled, every committed EOS config parsed otherwise, its
  addresses and descriptions lost.  `router bgp` is now read by
  relative depth: the section's own lines are at the shallowest
  indentation of any of its lines, a `vrf <name>`, `vlan <id>`,
  `vlan-aware-bundle` or `address-family` block opens only there and
  holds every line deeper than it, and a `!` closes no block.  An
  empty line closes nothing, in `router bgp` or in an interface or
  VLAN stanza, which reads every indented line as its own as before.
  Each committed EOS config re-indented with tabs, two or four spaces
  a level, and with its line ends doubled (`\n\n` and `\r\r\n`), now
  parses to the tree it gives as committed, whole; no committed
  capture of any codec, as committed, moves.  One hand-edited shape
  reads as less than before: a block header indented deeper than
  another line of the section's own opens no block (Known
  limitations).  If you translated an EOS config indented with tabs
  or another width, or with empty lines in it, with 0.7.7 or earlier,
  translate it again: the old output may lack its MAC-VRFs, route
  distinguishers and route targets, or its addresses and
  descriptions.

- **An IOS XR interface ended at the `!` that closes a submode inside
  it.**  The interface parser ended an `interface` stanza at a `!` of
  any depth, and an interface that holds a submode (`ptp`, `lldp`)
  closes the submode with a `!` one level in: every line of the
  interface after the submode was read by nothing.  On the committed
  `iosxr_design_cst_pa3_xr752.cfg`, `TenGigE0/0/0/20` and
  `TenGigE0/0/0/21` each lost one IPv4 and one IPv6 address, onto
  every target, in jobs that said nothing of it.  A stanza now ends at
  a line in column 0 (its own `!` is one); a submode's `!` does not
  end it, and a line indented deeper than the stanza's own first body
  line is the submode's, not the interface's -- for the interface's
  record, for the member list of the LAG a `bundle id` line names, and
  for a `username` block alike.  The rule is the shared stanza
  scanner's default, which only the IOS XR interface parser used;
  every other caller of the scanner passes a column-0 rule of its own,
  as it already did.  Every other committed capture of every codec
  parses as before, field for field.  If you translated an IOS XR
  config whose interfaces hold a submode before their own lines with
  0.7.7 or earlier, translate it again: its addresses, MTU, VRF and
  `shutdown` after the submode were not carried.

- **An IOS XR config without its indentation was read as other
  records, and the job said `completed`.**  IOS XR places each line of
  a configuration by its indentation when it loads a file (Cisco's CLI
  model and a Cisco engineer's router output; no manual says it in a
  sentence, and what the router does with such text typed at its
  prompt is not established): a line at
  the left margin is a line of the top level, and a file that lost its
  indentation loads with its lines in the wrong submode.  The parser
  read such a text by the same rule, and so made records of lines
  nested under routing protocols, MPLS and config groups: over the 11
  committed IOS XR captures and the synthetic config with every line's
  leading white space removed, 61 interfaces and 29 routing instances
  more than the texts hold, among them interfaces named `all` and
  `'Bundle-Ether.*'` and a LAG nothing declares, with no address, no
  description, no route, and local users with no secret and no
  group.  Of their jobs onto IOS XR, Junos and IOS-XE CLI, 25 of 36
  said `completed` and the rest `partial` for another reason, and none
  said a line was not read.  The `!` lines do not give the
  tree back: they say how many submodes close, not which line opened
  one.  Such a text -- no line indented, and the lines of a stanza the
  parser reads at the left margin -- is now refused before anything of
  it is read: the job is `failed`, and its error is `parse failed:`
  and a sentence that says the text has no indentation, why neither
  the router loading it nor the parser can tell where a stanza of it
  ends, the number of the first line that opens a stanza with the line
  after it at the left margin, and asks for `show running-config` as
  the router prints it.  The sentence quotes nothing of the text.
  Detection still proposes IOS XR for each committed capture in that
  form, so the migrate page offers no other vendor for it; a short
  text with no interface of an IOS XR name (a user and a VRF, say) is
  detected as IOS-XE CLI, printed or not, and the page offers IOS-XE
  beside the sentence.  A text in which only some lines lost their
  indentation is read by its indentation, as the router reads it.  A
  translation made from such a text with 0.7.7 or earlier holds
  interfaces and VRFs the router does not have, and none of its
  addresses: make it again from `show running-config`.

- **An IOS XR line that states an interface's setting on the
  `interface` line was a second record of the interface, its setting
  lost.**  `interface <name> description ...` (or `ipv4`, `ipv6`,
  `shutdown`, `mtu`, `vrf`, `bundle`, `encapsulation`, after the name
  and an `l2transport` if it has one) in column 0 is the form `show
  running-config formal` prints, one line a setting with its whole
  path (by the shape Cisco shows it printing for class and policy
  maps), or a one-line command typed into a printed config; `show
  running-config` prints none.  A whole formal config was read as a
  record of an interface for each of its lines (over 500 for the 155
  interfaces of the 11 committed IOS XR captures and the synthetic
  config, written in that form), with no address, no route and no
  secret.  Such a line is now refused the same way, with its line
  number and a request for `show running-config` without `formal`.
  The `interface preconfigure <name> ...` one-liner, whose row in
  `dropped_tier3_sections` carried the setting's value, is refused
  with it.  A translation made from a formal config with 0.7.7 or
  earlier lost every interface setting: make it again from `show
  running-config`.

- **An AOS-S stanza ended at the first line that was not indented.**
  The parser ended a `vlan`, `interface` or `vrrp vrid` stanza at its
  `exit` or at any line in column 0, read that line again at the top,
  and skipped every indented line after it.  HPE describes the CLI by
  commands -- a command enters a context, `exit` returns to the one
  before, `end` to the Manager level, a command that enters another
  context leaves the open one -- and no HPE switch guide says
  indentation plays a part.  So a config pasted with its indentation
  lost was read as nothing: `hpe_community_5406rzl2_kb1515.cfg`, a
  KB.15.15 capture committed with every line at column 0, its
  indentation lost between the switch and the repository, was three
  VLANs with no name, no port and no address, and no interface at
  all, in jobs that said `completed` onto most targets (AOS-S itself
  among them), and no job said a line was not read.  It is now its 48
  ports, the VLANs' names, 137 tagged and 1 untagged memberships and
  the two VLAN addresses.  In the template render
  `aruba_central_5memberstack_rendered.cfg` the `ip address` of each
  of its three VLANs stood at column 0 and ended the stanza: the three
  addresses are read now.  A stanza ends at its `exit` or an `end`
  (in any letter case: `EXIT` is the same command), at a line in
  column 0 that enters another context, or at a line in column 0 that
  the top of the config reads (`ip route ...`, `trunk ...`); any other
  line in column 0 is the stanza's.  One predicate decides it for the
  three stanza readers, the `oobm` stanza, the reader the renderer
  asks whether a VLAN stanza gives its ports back, and deployment
  detection's `stacking` / `vsf` body, and it is built from the
  top-level loop's own patterns (a test holds the two together).
  Every committed AOS-S input, its leading white space removed, now
  parses to the tree of the text as committed, and the other AOS-S
  inputs read as before, field for field.  Two consequences of
  reading the lists: a VLAN name with a line break in it no longer
  cuts its stanza short unless the rest of the name is a line of the
  top, and kb1515's jobs onto other vendors are now `partial` where
  most were `completed`, listing the letter-slot ports (`A1`-`B24`)
  and `Vlan2` / `Vlan3`, which the port translator cannot read and
  which the job used to carry none of.

  **`oobm` is a stanza.**  Its lines are the management port's and
  none is read: HPE configures the OOBM address and gateway "within
  the OOBM context".  Indented, its body was skipped already; written
  at column 0, its `ip default-gateway` was read as the switch's
  default route, and its `interface enable` made an interface called
  `enable`.  The words of the context (`ip address`, `ip
  default-gateway`, `enable`, `disable`, `interface enable|disable|
  speed-duplex`) do not end it, indented or not.  Its `exit` does (a
  stack member's `member N` block in it has its own first), an `end`
  does, and so does a line in column 0 that enters another context
  or that the top of the config reads and is no word of the context
  (`hostname ...`): an `oobm` with no `exit` keeps the management
  port's gateway and loses no line of the switch's after it.

  **A port's VLAN lines are read.**  `tagged vlan <list>`, `untagged
  vlan <id>`, `no tagged vlan <list>` and `no untagged vlan <id>` in an
  `interface` stanza, and `[no] interface <ports> tagged|untagged vlan
  <list>` on one line at the top, were passed unread: a port named so
  stayed untagged in VLAN 1, in a job that said nothing.  Each is now
  the VLAN's own line of the same meaning, where it stands in the
  text, the later line winning, and an `untagged vlan` line moves the
  port out of the VLAN it was untagged in.  What a later line takes
  out of a VLAN's list is what the list held when that line was read,
  so a port moved out of VLAN 1 and back into it is in VLAN 1 (taking
  it out of every entry would leave it in no VLAN).  A line that
  names a VLAN no `vlan` stanza above it declares makes no VLAN; it is
  left out and has a row in `dropped_tier3_sections`.  The order is
  the switch's own, and it has a consequence: a config that puts its
  `interface` stanzas above its `vlan` stanzas (the order `show
  running-config` prints the two kinds in) has every such line left
  out, each said in a row; move the `vlan` stanzas up.  The rows are
  bounded in number and in length: a row quotes the first characters
  of its line and the first few ids it names, and counts the rest.  A
  stanza for several ports (`interface 1,3`, which entered no stanza
  the parser read, and `interface 1-4`, which made an interface named
  `1-4`) gives its VLAN lines to each port it names, makes no record
  named after the list, and says in a row what else it sets: that is
  not translated.  `forbid` is not read in either context (GVRP is
  not modelled).  The renderer is unchanged: it writes every
  membership under `vlan N`, as the switch's full configuration
  prints it.  The product of a line's ports and its VLANs is counted
  before it is made, in a stanza as on one line and for the `no`
  lines too (each line of a stanza stamps every port of its header
  again), and the loop that applies a stanza's lines looks at the
  deadline.

  **A VLAN id `int` cannot read ended the job.**  The VLAN-list
  helper the AOS-S, NX-OS, AOS-CX and IOS-XE CLI parsers share took a
  superscript digit (`1²`) for a digit, and a run of more digits
  than Python converts for a number: the job was `failed`, "unexpected
  error in stage parsing".  Such a token is no VLAN id now, as any
  other word is not.

  **Detection reads a stack's stanza by the same rule.**  Pasted
  without its indentation, a `stacking` / `vsf` stanza gave no
  member.  It ends at its `exit`, an `end`, a line in column 0 that
  ends a stanza for the parser, or a `flexible-module` / `module`
  line of the top (the stanza's own begin `member N`), so that a
  `stacking` with no `exit` does not take the top's `flexible-module`
  line for one of its own.

  **The tick rule's reader knows more loops.**  Deployment
  detection's loops over a config's lines (`for line in
  text.split("\n")`) never looked at the deadline, and the source
  reader in `tests/unit/migration/test_limits.py` knew only
  `.splitlines()`.  It knows both now, and a slice of either, and the
  four loops it then found go through `ticked`.  It also knows a list
  a loop over lines fills -- appended to there, or handed beside the
  lines to a call there -- and the loops over such lists it then
  found (in the AOS-S, Junos and IOS-XE CLI parsers) go through
  `ticked` too.

  **What to check in a job made before this release.**  An AOS-S
  source whose stanza bodies were not indented -- pasted from a
  forum, a web page or a template -- was translated with its VLANs'
  ports, names and addresses missing: translate it again.  An `oobm`
  block written at column 0 gave the output the management port's
  gateway as the switch's default route, and an interface named
  `enable`: check the output's default route.  A config that states a
  port's VLANs from the port's side (`tagged vlan` / `untagged vlan`
  in an `interface` stanza, or `interface <ports> tagged vlan ...`)
  lost those memberships: translate it again.  What remains is in
  Known limitations: the other block parsers on flat text, the AOS-S
  probe on flat text with no banner, an indented header, a line of
  the top inside a flat stanza, and a port tagged and untagged in one
  VLAN.

  **The render script dedented stanza bodies.**
  `scripts/render_aruba_central_template.py` moved to column 0 every
  line that began `ip` or `no`, a stanza's body lines included, on
  the strength of a comment that Aruba Central strips indentation
  (Central's help asks the reverse: "Ensure that the command text
  indentation matches the indentation in the running
  configuration.").  It now dedents a top-level keyword line only
  outside a stanza body.  The committed render is kept byte for
  byte, as an input whose bodies are partly flat; run on the current
  upstream template, the script now writes the same file with those
  five lines indented, which parses to the same tree.

- **A trunk that carries no VLAN untagged was left, on OS10 and AOS-S,
  to the switch's default VLAN.**  Both give a port that the output
  gives no untagged VLAN one all the same.  Dell: "By default, native
  VLAN of a port is the default VLAN ID of the switch."  HPE: "Any
  ports not specifically removed from the default VLAN remain in the
  DEFAULT_VLAN, regardless of other port assignments."  OS10 was
  written such a trunk with no access line, and AOS-S such a port on
  `tagged` lines alone, with no line that takes it out of VLAN 1 --
  in jobs that said nothing.  Such a port is a Junos trunk with no
  `native-vlan-id`, a Cisco or Arista trunk whose list leaves VLAN 1
  out, an AOS-S port only `tagged`, an OS10 trunk with no access line,
  an AOS-CX trunk of `vlan trunk native <N> tag`, and a trunk whose
  native VLAN the VLAN pane's map cleared.  Over the committed
  captures that was 58 source trunks onto OS10 (9 of them with VLAN 1
  on their allowed line) and 43 ports or trunk groups of outputs onto
  AOS-S, beside the 8 AOS-CX trunk groups whose native VLAN is off
  their list, which had a review line and stayed in VLAN 1 as well.

  **OS10:** a trunk with no native VLAN in the tree -- whatever its
  list, the empty one included -- is written `no switchport access
  vlan` after `switchport mode trunk`, under a review line, unless
  another record of the interface states its untagged VLAN (a native
  VLAN, or an access VLAN): OS10 applies an interface's stanzas in
  turn, and the line would take that VLAN back.  The review line:

  ```
  ! review: no untagged VLAN is stated for this trunk; an OS10 trunk with neither an access line nor the next line is an untagged member of the switch's default VLAN, and Dell's pages disagree on whether the next line leaves it with no untagged VLAN or with VLAN 1 -- check what this port is to carry untagged
  ```

  Where the allowed line holds VLAN 1 it adds `; no Dell page shows
  VLAN 1 on an OS10 trunk's allowed line` before the dash.  Dell's
  VLAN-stacking configuration notes (10.5.5 to 10.6.1) describe "pure
  trunk ports without any access VLAN membership", which "drop any
  untagged or tagged (with other than configured TPID) traffic on
  those ports", and reach them with this line; the command's own page
  says its `no` form "resets access VLAN membership on a L2 access or
  trunk port to VLAN 1".  The default VLAN's id (`default vlan-id`)
  is not read and nothing is filled in for it: no Dell example and
  no capture prints that line as configuration.  The OS10 parser
  reads a trunk with the line and one with neither as one tree, so an
  OS10 config's own `no switchport access vlan` on a trunk now comes
  back onto OS10, and a trunk with neither line comes back with it
  (no committed OS10 capture has such a trunk).

  **AOS-S:** VLAN 1's stanza is written `no untagged <names>` for
  every name the output tags in some VLAN, lists untagged in none,
  and names on no line of VLAN 1 -- after the `name` line and before
  `untagged` and `tagged`, the order of HPE's examples from 15.14 on.  A
  trunk group is named `Trk<n>`, as the other lines name it.  A tree
  with no VLAN 1 record gets a `vlan 1` stanza for it, first and with
  no `name` line, and a trunk that carries VLAN 1 tagged -- a Junos
  trunk of `vlan members all` -- is written `tagged` there.  The
  parser reads a `no untagged` line above the lists as removing
  nothing, which on lists that share no name is the tree they came
  from.  Onto AOS-S itself, `hpe_community_2930f_wc1607_intervlan.cfg`
  gets back the removal of its 13 ports that are tagged only (`no
  untagged 35-47`); two configs no switch printed -- the template
  render `aruba_central_5memberstack_rendered.cfg` and the synthetic
  kitchen-sink -- are written a removal they do not state, for ports
  their text puts on no line of VLAN 1 (in every full config HPE's
  16.09-16.11 guides print, a port another VLAN names is on a line of
  `vlan 1`).  The
  review line for a native VLAN its list leaves out now says what
  the output does where `no untagged` takes the port out (`... so no
  untagged line is written for this port and it is taken out of the
  default VLAN -- check ...`); for a trunk group, or a port of one,
  that no line takes out, it now says what HPE's sentences say where
  it said "not established" (`... a new AOS-S trunk group is placed
  in the default VLAN (VID 1), a static one is configured for VLAN
  membership as a port is, and the VLANs of a port that is in one are
  the group's -- check ...`).  HPE: "Creating a new trunk
  automatically places the trunk in the DEFAULT_VLAN ...", and the
  groups written are static (`TrkX (Static)` in HPE's table).

  The two guards read both targets' defaults from the text: an OS10
  trunk with neither access line is an untagged member of its
  switch's default VLAN, and an AOS-S port tagged somewhere, untagged
  nowhere and on no line of VLAN 1 is in VLAN 1
  (`tests/unit/migration/test_the_list_holds_the_native_vlan.py`,
  `tests/unit/migration/test_vlan_members_reach_the_output.py`).  No
  committed capture is left to either default now, and every check
  of the fix is handed the old output and fails.  The expectations of
  `juniper_junos__aruba_aoss` (`vlans[].id`) and
  `cisco_iosxe_cli__aruba_aoss` (`vlans`) are `lossy`: a source with
  such a port and no VLAN 1 comes back with a VLAN 1 record it did
  not have.  On one Junos capture that added record hides, under the
  count drift, an existing defect: an address on a VLAN the Junos
  tree gives none (the `juniper_junos__aruba_aoss` expectation says
  which).  It is not mended.  What remains is in Known limitations:
  an AOS-S trunk that carries nothing, and what OS10 does with the
  line.

- **A trunk that carries no VLAN untagged was written for IOS-XE,
  NX-OS, EOS and AOS-CX as one that carries VLAN 1 untagged.**  On
  those four a trunk with no native line has native VLAN 1 (the
  vendors' sentences are in the entry below).  A port that carries
  NO VLAN untagged at its source and has VLAN 1 on its list was
  written a trunk with no native line, so the switch made VLAN 1 its
  untagged VLAN: a VLAN the source carried TAGGED.  Such a port is a
  Junos trunk with no
  `native-vlan-id` (Juniper: "By default, the untagged packets are
  dropped on trunk interfaces.") whose members hold VLAN 1 or are
  `vlan members all`; an AOS-S port only `tagged` in VLAN 1; a
  trunk whose native VLAN the VLAN pane's map dropped or merged;
  and a Cisco, Arista or AOS-CX trunk whose native VLAN is sent
  tagged.  The job said nothing, but for one warning on a map drop
  beside every VLAN.  Over the committed captures that was the five
  Junos trunks of `vlan members all` onto each of the four -- 20
  ports of outputs, in jobs `partial` for other reasons -- and the
  four AOS-CX LAGs below onto IOS-XE, NX-OS and EOS.  It has been so
  for as long as each pair has existed.

  Each of the four is now written its own form for a trunk that
  carries no VLAN untagged, where the tree gives the trunk no native
  VLAN and its list holds VLAN 1.  **AOS-CX:** `vlan trunk native 1
  tag` before the allowed line (HPE: "Only incoming packets that are
  tagged with the matching VLAN ID are accepted. Incoming packets
  that are untagged are dropped except for BPDUs. Egress packets are
  tagged.").  **EOS:** `switchport trunk native vlan tag` (Arista:
  "tag interface drops all untagged frames."; what the interface
  sends for VLAN 1 is not on Arista's page).  **IOS-XE and NX-OS:**
  `vlan dot1q tag native`, the one form Cisco documents for it on
  the Catalyst 9300 and the Nexus 9000 -- and it is the switch's,
  not the port's (Cisco, of IOS-XE: "To enable tagging of native
  VLAN frames on all IEEE 802.1Q trunk ports, use the vlan dot1q tag
  native command in global configuration mode."; of NX-OS: "This
  configuration is global; trunk ports on the device either do or
  do not retain the tagging for the native VLAN.").  So it is
  written, once, before the interfaces, only where no port the check
  reads blocks it.  The check reads the ports written in trunk mode,
  the ports with trunk lines and no mode, and the ports in a mode no
  mode line is written for (dynamic, private-vlan, dot1q-tunnel,
  fex-fabric and the like): the line is written where no trunk
  carries a VLAN untagged, at least one trunk the tree gives no
  native VLAN holds VLAN 1, and no port is in such a mode or holds
  trunk lines in no mode.  A port written with no mode and no trunk
  line is not counted: on a Catalyst such a port is in dynamic auto
  by default, and should it become a trunk the line tags its native
  VLAN as well.  Otherwise each such trunk is written no native line
  and, where the native line would be, a review line:

  ```
  ! review: this trunk carries no VLAN untagged in the translated config; on IOS-XE a trunk with no native line has native VLAN 1, and this one's allowed list holds VLAN 1; vlan dot1q tag native would tag it, and tags the native VLAN of every 802.1Q trunk of the switch -- check what this port is to carry untagged
  ```

  (on NX-OS: `on NX-OS a trunk with no native line uses the default
  VLAN, VLAN 1, ...`, and `changes the native VLAN of every trunk of
  the device`).  The job adds nothing else.  Over the committed
  captures the five Junos trunks are written the line on IOS-XE and
  NX-OS and the port's form on EOS and AOS-CX.  Of the four AOS-CX
  LAGs, two (on the two `aoscx_dcn_arch3_*leaf1a` captures) are
  written the line on IOS-XE and NX-OS; the other two are on
  captures whose other trunks carry VLAN 1 untagged, and are written
  the review line there -- in jobs that say `completed` on NX-OS,
  and `partial` on IOS-XE for a port the job drops.  Junos is not
  changed as a target; OS10 and AOS-S are the entry above.

  **The words that say a native VLAN is sent tagged are read.**
  AOS-CX `vlan trunk native <N> tag` was read as native VLAN N
  UNTAGGED, the word thrown away.  The committed captures have four
  such lines, each `vlan trunk native 1 tag` beside `vlan trunk
  allowed all` on a LAG (two in Aruba's published sample
  configurations, two in configurations made by tools), and every
  target was written VLAN 1 untagged for them: Junos `native-vlan-id
  1`, OS10 `switchport access vlan 1`, AOS-S `untagged`, AOS-CX
  `vlan trunk native 1` (the word lost onto its own platform), and
  the other three by their default -- since AOS-CX was added, in
  0.1.6.  Such a trunk now has no native VLAN in the tree, a trunk that carries
  none untagged: Junos `vlan members all` with no `native-vlan-id`,
  AOS-S `tagged` in VLAN 1, OS10 `no switchport access vlan` under
  its review line with VLAN 1 on its allowed line (the entry above;
  what OS10 then carries untagged is a limitation, below),
  and the forms above.  The id is not kept: such a trunk
  takes only tagged frames and tags what it sends, so `native 20
  tag` and `native 1 tag` beside one list carry the same VLANs, and
  it comes back onto AOS-CX as `vlan trunk native 1 tag` where its
  list holds VLAN 1 and with no native line where it does not.  On
  IOS-XE and NX-OS `vlan dot1q tag native exclude control` (a form
  Cisco documents for the Nexus 7000) was not recognised, and a
  trunk under it was given native VLAN 1; it is read now.  `no
  switchport trunk native vlan tag` on a port -- by which, on a
  Catalyst 9500 High Performance switch, a trunk leaves `vlan dot1q
  tag native` -- gives that trunk its default again.  A native VLAN
  a trunk states under the line, or beside its own `tag`, is sent
  tagged, and is no longer kept in the tree (it was written as the
  trunk's untagged VLAN on every target).  On EOS the id and `tag`
  are one argument of one line, and the one met last stands.  No
  committed capture has the Cisco words.

  Onto its own platform every committed capture comes back byte for
  byte as before, but the four AOS-CX captures, which now come back
  with their `vlan trunk native 1 tag`.  A Cisco config under `vlan
  dot1q tag native` comes back with the line where at least one
  trunk under the line holds VLAN 1 and no port the check reads
  blocks it (`exclude control` is not kept).  Where a port blocks
  it -- a trunk that carries a VLAN untagged (a trunk that leaves
  the line by `no switchport trunk native vlan tag` and holds VLAN 1
  is one), a port in a mode no mode line is written for, trunk lines
  in no mode -- the trunks under the line that hold VLAN 1 come back
  with review lines.  Where no trunk under the line holds VLAN 1 it
  comes back without the line, and those trunks without a native
  line: the same VLANs, by Cisco's sentence for a trunk whose list
  leaves VLAN 1 out.  An EOS trunk with
  `switchport trunk native vlan tag` comes back with it where its
  list holds VLAN 1; where the list leaves VLAN 1 out it comes back
  with no native line, and what EOS does with untagged frames on
  such a trunk is not established (a limitation, below).

  **If a switch was migrated onto IOS-XE, NX-OS, EOS or AOS-CX with
  release 0.7.7 or earlier, look at every trunk that was written no
  native line and has VLAN 1 on its allowed list, or no allowed
  line, where the source trunk was a Junos trunk with no
  `native-vlan-id`, an AOS-S port tagged in VLAN 1, a trunk whose
  native VLAN was sent tagged, or one whose native VLAN you dropped
  or merged in the VLAN pane: the switch carries VLAN 1 untagged on
  it, and the source did not.  And a trunk migrated FROM AOS-CX
  with `vlan trunk native <N> tag` was written VLAN N untagged on
  every target.**

- **VLAN 1 of a Cisco, Arista or AOS-CX trunk that states no native
  VLAN was written TAGGED on Junos, OS10 and AOS-S.**  A trunk with
  no `switchport trunk native vlan` line (on AOS-CX, no `vlan trunk
  native` line) has its platform's default for a native VLAN.  Cisco,
  of IOS-XE: "The native VLAN is VLAN 1 by default."  Arista: "The
  default native VLAN for all interfaces is VLAN 1."  HPE, of AOS-CX:
  "By default, VLAN ID 1 is assigned as the native VLAN ID for all
  trunk interfaces."  Cisco, of NX-OS: "If you do not configure a
  native VLAN ID, the trunk port uses the default VLAN.", and on
  the same page: "The default VLAN is VLAN1."  So where such a
  trunk's
  allowed list holds VLAN 1 -- the list names it, or the trunk
  states no list at all, which is every VLAN -- the switch carries
  VLAN 1 without a tag.  The canonical tree did not say so.  The
  trunk had no native VLAN there, VLAN 1 was a tagged VLAN of it
  like any other, and the three targets that state the untagged
  VLAN in a line of their own were written none: on Junos the port
  was a member of VLAN 1 with no `native-vlan-id` (Juniper: "By
  default, the untagged packets are dropped on trunk interfaces."),
  on OS10 VLAN 1 stood on the allowed line, which names tagged
  VLANs, and on AOS-S the port was `tagged` in VLAN 1.  The job said
  nothing: no warning, no lossy path.

  Over the committed captures, 32 trunks of those four platforms
  state no native VLAN and 12 of them have VLAN 1 on their list (9
  of IOS-XE and 3 of NX-OS; 7 of the 12 because they state no list).
  For those 12, VLAN 1 was written tagged on Junos for all 12, on
  OS10 for 10 and on AOS-S for 6, and 4 more had no VLAN line on
  AOS-S at all.  (The rest are ports AOS-S has no name for, which
  the job drops and lists, and ports that an OS10 job writes with
  others under one name, and lists.)  It has been so for as long as
  each pair has existed: IOS-XE and EOS onto Junos and AOS-S since
  the first release, NX-OS as a source since 0.1.4, AOS-CX since
  0.1.6, and all four onto OS10 since 0.7.5.

  Each of the four parsers now puts its platform's default into the
  tree, where the parser of a trunk that states no allowed LIST
  already puts the platform's list: from one table
  (`TRUNK_THAT_STATES_NO_NATIVE` in `codecs/_helpers.py`), for an
  interface and not for a stanza, after its list is known.  A trunk
  that states no native VLAN and whose list holds VLAN 1 has native
  VLAN 1, and VLAN 1 has a record with the port as its untagged
  member, whether or not the config declares VLAN 1.  Where the
  list leaves VLAN 1 out (`switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20`;
  `2-4094`) nothing is filled in, and the trunk has no native VLAN
  in the tree: 20 of the 32.  That is a native VLAN outside its
  list, and what a switch does with one is each vendor's to say.
  For VLAN 1 on IOS-XE, NX-OS and AOS-CX the vendor reference has
  Cisco's and HPE's sentences (no user traffic; data traffic
  blocked; not forwarded).  For EOS, 8 of the 20, it is not
  established: "no untagged VLAN" is how netcanon reads such a
  trunk, and says nothing about the switch.  **The default is a
  trunk's.**  It is given to a port that SAYS it is a trunk --
  `switchport mode trunk`, or on AOS-CX a `vlan trunk` line, which
  is how a trunk is stated there -- and to no other.  A port in
  another mode that keeps trunk lines, and a port with a trunk line
  and no mode line, get nothing from it, as they get nothing of the
  platform's list (the limitation on such a port, below).  All 32
  trunks of the captures say they are trunks.  Nothing is filled
  in where the text says the native VLAN is sent tagged (`vlan
  dot1q tag native`, `switchport trunk native vlan tag`): a native
  VLAN put there would be read as untagged.  (What else those
  words now make of a trunk is in the entry above.)  OS10 and Junos are not
  changed.  A Junos trunk has no default, and an OS10 trunk's is the
  default VLAN of its switch, a setting no trunk states (no
  committed capture has an OS10 trunk without an access VLAN line).

  So the same 12 trunks are now written a line that states VLAN 1
  as their untagged VLAN: on OS10 `switchport access vlan 1` with
  VLAN 1 off the allowed line, on AOS-S `untagged` in VLAN 1 (10
  of the 12, under 9 port names: two the job reports as fused
  share one; the two the job drops are as they were), on AOS-CX `vlan
  trunk native 1`, which its captures print on every trunk, and on
  Junos `native-vlan-id 1` (with `set vlans VLAN-1 vlan-id 1` where
  the source declared no VLAN 1).  On Junos, 5 of the 12 name VLAN
  1 among their `vlan members`.  The other 7 are trunks of every
  VLAN and are written `vlan members all` beside `native-vlan-id
  1`.  Juniper's page asks for the logical interface to be a member
  of the native VLAN and its procedure names that VLAN on `vlan
  members`; whether `all` takes the native VLAN in is not
  established.  **Before deploying a Junos trunk written `vlan
  members all` beside `native-vlan-id`, check on the switch that
  it receives untagged frames into the native VLAN, or name that
  VLAN on `vlan members` as Juniper's procedure does.**

  **IOS-XE, NX-OS and EOS are written no native line for VLAN 1 on
  a trunk whose list holds it**, from any source.  It is their
  default as well, no real capture of the three prints the line,
  and by the sentences above the trunk is the same with it and
  without: a trunk that stated no native VLAN comes back as it
  went.  That takes `switchport trunk native vlan 1` out of outputs
  that had it -- for an AOS-S port untagged in VLAN 1 and tagged in
  others, an OS10 trunk whose access VLAN is 1, an AOS-CX trunk
  with `vlan trunk native 1`.  Over the committed captures that is
  115 lines in 43 outputs (39 lines in 15 outputs for IOS-XE, 39 in
  15 for EOS, 37 in 13 for NX-OS), and no other line of those
  outputs moves.  A native VLAN 1 that its list leaves OUT is
  written as before, on all three: it is stated and not carried,
  which no default is.  And on IOS-XE a port that is not
  `switchport mode trunk` keeps a `switchport trunk native vlan 1`
  line it states: no default is put for such a port, so the line
  is all there is.

  **An IOS-XE or EOS output now has a `vlan 1` line where a trunk of
  the source carries VLAN 1 untagged by its platform's default**
  (and an NX-OS or AOS-CX output declares VLAN 1 then too: `vlan
  1,10,20`, `vlan 1`; every committed capture of those two declares
  VLAN 1 already, so none shows it).
  Such a trunk brings VLAN 1 into the tree, with the trunk as its
  untagged member, and both renderers write a `vlan` line for every
  VLAN of the tree -- as they did before for a VLAN 1 that a short
  allowed list names, that an access port is in, or that has an
  interface of its own.  So a config with a trunk that states no
  native VLAN, and no word for VLAN 1, comes back onto its own
  platform with one line it did not have: `vlan 1` (and the `!`
  that closes the VLAN block, where it declared no VLAN at all).
  No real capture of either platform prints that line.  No sentence
  the vendor reference quotes says what either switch does with
  it, or that VLAN 1 is there without it, so nothing is claimed
  for it here: it is written because the tree has the VLAN, and
  the tree does not keep whether the text had the line.  It is a
  line to expect when an output is compared with its source.  Over
  the committed captures two outputs gain it, both from one IOS-XE
  capture whose four trunks state neither a native VLAN nor a list
  and which declares no VLAN: onto IOS-XE itself and onto EOS.  That
  is also the ONLY difference in any capture's output onto its own
  platform, with a job and without: the one IOS-XE capture gains
  `vlan 1` and the `!` after it, and the output of every other
  capture onto its own platform is byte for byte what it was.

  **If a switch was migrated from IOS-XE, NX-OS, EOS or AOS-CX onto
  Junos, OS10 or AOS-S with release 0.7.7 or earlier, look at every
  trunk whose source had no native VLAN line and had VLAN 1 on its
  allowed list, or no allowed list.  VLAN 1 is tagged on it where
  the source carried it untagged: translate it again and compare
  the trunk's lines.**  What else moves with it:

  - A client that reads the canonical tree sees `trunk_native_vlan:
    1` on such a port, and VLAN 1 among the VLANs with the port in
    `untagged_ports`.  The VLAN pane offers VLAN 1 for such a
    config, and a map that renumbers VLAN 1 moves the trunk's
    untagged VLAN with it.
  - `fortigate_cli`, `mikrotik_routeros` and `opnsense` write every
    VLAN of the tree as a tagged VLAN device, the untagged one
    among them (a known limitation, below).  A source that declares
    no VLAN 1 and has such trunks now reaches them with a VLAN 1
    device, where it had none: three outputs of the committed
    captures (one IOS-XE capture of four default trunks).  The
    source carries VLAN 1 without a tag, so that device is further
    from it than no device was.
  - What a config makes is counted (`memberships`).  A trunk of
    every VLAN is on VLAN 1 as well, untagged, so a config of such
    trunks that declares no VLAN 1 counts one VLAN more than it
    declares, and one membership more a trunk for the untagged
    place.  The text that reaches every limit of `small` at once is
    two VLANs smaller for it (256 trunks and 193 VLANs, where it
    was 195), and `deploy/VERIFY.md` proofs 15 to 17 use that text;
    the times and the memory the demo's documents give for it were
    measured with the text as it was.
  - Over the committed captures 146 of 3,105 parse, render and plan
    digests move (3 parse, 61 bare, 82 plan; 62 outputs of jobs), and
    no job status does.

  The other half is not mended, and is the first of the limitations
  below: a port that carries NO VLAN untagged, written for a
  platform whose trunk has a default native VLAN.  Guarded by
  `tests/unit/migration/test_the_list_holds_the_native_vlan.py`,
  which holds every tree to its platform's default -- a trunk that
  says it is one has it, and no other port does, read from the
  text and from no parser -- reads each output's text with that
  default applied, and pins the cells of the open half one by one.
- **The untagged VLAN of an AOS-S or Dell OS10 trunk was written as a
  native VLAN outside the allowed list.**  An AOS-S port that is
  `untagged` in one VLAN and `tagged` in others, and an OS10 trunk
  with a `switchport access vlan` line, carry that VLAN untagged: on
  both platforms the untagged VLAN is a statement of its own, beside
  the tagged ones.  The canonical tree kept it beside the list as
  well, and the renderers of **IOS-XE CLI, NX-OS, EOS, AOS-CX and
  Junos** write a trunk's list as it stands.  So the port came out as
  `switchport trunk native vlan 10` beside `switchport trunk allowed
  vlan 20,30` (on AOS-CX `vlan trunk native 10` beside `vlan trunk
  allowed 20,30`; on Junos `native-vlan-id 10` and `vlan members`
  without it).  Where the allowed list decides what a trunk carries,
  that is a port with no untagged VLAN: the hosts behind it lose
  their network.  How far that goes is each vendor's to say.  HPE
  says it of AOS-CX in so many words ("If the native VLAN is not
  included in the allowed list, all untagged frames that ingress on
  the trunk interface are dropped.").  Cisco says it of IOS-XE and
  NX-OS for VLAN 1, the default native VLAN; for another VLAN it
  follows from Cisco's rule for the list and is no sentence of
  Cisco's.  Juniper states it, for the grammar written here, as what
  a unit needs in order to receive untagged packets.  For EOS it is
  not established.  The job said nothing either way: no warning, no
  lossy path, `completed`.

  It was every such trunk, not some.  Over the committed captures:
  all 8 AOS-S trunks and all 29 OS10 trunks that have an untagged
  VLAN, on each of the five targets they reach as a trunk -- 135
  ports of outputs, 92 of them in jobs that said `completed`.  It has
  been so in every release that has the pair: AOS-S onto IOS-XE CLI,
  EOS and Junos since the first release, onto NX-OS since 0.1.4 and
  AOS-CX since 0.1.6; OS10, as a source onto all five, since 0.7.5.

  A trunk's allowed list is now what the trunk CARRIES, its native
  VLAN among them, in the tree and so in every output: the same port
  is `switchport trunk native vlan 10` beside `switchport trunk
  allowed vlan 10,20,30`, which is how HPE's own side-by-side of the
  two grammars writes an AOS-S port for AOS-CX.  A native VLAN the
  list does NOT hold is stated and not carried, and that is kept
  too: such a trunk of IOS-XE, NX-OS, EOS, AOS-CX or Junos comes
  back, on those five, with the lines it had.  One table says how
  each platform's text states it (`NATIVE_VLAN_AND_THE_LIST`), the
  OS10 parser puts a trunk's access VLAN into its list and the OS10
  renderer takes it out again, and the two projections between a
  port's own fields and the VLANs' member lists agree with each
  other, which they did not.  Every committed OS10 and AOS-S capture
  comes back onto its own platform byte for byte as it did.

  *The other way round,* three things were written that the source
  does not state.  The first is no longer WRITTEN, which is not to
  say that the switch now drops the VLAN.  A trunk whose native VLAN
  is NOT in its allowed list was written `untagged` in that VLAN on
  AOS-S, and with `switchport access vlan` on OS10 -- a port that
  carries a VLAN the source list leaves out (11 trunks of the
  committed captures, eight of them LAGs, all VLAN 1; 20 interfaces
  of outputs, each in a job that was `partial` for another reason).
  AOS-S is now written no `untagged` line for such a port, and a
  `; review:` line in that VLAN's stanza names it and says so.  Over
  the committed captures that is nine names in four outputs, and
  only ONE of the nine is a port.  The other eight are trunk groups
  (`Trk<n>`) that the output does not make: AOS-S has no name for
  their member ports, the job drops and lists those, and the output
  says of each such LAG that it has no members.  (The last two of
  the 11 are ports AOS-S has no name for, which the job drops and
  lists as well.)  No `untagged` line is not the same as no VLAN,
  though.  HPE, of AOS-S: "In the factory default configuration,
  all ports are assigned to the default VLAN (DEFAULT_VLAN;
  VID=1)." and "Any ports not specifically removed from the default
  VLAN remain in the DEFAULT_VLAN, regardless of other port
  assignments."  So a PORT that is written this way is, by those
  sentences, in VLAN 1 on the switch unless it has been removed
  from it -- the VLAN the earlier output had it carry -- and its
  review line says what the two sentences say, and asks what the
  port is to carry:
  `; review: port 3 -- native VLAN 1 is stated for this trunk and
  its allowed list leaves it out, so no untagged line is written
  for this port; in the factory default configuration an AOS-S port
  is in the default VLAN (VID 1), and it remains there until it is
  removed -- check what this port is to carry untagged`.  The two
  sentences speak of ports, and neither says whether that
  membership is tagged or untagged, so the line does not either.
  For a trunk group, or for a port once it is in one, no sentence
  of HPE's was found.  The line for a `Trk<n>` name, and for a port
  that the same output puts on a `trunk` line, has this where the
  other has HPE's sentences: `which VLAN an AOS-S trunk group, or a
  port that is in one, is in by default is not established`.  (Both
  forms have changed since: a name the output tags in some VLAN is
  now taken out of VLAN 1, and its line says so, and the line for a
  trunk group gives HPE's sentences for one -- the first entry of
  this section.)
  OS10 is written `no switchport access vlan` under a `! review:`
  line, because Dell's own pages do not agree on whether that line
  leaves a trunk with no untagged VLAN or with VLAN 1.  Neither
  review line calls the VLAN the source's: after a VLAN map its id
  is the output's.  The OS10
  parser, which passed that line over, now reads it, on any switched
  port: a trunk is left with no native VLAN, and an access port with
  no access VLAN stated.  The second: an OS10 trunk was written
  with one VLAN on its access line AND on its allowed line whenever
  the source list named its native VLAN (47 trunks of those outputs),
  which Dell says an interface cannot be: the allowed line now names
  the tagged VLANs only.  The third: an OS10 trunk with an access
  VLAN and no allowed line -- the two Dell peer links of the
  committed captures -- was read as a trunk of NO VLAN, and written
  `switchport trunk allowed vlan none` beside the native line (on
  AOS-CX: no `vlan trunk` line at all, under a `review:` line).  It
  is a trunk of that one VLAN, and is written so.

  *The VLAN pane's map* is held to the same reading.  A map could
  bring a native VLAN that its trunk's list leaves out INTO the
  list, and the output then had the trunk carry that VLAN untagged,
  which the source did not.  Two different things can have
  happened, and they are told apart by the id of the list that the
  map puts on the native VLAN's id: is it a VLAN the list names --
  a VLAN the config has (one it declares, an access port's VLAN, or
  one that a trunk names as its native VLAN or in a short allowed
  list: the rule for which VLANs are translated at all), or any id
  of a short allowed list, declared or not -- or only a number that
  a longer list covers with a range?

  *A merge.*  Native VLAN 10 beside a list of 20 and 30, and VLAN 10
  given the id 20, or 20 the id 10.  The trunk then stated the
  merged VLAN as its native VLAN with that VLAN on its list, so a
  VLAN the source carried tagged was written UNTAGGED on IOS-XE,
  NX-OS, EOS, AOS-CX, Junos and OS10, and on AOS-S the port was
  listed `untagged` and `tagged` in it.  The native VLAN of such a
  trunk is now cleared, and the job says so: `vlan_rename: interface
  'GigabitEthernet1/0/1' had native VLAN 10 outside its allowed
  list, and the map merges it into VLAN 20, which the trunk carries
  tagged — native VLAN cleared`.  The VLAN stays tagged on all
  seven.  The trunk then has no native VLAN, and on a target whose
  trunk has a default the first of the limitations below applies.

  *A number no VLAN had.*  `switchport trunk native vlan 1000`
  beside `switchport trunk allowed vlan 2-999,1001-4094` -- a
  parking VLAN as the native VLAN, and a list of every other id --
  and VLAN 1000 given the id 900.  (Or `allowed vlan except 10`, and
  10 given the id 4000.)  The config has no VLAN 900; the list
  names that number only because its range covers it.  The output
  had `native vlan 900` beside a list that held 900: the parking
  VLAN, which the source trunk did not carry, carried untagged.
  Nothing is merged here, and nothing is cleared.  The new id is
  taken OUT of the list and the native VLAN is kept -- `native vlan
  900` beside `2-899,901-999,1001-4094`, and on AOS-S and OS10 the
  review line described above -- so the trunk carries that VLAN on
  none of the seven, as before the map.  The job says so in other
  words than a merge's: `vlan_rename: interface 'Ethernet1' had
  native VLAN 1000 outside its allowed list, and the map gives it
  the id 900, which the list named only as a number no VLAN of the
  config had — 900 is taken out of the list, and the trunk does not
  carry native VLAN 900`.

  Both are done for every port that states the two lines, whatever
  its mode: a port in a dynamic mode, or with no mode line, can
  become a trunk, and IOS-XE is written such a port's trunk lines.
  (No VLAN is made from the trunk lines of such a port, and its
  short list is read as a trunk's is: `native vlan 10` beside
  `allowed vlan 500`, with 10 given the id 500, is a merge in any
  mode.)
  A native VLAN its list holds is renumbered with the list as
  before, and so is one that is still outside the list afterwards.

  **If a switch was migrated from AOS-S or OS10 onto IOS-XE, NX-OS,
  EOS, AOS-CX or Junos with release 0.7.7 or earlier, look at every
  trunk that has a native VLAN line: where the allowed list (`vlan
  members` on Junos) does not name that VLAN, untagged traffic on
  the port is at risk, and on AOS-CX it is dropped.  Add the VLAN to
  the list.**  If one was migrated the other way, onto AOS-S or OS10,
  look for a port that is `untagged` in a VLAN (has `switchport
  access vlan` on a trunk) where the source trunk's list left its
  native VLAN out, and for an OS10 trunk that names one VLAN on both
  lines.  And if a VLAN was renumbered, or given the id of another,
  in the VLAN pane with one of those releases, compare each trunk's
  native VLAN with its allowed list in the output and in the source:
  a native VLAN that the source list left out may be ON the list in
  the output, and carried untagged.  A client that reads the canonical tree sees
  `trunk_allowed_vlans` hold the untagged VLAN of an OS10 or AOS-S
  trunk from now on, and a trunk that states a native VLAN outside
  its list is no longer among that VLAN's `untagged_ports`.  Three
  outputs for OPNsense move with it, on the committed captures: the
  parent of a VLAN device is a port whose list names the VLAN, so
  the device of an AOS-S or OS10 trunk's untagged VLAN is now on
  that trunk.  In two OS10 outputs VLAN 1's device moves there from
  the management port; in one AOS-S output VLAN 10's moves there
  from a port that was never in VLAN 10, and VLAN 1's from one port
  of VLAN 1 to another.  Each is still written as a TAGGED device,
  which is among the limitations below.  No FortiGate or RouterOS
  output of the committed captures moves.  And where several source
  ports are written under one name -- a job that lists them and is
  `partial` -- the port made of them has its untagged VLAN in its
  list as well.  Guarded by
  `tests/unit/migration/test_the_list_holds_the_native_vlan.py`,
  which reads what a device carries untagged on each side by its own
  platform's grammar, from the output parsed again and from the
  output's text, and holds every job onto AOS-S to its review line,
  whole and in the form for what the name is; the map's part is in
  `tests/unit/migration/test_a_vlan_drop_and_a_trunks_list.py`,
  which also holds that no map makes a port carry untagged a VLAN
  it did not carry untagged before.
- **A word of the config is no longer written into the output as an
  interface's name.**  A field that holds a port name is given a port
  name or nothing, and an interface is made only for a name the
  config configures something under.  Four parsers broke one half of
  that or the other, each in every release up to and including 0.7.7
  (IOS XR since the codec shipped), and each in jobs that could say
  `completed`:

  - *IOS XR `interface preconfigure <name>`.*  The stanza is
    configuration the router holds for an interface it does not have
    until the line card is put in.  It was read as an interface
    called `preconfigure`, and every target's output had one
    (`interface preconfigure`, `edit "preconfigure"`, `ethernet
    preconfigure {`), IOS XR's own included.  It makes no interface
    now, nothing in the stanza is read (a `bundle id` there no longer
    adds a member to the bundle, an `encapsulation dot1q` no longer
    adds a VLAN), and the job lists it as it lists every statement a
    source held and did not run: `preconfigure: interface <name>
    (held for an interface the source does not have; not
    translated)`.  Such a row is not counted as a section, the rows
    are bounded, and a text that is nothing but such stanzas is
    `partial`, not `completed`.  Nor is the stanza read as the port
    it names: on the committed capture that has one, that port is a
    cage the config already has under another speed, and seven
    targets would write the two under one name.
  - *A type and its number written apart* (IOS-XE and IOS XR:
    `interface ethernet 1/11`, `interface Bundle-Ether 10`).  IOS
    reads the two words as one name, and `show running-config` prints
    them together, so the form is in typed and documentation-shaped
    text.  The name was the first word alone: two such stanzas made
    one interface called `ethernet`, written twice.  The two words
    are one name now, in the letters the config has (`ethernet1/11`).
    A keyword is not a type: an `interface range ...` stanza was an
    interface called `range`, and an `interface breakout <port> map
    <profile>` line — OS10's, in a text read as IOS-XE or IOS XR —
    one called `breakout`.  Neither makes an interface now, neither
    is translated, and the header line of each is listed, as a
    section.
  - *IOS-XE `ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 loopback 66 100`.*  A route out
    an interface written the same way was a route out `loopback` at
    distance 66, the 100 lost.  It is `loopback66` at distance 100,
    in `ip route` and `ipv6 route` alike.  A type word with an
    address after it (`ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 Dialer 10.0.0.1`) is
    read as it was: the address is the gateway.
  - *OPNsense `<dhcpd><lan>`.*  A DHCP pool is keyed by a zone, and
    the zone's NAME was put where the pool's interface goes: Junos
    bound its DHCP server to `interface lan`, FortiOS wrote `set
    interface "lan"`, and OPNsense's own output had `<dhcpd><lan>`
    beside an `<interfaces>` with no `<lan>` in it.  The pool is on
    the device the zone is assigned to (`<interfaces><lan><if>`),
    and follows that port where it is renamed.  A target that names
    a pool after its interface names it after the port now: `ip dhcp
    pool lan` is `ip dhcp pool GigabitEthernet0_0`, and Junos
    `pool_lan` is `pool_ge_0_0_0`.  A pool whose zone `<interfaces>`
    does not have has no interface to be on: it is left out, and the
    job lists the zone (`<dhcpd><opt9>: no <opt9> in <interfaces>,
    so its DHCP pool has no interface`).
  - *Junos `set interfaces irb unit 100 ...`.*  The line configures
    the unit, and an empty interface `irb` was made beside `irb.100`
    (and `st0` beside `st0.1`, `lo0` beside `lo0.1`).  No platform
    has a name for it, so it was written under its Junos name
    (`interface irb`, `edit "irb"`) and held the job as a name left
    as the source has it; Junos onto Junos gained a `set interfaces
    irb` line the source did not have.  An interface is made for a
    name a line configures: the first word of a line on the device
    itself or on its unit 0, whether or not the parser reads the
    rest of the line (`irb mtu 9100`, `irb gratuitous-arp-reply`, a
    bare `set interfaces st0`, `st0 unit 0 family inet` — the
    unnumbered tunnel a route to `st0.0` goes out of), and
    `<name>.<N>` for a line under unit N.  A name the port
    classifier reads as a port or as an `ae` bundle keeps its
    record whatever the config says of it (`ge-0/0/3` with only
    tagged units).  That is not yet every port: a channelized
    `xe-0/0/6:2`, a `so-0/0/0` or a `reth0` is a name it does not
    read, and with nothing but units above 0 has its units and no
    record of its own.  A bare `set interfaces st0 unit 1`, which
    made `st0` and no `st0.1`, makes `st0.1`.  And a device that has
    a record is no longer discarded when a unit beside it is folded
    onto its VLAN — an MTU or a unit-0 address on `irb` was lost
    that way, and nothing said so.

  **If a config with one of these forms was translated with release
  0.7.7 or earlier, look in the output for an interface called
  `preconfigure`, `ethernet`, `range`, `breakout`, `loopback`,
  `lan`, `irb` or `st0`.**  The list of what was not translated has
  three new kinds of row: `preconfigure: interface <name> (...)`,
  which like an `inactive:` row is not a section; and an `interface
  range` or `interface breakout` header and `<dhcpd><zone>: ...` for
  a pool left out, each counted as a section.  A translation onto
  OPNsense reports `/dhcp-servers/pool` as lossy from now on: a pool
  is written under the zone of its interface, one that names no
  interface under `<lan>`, and a pool under a zone the output has no
  interface for serves nothing there (read back, it is left out).
  Over the
  committed captures: four OPNsense configs have their pool on the
  device of its zone (in one of them a placeholder the capture
  itself uses, `mismatch0`; two of them had `interface lan` in a
  `completed` Junos job), and two Junos jobs that were `partial` for
  the empty `irb` alone are `completed`.  Not mended here, each
  older than this release: IOS-XE `ip route <prefix> <mask> dhcp`
  still keeps the keyword where the route's interface goes — the
  line is written back to IOS-XE as it was, other platforms are
  given a route out an interface called `dhcp`, and onto Junos the
  validation report holds the job; NX-OS still reads `interface
  port-channel 1` as `port-channel`; an IOS XR `router static` line
  and an AOS-CX `ip route` line still read a spaced interface a word
  at a time (AOS-CX writes `loopback 77` itself, and reads its own
  line back as distance 77); an EOS DHCP pool's NAME is still where
  the pool's interface goes; and a Junos output never has the line
  `set interfaces st0 unit 0 family inet` itself — for an empty
  `st0` it has a bare `set interfaces st0` where the config has a
  unit of it too or a routing instance names it, and no line where
  it stands alone.
- **An AOS-S port with no `interface` stanza was in no line of the
  output, and its VLANs with it.**  An AOS-S switch prints an
  `interface` stanza only for a port that has a setting of its own.
  Every other port is in the config through the `untagged` /
  `tagged` lists of its VLANs, or as a member on a `trunk` line, and
  a switch's own config can have no `interface` stanza at all.  The
  parser made a port record only for a stanza, and most targets
  write a port -- its VLANs, its LAG -- from the port's own record.
  Onto **NX-OS, AOS-CX, OS10 and IOS-XR** the output had no line for
  such a port, in a job that could say `completed`: `port_renames`
  listed the port under a name the output did not have, and the
  validation report counted its VLAN membership as supported.  On a
  committed capture of a standalone 2930F, 181 of 182 VLAN port
  memberships were missing from an NX-OS output in a `completed`
  job; over the committed AOS-S captures, 297 on each of the four
  targets.  A `trunk` member with no stanza was likewise no member
  of its LAG on those four targets and on EOS, IOS-XE CLI and Junos.
  It has been so in every release that has the target: NX-OS since
  0.1.4, IOS-XR since 0.1.5, AOS-CX since 0.1.6, OS10 since 0.7.5.
  (EOS, IOS-XE CLI and Junos wrote the VLANs: their renderers made
  the missing record themselves.)

  The parser now gives a record to every port a VLAN's list or a
  `trunk` line names: the record a stanza with no lines makes.
  Every target writes the port.  Where it has a form for a port's
  VLANs and LAG they are on the port's stanza (`switchport access
  vlan`, `vlan trunk allowed`, `channel-group`, `lag`); where it has
  none -- IOS-XR, IOS-XE over NETCONF, VyOS, FortiOS, RouterOS,
  OPNsense -- the port is written without them and the validation
  report lists the port's membership as unsupported; onto IOS-XR,
  IOS-XE over NETCONF and VyOS it used to list nothing that said
  so.  With both devices declared such a port is
  found by its hardware like any other, under the name an operator
  gives it.

  **To re-check on a device migrated before:** an AOS-S switch moved
  onto NX-OS, AOS-CX, OS10 or IOS-XR.  Every port that has no
  `interface` stanza in the AOS-S config -- on a switch's own config
  that is most of them -- was left out: compare the `untagged` and
  `tagged` lines of each `vlan` in the source with the `switchport`
  (or `vlan access` / `vlan trunk`) lines of the output port by
  port, and give each missing port its lines.  For a `trunk` line,
  also on EOS, IOS-XE and Junos: check that each member carries its
  `channel-group` (`lag`, `bundle id`, `802.3ad`).  A port that had
  a stanza of its own was written as it is now.
- **A trunk that allows no VLAN no longer comes out allowing every
  VLAN, and a trunk of every VLAN no longer comes out carrying
  none.**  The canonical tree had one value, an empty list, for three
  statements: a trunk that allows no VLAN (`switchport trunk allowed
  vlan none`, a list emptied by `remove` or `except`, a Dell OS10 or
  Junos trunk that lists nothing, a trunk whose VLANs were all dropped
  in the rename modal), a trunk that states no list (every VLAN on
  IOS-XE, NX-OS and EOS), and AOS-CX's own `vlan trunk allowed all`.
  Each renderer picked one reading for all three.  IOS-XE, NX-OS and
  EOS wrote the empty list as a trunk with no allowed line, and
  AOS-CX as `vlan trunk allowed all`: every VLAN, for a trunk that
  carried none.  Junos, OS10 and AOS-S wrote it as a trunk that
  carries none: for a Cisco uplink that carried everything.  The job
  said `completed` and reported nothing, and a test that read the
  output back with the target's parser saw nothing either, because
  that parser read its own default as the same empty list.  In the
  committed captures: two Dell peer links that carry one untagged
  VLAN came out as trunks of every VLAN on four targets, and 23
  trunks of every VLAN — two vPC peer links and their members among
  them — reached Junos, OS10 and AOS-S carrying nothing.
  A list now means what it says.  On a trunk an empty list is NO
  VLAN, a list of every id (1-4094) is EVERY VLAN, and any other list
  is the list.  The parser, which knows its platform, puts what a
  trunk with no allowed list carries there, from one table: every
  VLAN on IOS-XE, NX-OS, EOS and AOS-CX; none on OS10 and Junos
  (each vendor's sentence, with its source, is in
  `docs/vendor-references/cisco_iosxe_cli_to_juniper_junos/vlans.md`).
  `add` and `remove` on an interface's first allowed line start from
  that list, as they do on the device (`remove 10` on a Cisco trunk
  with no earlier line was read as no VLAN, and is every VLAN but 10).
  What an interface states is kept by its NAME — the one its header
  line writes — so a stanza that is met twice is one interface: a
  trunk of VLAN 10 whose stanza appears again with only its mode line
  is a trunk of VLAN 10 both times, and `add 30` in a second stanza
  is added to the interface's own list.
  And the platform's list is given only where the interface SAYS it
  is a trunk: the NX-OS and EOS parsers take a port for a trunk from a
  trunk line alone, and a trunk taken that way gets nothing from the
  default (Known limitations, below).
  Each renderer writes its target's form: IOS-XE, NX-OS and EOS write
  `switchport trunk allowed vlan none` for no VLAN and no allowed line
  for every VLAN — they wrote the 4,094 ids on one line of some
  19,000 characters, or `1-4094`, which names ids NX-OS keeps for
  itself — AOS-CX writes `vlan trunk allowed all` for every VLAN and
  for no other list, and Junos, OS10 and AOS-S write what they did.
  **If a config was translated with release 0.7.7 or earlier, check
  every trunk whose allowed list is empty or absent on either side.**
  Every committed capture comes back through its own codec byte for
  byte as it did (230 outputs, and 474 over the development
  captures).  Same-vendor texts that no capture holds do change, two
  of them
  each to what the device prints: `switchport trunk allowed vlan all`
  (or `1-4094`) comes back from IOS-XE, NX-OS and EOS as a trunk with
  no allowed line, and an AOS-CX `vlan trunk native <N>` with no
  allowed line comes back with `vlan trunk allowed all` beside it (as
  does `vlan trunk allowed 1-4094`).  A third changes to something
  the source did not print: an NX-OS or EOS port with a trunk line
  and no `switchport mode trunk`, which was and is written back as a
  trunk, now has `switchport trunk allowed vlan none` under it (Known
  limitations).  Of the 1,495 outputs every
  capture makes onto every codec, 57 change, none of them onto its
  own; no job changes status and, with no VLAN map given, no job's
  warnings change.  What else moves with it:
  - *The VLAN pane.*  A trunk that allowed only VLANs you dropped is
    written as a trunk of no VLAN — it was every VLAN on four targets
    — and the job says so: `vlan_rename: interface
    'GigabitEthernet1/0/1' is a trunk that allowed only VLAN 100
    which was dropped — the trunk now allows no VLAN`.  A trunk of
    every VLAN is left as it is by a drop or a renumber: a trunk that
    said `all` came out as `1-99,101-4094` when VLAN 100 was dropped
    or given another id.  And it is no reference to any one VLAN: a
    map entry for a VLAN the config does not have is still reported
    (`VLAN 555 is present nowhere in the parsed config ... entry
    ignored`), whatever trunks of every VLAN the config holds.
  - *The validation report* names
    `/interfaces/interface/trunk-allowed-vlans` for a trunk that
    states no list, where the target drops it.  It was not walked:
    the list was empty.
  - *The VLAN parent on OPNsense, RouterOS and FortiOS*, which have
    no trunks and hang a VLAN on one port.  Each looks through the
    source's trunks for one that carries the VLAN, and a trunk that
    states no list carries every VLAN now.  A trunk that NAMES the
    VLAN is looked for before a trunk of every VLAN, so an output is
    as it was wherever a trunk names the VLAN.  Four committed
    outputs change, all onto OPNsense.  In three, VLANs that no trunk
    names move from a parent chosen without looking to the LAG that
    carries every VLAN (two AOS-CX captures, and the vPC peer link of
    an NX-OS one).  In the fourth, a Junos QFX, VLANs move from a LAG
    that says `vlan members all` to the port that names them.
  - *What it costs.*  A trunk that states no list is 4,094 ids in the
    tree on those four platforms, which is what a trunk that states
    `1-4094` already cost: some 35 KB a trunk.  A thousand of them
    (60 KB of text) are 36 MB of tree where they were 3; ten thousand
    (0.6 MB) are 364 MB, the figure for ten thousand that state
    `1-4094`, and take what those take: a second to read, and under
    four to translate to Junos (the stated list took seven, until
    the Junos renderer asked the shared reading of "every VLAN").
    Reading them still grows with their number and no faster.  Those
    are what the lists cost where they are made.  The config limits
    (under Security, above) count such a trunk as the 4,094 ids it is,
    as they count the word `all`, BEFORE its list is made -- and with
    it the every-VLAN list a first `add` or `remove` starts from, and
    the list each record of a stanza met again is given: the default
    set reads 4,098 such trunks and refuses the next (ten thousand are
    refused in half a second, at 159 MB), and the public demo's reads
    256.  Such
    trunks beside as many VLAN interfaces are a product — N trunks in
    each of M VLANs — as they are with the list stated.  A thousand
    of each takes one to two seconds onto OPNsense, RouterOS and
    FortiOS, which is what the stated list took, or less: just over
    a second onto FortiOS, where it took more than four, because that
    renderer scored every port again for every VLAN interface and now
    scores them once a render.  SECURITY.md has both under "What a
    request may make, and for how long".
  New tests render a trunk that says none, nothing and all — in each
  source's own grammar — onto every codec, and read the output as
  text with a reader of their own as well as with the target's parser
  (`tests/unit/migration/test_a_trunk_says_none_nothing_or_all.py`);
  a stanza met twice and a trunk line with no mode line are among
  them; and a public codec that makes trunks fails there until it
  says what a trunk with no list carries on its platform.

- **NX-OS counted a `vlan <range>` line twice.**  Two passes of the
  parser read the line and both expanded it, so `vlan 2-2502` (2,501
  ids) was charged as 5,002 "over 2 lists": a limit refused half of
  what it says it allows, and a refusal printed twice the count.  The
  second pass only has to know whether the line opens a stanza of one
  VLAN, and no longer expands it.
- **A trunk that leaves a VLAN out does not get it back on Junos.**
  The Junos renderer wrote any trunk list of 4,000 VLAN ids or more
  as `vlan members all`, which on Junos is every VLAN the switch has
  and every VLAN it is given later.  So `switchport trunk allowed
  vlan 1-99,101-4094` came out as `all`, with VLAN 100 back on the
  trunk, and `2-4094` with VLAN 1 — in a job that said `completed`
  and reported nothing.  `all` is now written only for a list of
  every id (`1-4094`).  Any other list is cut into runs of
  consecutive ids: a run made only of VLANs the output defines is
  written by name, as before; any other run is written as one range
  of ids, which covers the defined VLANs inside it (`vlan members
  1-99`, `vlan members 101-4094`).  Junos documents ids and ranges
  as members beside names, and this parser already read them.  A
  list of 129 to 3,999 ids was a line per id, each a name
  `VLAN-<id>` for a VLAN the output does not define (`1-3999`:
  3,999 lines); that is one range now.  A list of 128 ids or fewer
  is unchanged: its VLANs are made, and named.  A VLAN whose own
  name is `all`, another VLAN's number or a range of numbers is
  written as `VLAN-<id>` with a `# review:` line: a member list
  reads those names as every VLAN, or as ids.  The shared projection read
  `2-4094` as "all VLANs" and stamped the trunk onto every declared
  VLAN, VLAN 1 included, so AOS-S tagged the port in VLAN 1; it
  stamps the VLANs the list holds.  **If a trunk with a wide list
  that leaves VLANs out was translated to Junos with release 0.7.7
  or earlier, check its `vlan members` line: it says `all`, and the
  VLANs the source left out are on it.**  Not verified on a device:
  that a switch commits a member range most of whose ids have no
  VLAN.  Juniper's pages give the grammar, and an example of a
  range with no VLAN defined; none says so in words.  Two committed
  captures change (an Arista MLAG peer link allowing `2-4094`:
  `vlan members 2-4094` now).  They are the only committed trunks
  that leave a VLAN out, and the VLAN 1 they gained had been written
  down in a test as an asymmetry to accept.  A test now renders such
  trunks onto every codec and reads the output back three ways.
- **A Junos text with comments that are never closed cost the square of
  its lines.**  Comments were cut out of hierarchical text by a pattern,
  run over every Junos text before its form was known; from each `/*`
  it read on for the `*/`, to the end of the text when there was none.
  8,000 set-form lines that each hold a `/*` (a third of a megabyte)
  took seven seconds, sixteen times what a quarter as many took.
  Comments are now known in the tokeniser's own walk, where a token can
  begin, and set-form is known for set-form by its first statement.  The
  search in `tests/unit/test_untrusted_text_cost.py` had not built that
  text — it writes a run after one opener, not the opener many times —
  and has one for it now.
- **One long word in a Junos line cost its square.**  The words of a
  `set` line were split by Python's `shlex`, which builds a word by
  adding a character at a time to a string it keeps, and so copies the
  word for every character of it.  A word of 400,000 characters — a
  description, a login message, in quotes or not, in either form — took
  over a second to split, and one of 1.6 MB about three minutes.  The
  words are now read in time that fits the line, by a splitter that is
  held to `shlex`'s own answers: every short line there is over the
  characters that matter, and longer lines at random, are split both
  ways and compared.  Parsing the committed Junos captures takes under
  a third of the time it did, and none of them reads differently.
- **Junos SNMPv3 users cost the square of their number.**  Each `set
  snmp v3` line found its user by reading every user so far: 32,000
  `security-to-group` lines took fifteen seconds.  The user is found by
  name now.  `tools/stanza_cost_search.py` had not reported it — at the
  sizes it reads, the time the lines took to split hid the growth — and
  with that time gone it also reported, for Junos, many addresses on
  one unit: the cost the Security entry above mends (a list of one
  record that a line adds to).  With both, it reports no Junos unit.

### Fixed

- **A hierarchical Junos config is read as a device prints it, and as
  it leaves a terminal.**  The hierarchical output of `show
  configuration` begins `## Last commit: ...` and `version
  21.4R3.15;`, and marks its secrets `## SECRET-DATA`.  The parser
  read the hierarchical form only if it began with a block: with the
  `version` line first the text was taken for set-form, where no line
  of it is a statement, and the config was read as empty — a job that
  rendered nothing and gave no reason.  A `## SECRET-DATA` marker was
  read as words of a statement (`set system login user admin
  authentication ## SECRET-DATA`), and that put every block after it
  one level out: in a small config the next user was written outside
  `login` and lost, and the `snmp` block was not read at all.  No
  probe knew the form, so detection offered no codec for it.  And the
  list of what was not translated was empty for it: the Tier-3
  detector was handed the text as it came, and its patterns begin
  `set`, so a firewall's filters, NAT and policies were dropped with
  no row to say so.

  Read now: comments — `#` where a statement can begin, `/* */` where
  a word can, and nowhere else (`member ge-0/*/*;` and a group's
  `<*/*>` were cut as comments, with every block up to the next
  `*/`); statements ahead of the first block; the lines of the
  session a capture was copied from (`{master:0}`, the prompt with or
  without its command, `[edit]`, a pager's `---(more)---`), a
  Markdown fence, a byte-order mark, carriage returns; the tags a
  device prints (`inactive:`, `protect:`) and the operators of a load
  file, which no device prints (`replace:`, `active:`, `unprotect:`;
  a statement under `delete:` is left out and listed); a block with
  nothing in it; what `display max-depth` elides.  Both forms list
  the same Tier-3 sections.  A `}` that closes nothing, and a `/*`
  opened after the first block and never closed, are refused with a
  sentence, where the read used to end there in silence, and a
  missing `;` before a `}` no longer closes two blocks.  (A `/*`
  left open ahead of the first block is not refused: the text is
  then not taken for the hierarchical form at all.)  The rows for
  statements left out are bounded: statements that read alike share
  a row that counts them, and past two hundred rows one last row
  counts the rest.  Detection offers Junos for the form: its
  last-commit line counts beside a second sign of Junos (by itself
  the line is a comment, and a page of prose that quotes it is not
  claimed), and so do two of `version X;`, `system {` and `host-name
  X;`.

  Measured on 18 public `show configuration` captures as they were
  fetched, none of them committed: before, none was read (17 came out
  as an empty config, one was refused, and detection offered a codec
  for none); now each gives the tree its `display set` form gives.
  0 of 2,998 digests of the committed captures differ from before,
  and detection is unchanged for every file under `tests/fixtures`.

  Not read: the wildcards of an interface-range `member` and of a
  group (`<*>`) are not expanded — each is an interface of that
  name, in both forms; a `member-range` is not read at all, so the
  ports it names get nothing of the range; and `apply-groups
  "${node}"` is not resolved.  Every committed capture is set-form:
  the hierarchical reader is held by built configs, each beside its
  set form typed by hand.
- **A deactivated Junos statement is not translated as if it were in
  force.**  `deactivate interfaces ge-0/0/2` (`inactive: ge-0/0/2 {`
  in the hierarchical form) marks a statement the device holds and
  does not run.  The parser skipped the `deactivate` line and read
  the `set` lines under it, so an interface the source had switched
  off came out with its addresses on the target, in a job that said
  nothing; in the hierarchical form it became an interface named
  `inactive:`.  The statement and everything under it is now left
  out and listed with what was not translated, as `inactive:
  <path>`; the banner says in a sentence that such a row is not
  something to apply by hand, and does not count it among the
  sections that are.  The row names the statement and never a
  secret: a path is cut after the word that names one (`inactive:
  snmp community ...`), and a leaf is named without its value.  What
  an applied group or an interface-range would give to a deactivated
