  path is left out with it — no Juniper page was found that says so
  in as many words; batfish reads it this way — and a group whose
  every line was left out is no longer applied.  A text whose only
  rows are of this kind is not taken for a recognised config: the
  job is `partial` and says why.  **If a Junos config with
  deactivated statements was translated with release 0.7.7 or
  earlier, check the output for what the source had switched off.**
  A Junos to Junos job does not write the statement back as
  inactive: it is gone from the output.  Not handled: a reference to
  a deactivated statement from one that is in force — an OSPF
  interface line; a port a routing instance still names; the member
  ports of a LAG whose own interface is deactivated, which still
  make the LAG, as a static bundle with none of its own settings.
- **The rename modal held Apply on a job the server called
  `completed`.**  A Junos config that names its VXLAN source as
  Junos does — `vtep-source-interface lo0.0`, where the interface
  is `lo0` — has two names that both read `Loopback0` on EOS, and
  they are one interface.  The modal compared the two rows' targets
  as text, counted "2 collisions", and held Apply until `lo0.0` was
  renamed or dropped, either of which breaks the VTEP source.  With
  no devices declared the job now says itself which names it wrote
  as one interface (`fused_ports`, see Changed), and the modal takes
  its word for the rows the job was made with: a pair it does not
  list is not marked, counted or held.  Two rows given one name in
  the fields before Apply are in no job yet, and hold Apply as they
  did.  With a port plan on screen nothing changes.
- **A translation changed port names nobody had mapped, and put a
  sub-interface on its parent port or left it behind.**  Every job
  runs the port translator on each name no rename-map entry decides
  (an absent `port_rename_map` is read as `{}`): the source codec
  classifies the name and the target codec writes what it was told.

  *Between two configs of one vendor* that round trip is not the
  identity on several codecs' own names (AOS-S, IOS-XE CLI, OS10,
  FortiOS, Junos and VyOS, over the committed inputs), so a job
  that said `completed`
  came back with names changed and ports missing.  Of the 112
  committed captures and kitchen sinks, 20 did: Junos `fxp0` and
  `me0` as `em0`; FortiOS `dmz`, `modem` and `fortilink` as `dmz1`,
  `modem1` and `fortilink1`; IOS `Ethernet0/0` as `FastEthernet0/0`;
  a Catalyst's `Mgmt-vrf` port and every Dell OS10 breakout lane
  (`ethernet1/1/1:1`) **dropped**; a Junos tagged unit `ge-0/0/1.54`
  written onto `ge-0/0/1` — `unit 54` and its `vlan-id` gone, its
  address on unit 0 — and every per-instance loopback unit `lo0.N`
  onto `lo0`, one unit that several routing instances then claimed;
  both `vif`s of a VyOS port gone with their addresses.  Now a name
  nobody mapped **stands**: with no entry, the output of such a job
  is the output of parse and render alone.

  *Across vendors* no classifier keeps a unit.  A Junos or VyOS
  sub-interface was written under its PORT's name (`interface
  Ethernet1` twice, the tag on the second), and an IOS-XE, EOS, NX-OS
  or IOS-XR one stayed in the other vendor's config under its own
  (`set interfaces GigabitEthernet0/0/1.54 unit 0 ...`).  Now a
  sub-interface **goes where its port goes, with its unit**:
  `ge-0/0/1.54` is `Ethernet1.54` with its `encapsulation dot1q`,
  and `GigabitEthernet0/0/1.54` is `ge-0/0/1` `unit 54` with its
  `vlan-id`.  It is dropped with a port that is dropped (listed in
  `port_drops`, with a warning each), and it follows an entry of a
  rename map that moves or drops its port — it stayed on the port's
  old name, or brought a dropped port back.  That holds for a unit
  typed in another letter case than its port (`interface
  gigabitethernet0/0/1.54` under `interface GigabitEthernet0/0/1`)
  where the source platform's names have no case.  With both devices
  declared it follows the port it was PAIRED with across vendors too,
  and `port_mapping_plan.sub_interfaces` says where each went; there
  the units of a port were given one name between them and all but
  one dropped.

  A unit's 802.1Q tag is not in its name: it travels in the parsed
  tree.  A unit that went with its port and has none there — the
  AOS-CX and OS10 parsers read no tag for a sub-interface, and a
  config may state none — is written as an interface with no VLAN,
  on a target that would have carried the tag, and there is no tag
  for the validation report to list.  The job says it: one warning
  for each such unit (`... went with its port to 'Ethernet1.54'
  with no 802.1Q tag ...`), and with both devices declared the unit
  is recorded in `port_mapping_plan.untagged_units` instead of
  `sub_interfaces`, stays among the names that need a decision, and
  the job is `partial` until an entry names it.

  With both devices declared two more kinds of unit go where their
  port goes and are not counted as having followed: one typed in
  another letter case than its port, and a unit of a unit
  (`ge-0/0/1.54.2`).  The plan takes a name for a unit of a port
  only where the name spells the port as the config does.  It
  records each in `port_mapping_plan.unvouched_units` with the name
  it has in the output, says in a line that it moved with its port
  and why the plan does not vouch for it, and holds the job
  `partial` until an entry names it.  In the rename modal the row
  of such a unit, and of one that went without a tag, says the
  same, and a row an entry of yours decided says that.  An entry
  that names a sub-interface onto a unit of a port the target lists
  (`Ethernet1.54`) is not reported as a target the device does not
  list: that is where the plan's own line says to put it.

  **Re-check a config translated with 0.7.7 or earlier**, and
  translate it again, if either holds:

  - source and target were the same vendor.  Compare the interface
    names of the output with the input's.  Each difference above was
    listed in the job's `port_renames` or `port_drops`, which a
    client that read only `status` did not see;
  - the source had sub-interfaces (`<port>.<unit>`, a Junos `unit N`
    other than 0, a VyOS `vif`) and the target was another vendor.
    Look for two stanzas of one interface, a missing `encapsulation
    dot1q` or `vlan-id`, and an interface under the source vendor's
    name.

  What is as it was.  A unit of a **loopback** across vendors is
  still put on the target's loopback beside `lo0`, with the warning
  that two names share it (and, with no devices declared, in a job
  that is `partial` for it: see Changed).  Three kinds of unit are
  not sent after
  their port across vendors and are left to the source classifier,
  as they were — which leaves a name it does not know under its
  source name, with a warning (and, with no devices declared, in a
  job that is `partial` for it: see Changed): a unit of a
  **management port** —
  one its name says is one (EOS `Management1.5`), and one its parser
  marks from context (the Catalyst port in `Mgmt-vrf`); a unit of a
  port the source classifier does not know (a channelized Junos
  `xe-0/0/6:2.10`); and an interface **numbered 0** (a hand-written
  `interface Gi0/0/1.0`, or `.00`), which would be the port's own
  unit 0 on Junos.  Nor is a name that ends in more than ten
  digits sent after its port across vendors — no grammar read here
  numbers a sub-interface that high, and FortiOS and VyOS make a
  VLAN id of the number — so it is left as it was, like any name
  the classifier does not know.  A target with no routed sub-interface (AOS-S, AOS-CX,
  OS10, RouterOS, OPNsense, IOS-XE over NETCONF) gets an interface
  named `<port>.<unit>` without the tag; where the parsed source
  holds a tag the validation report lists it and the job is
  `partial`.  A unit now goes with a port the translator drops,
  where it stayed behind (NX-OS sub-interfaces onto AOS-S, which has
  no name for `Ethernet1/1`).  And Junos `vlan-tagging` on the parent
  port was read and written on no path (it is written now: a
  sub-interface's tag statement is read whole, above).

  One more thing to check on an output with sub-interfaces.  VyOS
  and FortiOS take the VLAN id from the NUMBER in the interface's
  name (`vif <unit>`, `set vlanid <unit>`), so a source unit whose
  number is not its tag — IOS `GigabitEthernet0/0/1.54` with
  `encapsulation dot1Q 300` — comes out tagged 54; both list the tag
  as unsupported, so the job is `partial`.  From a source whose
  parser reads no tag the same number is written, and it is the
  warning above that says so.

  **A job now lists the names that are no hardware port.**  A LAG, a
  VLAN interface, a loopback or a tunnel had a row in the rename
  modal only when the job renamed it — between two configs of one
  vendor that was a rename in letter case (`trk1` to `Trk1`) — or a
  "could not classify" warning quoted it.  A job from a vendor to
  itself does neither now, so such a name would have had no row
  and could have been renamed only through the API.  Every job
  carries `source_other_names` beside `source_ports`: the names the
  port translator rewrites that are not hardware ports.  The modal
  draws a row for each that nothing else gave one, in a section of
  its own ("Other names in the config") after the ports, with the
  field and the drop / keep link every row has; a config that is
  one loopback opens the modal.

  No codec is touched: every parsed tree and every bare render of
  the committed fixtures is unchanged, and so are the cross-mesh
  results.  Of 1,443 plan jobs over those fixtures (each onto each
  codec, an empty map) 126 differ in a name or the output and 36
  more in their warnings alone; of 2,522 replayed on the real
  captures with port maps built from each capture's own names (its
  ports rotated, two ports given names of the operator's own, one
  port dropped) 183 and 65.  In every one the code as it was, given
  one explicit entry per name that ended elsewhere, produces the
  same names and the same output, and every such name is a unit or
  a same-vendor name nobody mapped; no job's status changes, and
  the four demo scenarios are byte-identical.  (Every job also
  carries the new `source_other_names`, which is left out of that
  comparison and checked on each for what it should hold.)  New:
  `tests/unit/migration/test_units_follow_their_port.py`, which
  compares the translator's output with something it had no hand in
  — the bare pipeline's output for every committed input, and each
  sub-interface found in the output by its address, from each of
  the six grammars that name one onto every codec.  The guards that
  were there compared one output of the translator with another.

- **An AOS-S LAG is one name, not two.**  The device writes a LAG
  `trk1` where it is defined and `Trk1` where a VLAN lists it or an
  `interface Trk1` stanza configures it, and both spellings were kept.
  Every `/plan` request runs the port translator (an absent
  `port_rename_map` is read as `{}`), so every job for such a config
  carried `multiple source ports map to 'Trk1' (sources: Trk1, trk1)
  ... their VLAN membership will be merged`, with nothing merged; onto
  any other vendor `port_renames` had a key for each spelling, which
  the rename modal drew as two rows aimed at one target, counted as a
  collision, and would not apply until one was dropped; and an entry
  of a rename map for one spelling left the other where it was — a
  LAG no VLAN listed, or a VLAN listing a LAG nothing defined, in a
  job that said nothing.  The AOS-S parser now writes a LAG one way,
  `trk<n>`, wherever it reads one — whatever letter case a line has
  it in, and whether or not its `trunk` line is in the text — so there
  is one name: one key, one row, and a drop or a new name takes the
  whole LAG.  The text an AOS-S config comes back as is unchanged
  (`trunk 51-52 trk1 lacp`, `tagged Trk1`, `interface Trk1`): the
  renderer writes each form where the device does.  A spelling no
  device prints (`tagged TRK1`) comes back in the device's form.  A
  second `interface` stanza for an interface goes on with the first,
  and a second `trunk` line for a LAG adds its ports to the first:
  one record each, as the device reads them, with an address the
  second stanza states again kept once.  A next hop that names the
  LAG (`ipv6 route <prefix> Trk1`) is read in the one spelling too,
  so the route goes where the LAG goes.
- **A rename-map key in another letter case reaches its port** where
  the source platform's names have no case: `Trk1`, `trk1` and `TRK1`
  are all the LAG the config calls `trk1`.  It was "does not exist in
  the parsed config; entry ignored".  Only where the config writes
  the name one way and that spelling has no entry of its own; of two
  keys that are spellings of one name the first is taken, and the
  other is reported as another spelling unless the two entries agree.
  The same with both devices declared: the key replaces the pairing's
  entry for that port, and the plan counts the port as decided.  On
  FortiOS and RouterOS, where an operator chooses interface names, a
  key is still the name exactly, and `DMZ` and `dmz` are still two
  interfaces.
- **One port name written in two letter cases counts as one source**
  where the source platform's names have no case (a hardware port
  typed `a1` beside the device's `A1`), and if the two spellings do
  not end in one place the job now says so: `... are one name on
  aruba_aoss, written in more than one letter case, and do not end
  together`.
- **Two final names that differ only in letter case are one port** on
  a target whose names have no case, and the source ports sent there
  are reported, all of them (`multiple source ports map to 'Trk1'
  (also written 'trk1': one port on aruba_aoss)`), and written as
  one stanza.  They were grouped by the exact
  string: an entry that named the LAG as the device prints it in a
  VLAN's list (`{"5": "Trk1"}`), where the config's own name for it
  is `trk1` — or, from another vendor, as `trk1`, where the AOS-S
  formatter writes `Trk1` — put a port on the LAG in a job that said
  nothing.

- **Target profiles that named ports the device does not have.**  A port
  id picked from a target profile in the rename modal is written verbatim
  into the generated config, so a wrong id is a config that names a
  non-existent port.  A registry audit found a wrong port name or count in
  a third of the shipped profiles.  Each is now corrected -- from a capture
  committed here, from the vendor's own documentation, or from public
  real-device output of the exact model -- or removed.  Every replacement
  was checked against its sources by a second reader before landing.

  - **Aruba 2930F** (all four).  Uplinks were `1/A1`-`1/A4` on a switch
    with no module slot; they are `49`-`52` (`25`-`28` on the 24-port),
    continuing the access numbering.  The profiles now describe the
    standalone switch -- bare `1`..`52` -- which is the factory default and
    what the committed JL260A capture shows.  Also: `2930F-24G` was
    labelled JL258A (the 8-port model; it is JL253A), `2930F-48G` gave the
    1G-SFP JL260A 10G uplinks, `2930F-48G-PoEP` declared 2 uplinks of 4,
    and all four capped trunk groups at 24 where HPE documents 60.
  - **Aruba 3810M** (both).  The module list offered JL084A as "4x 40G
    QSFP+" and JL085A as "1x 40G QSFP+".  JL084A is the 3810M *stacking*
    module and JL085A a 250 W power supply.  The real flexible modules
    modelled are JL083A (4x SFP+) and JL078A (1x QSFP+); the 48G chassis is
    JL074A, not JL076A.
  - **Aruba CX 6300M.**  Filed under `aruba_aoss` with AOS-S ids
    (`1/1-1/48`, `1/A1-1/A4`) and `vsx-stacking`.  It is an AOS-CX switch:
    now `aruba_aoscx`, `1/1/1`-`1/1/48` + `1/1/49`-`1/1/52`, VSF, JL661A.
    Its LAG prefix is `lag ` with a trailing space, because AOS-CX writes
    `interface lag 1` and `lag1` is not a name the codec recognises.
  - **Cisco Catalyst 9300.**  C9300-24UX downlinks were
    `GigabitEthernet1/0/N`; they are `TenGigabitEthernet1/0/N` (0 of 24
    matched the committed capture).  C9300-48UXM listed 48 x
    `GigabitEthernet` at 5G; it is `TwoGigabitEthernet1/0/1-36` +
    `TenGigabitEthernet1/0/37-48`.  All six capped EtherChannels at 48;
    the limit is 128.
  - **Juniper.**  QFX5120-48Y used `xle-0/0/N` -- a QFabric 40G type no
    QFX5120 port carries; the factory-default names are `xe-0/0/0-47`.
    EX4600-40F listed its fixed QSFP+ ports as `et-0/1/0-3` (an expansion
    module's ports); they are `et-0/0/24-27`.  Both said `me0` for
    management; it is `em0` / `em1`.  All three profiles gave 4094 VLANs
    under a source string naming a datasheet that prints 4093 / 4091 /
    4093; the QFX5120 said 128 LAGs where its datasheet says 80.
  - **Arista** (all four).  QSFP / OSFP cages were bare `EthernetN`; EOS
    names a multi-lane cage `EthernetN/1`.  The 7060CX-32S profile omitted
    its two SFP+ ports, and the 7280CR3-32P4's 400G ports are OSFP, not
    QSFP-DD.
  - **MikroTik CRS310-8G+2S+.**  Marked all eight copper ports PoE with a
    "170 W budget"; the switch has no PoE-out.
  - **Aruba AOS-S local-user ceiling.**  The six AOS-S profiles declared
    `max_local_users: 16`, which is not a vendor figure and drove a
    fit-check banner that was confidently wrong.  Now unset, so that banner
    is hidden for those targets.

  Over a dozen test assertions pinned the wrong values and moved in the
  same change, so they now guard the corrections instead of the errors.
- **A request the server could not echo was a 500.**  A validation
  error echoes the rejected value.  A value that cannot be written as
  UTF-8 (a lone surrogate, sent as the JSON escape `"\ud800"`) made
  that echo fail, on every endpoint; so did a rename-map name holding
  one, when the job that echoes it was serialised.  The 422 body is
  now written ASCII-escaped — same status, same `Content-Type`, and it
  parses to the same JSON — with a `NaN` or `Infinity` echoed as text
  so the body is always strict JSON, and such a rename-map name is
  refused with a 422 — in any of the four name-keyed rename maps, and
  whether or not the name would have been echoed: a request whose
  entry matched nothing in the config used to be answered.
- **One unreadable target-profile file stopped the application.**  A
  file under `target_profiles/` that is not UTF-8, is a directory, or
  has a key that is not a string is now logged and skipped, like one
  that fails validation.
- **A port could be deleted because another name was dropped.**  The
  port translator removed a name the target cannot express by
  matching it AFTER renaming, which also removed a different port that
  had just been renamed onto that name.  Such names are now removed
  before anything is renamed, and the warning that called the two
  ports "merged" is no longer raised for a name that was dropped;
  where two or more ports were renamed onto that name they now
  survive, and the translator's duplicate-name warning names them.  No
  committed capture is affected unless the request's own
  `port_rename_map` renames a port onto a name the target cannot
  express.
- **Reset all did not reach the server.**  Apply re-sends the previous
  request with the current overrides added, and a VLAN, local-user or
  SNMP map — or a target profile — that had been sent once and was
  then cleared stayed in the request and was applied again.  Cleared
  values are now removed from the request.
- **The SNMPv3 pane was not redrawn after Apply**, so it showed the
  previous job's rows until the modal was reopened.
- **A free-text port override could not be typed.**  The rename table
  was rebuilt on every key, and the field being typed in with it: typed
  `17`, the field held `1` and the focus was gone.  The table is now
  rebuilt when the field is left, at a moment when that cannot take a
  control out from under a click, and the control that had the focus
  has it again afterwards.
- **Apply could be disabled without a word.**  Two rows that end on
  one target name have always held it; the button now says why, beside
  itself and in its title.
- **Why an Apply was refused was gone in four seconds.**  The server's
  words were in a toast and nowhere else.  They are now the status
  line in the modal's footer, in red, until something in the modal is
  changed or the footer has its next thing to say; so is an Apply the
  server never answered.
- **Nothing paired was shown as a pairing.**  With a source device
  chosen by hand that is not the one the config is of, no port is
  paired: every name is "not on the source device".  After *Accept as
  shown* and Apply the strip was green, headed "Ports paired by
  position" over "0 paired", and the job `completed`.  The heading is
  now "No port was paired by position" and the strip amber.  And with
  a target device declared and **no** source device, Apply said
  "Applied. Rendered output refreshed." over an output that kept every
  port name: the strip now warns, with the count and the first of the
  names the target does not have, and the footer says the ports were
  not paired.  The footer is read from the strip, so the two cannot
  disagree; under a red strip it no longer says "Applied." and stops,
  and the toast is green only when the strip has nothing to say.
- **An override for a port named `__proto__` was shown and not sent.**
  RouterOS and FortiOS let an operator name a port anything.  The row
  showed the entry; the request was built by copying the map onto an
  ordinary object, where that key sets the prototype and makes no
  entry.  Entries are now copied one by one, to the request and to
  what the browser remembers.
- **An Apply could fail to end.**  Its request outlived the job it
  was pressed for and held the button for the next one; a request the
  server never answered was never given up; an answer the page could
  not read (a proxy's own page with a 200) left the footer empty, and
  a translation that failed read "Applied."  The request is now given
  up when its job is replaced and after two minutes, and each of
  those says "Not applied" in the footer, with why, and leaves the
  output as it was.
- **A device chosen, and the table still asking for names by hand.**
  The table's redraw waits while a mouse button is down, and a list
  the browser draws outside the page can take the release with it.
  The pointer moving with no button down, or a key, now ends the
  wait.
- **A toast could take a click meant for what was under it.**  On
  every page a toast is drawn above everything, and its tint lets
  what is under it show through.  A three-line error lay over the
  rename modal's Cancel and Apply at a laptop's height and swallowed
  both for as long as it showed.  A toast is a message and now takes
  no click.
- **A new translation left the open modal describing the last one.**
  The modal does not block the page.  Translating again behind it now
  redraws all of it from the new job.
- **The rename table listed an AOS-S config's ports as the config
  first mentions them** — 1, 48–52, 35–47, 2… for a 48-port
  switch, since AOS-S names its ports VLAN by VLAN.  Where the source
  device is declared (it is read from an AOS-S config by itself), the
  rows are in the device's own port order before Apply as well as
  after it.
- **Smaller things in the rename table.**  The rail's ports count is
  the number of rows drawn (it was one more for a config with two
  warnings about one name); a warning that quotes a *target* port no
  longer becomes a row for it; a name of any length wraps instead of
  widening the table; a section you opened stays open when the table
  is redrawn.
- **A VLAN, user or SNMP override could not be typed.**  The table
  that was rebuilt on every key was mended for ports only.  The VLAN,
  local-user, SNMP-community and SNMPv3-user tables still were:
  `private9` typed at a keyboard was `p`, the focus was gone, and `p`
  was the community Apply sent.  Each of them is now rebuilt when its
  field is left, the control that had the focus has it again
  afterwards, and a rebuild waits for a mouse button that is down, so
  "drop" pressed straight out of a field is not lost.
- **A VLAN id out of range was shown, and another one sent.**  A
  number that is no VLAN id was not stored, and the field was left
  showing it: after `409` and then `4095` the screen said 4095 and
  Apply sent 409.  Such a number now takes the place of the entry
  it was typed over: nothing is sent for that VLAN until it is put
  right, the field goes on holding it with a red edge, says why in
  its title, and is invalid to a screen reader.
- **A user called `constructor` opened with an override nobody had
  typed.**  The override maps of the VLAN, user and SNMP panes were
  ordinary objects, in which a name every object has — a local
  user `constructor`, an SNMPv3 user `toString` — reads as
  something inherited.  They are keyed by the names alone now, as the
  port map is, and so is what each pane reads of the job that came
  back.
- **Overrides kept for one config were sent for another of the same
  host name.**  The browser remembers your overrides by source codec,
  target codec and host name.  A second config with that host name
  opened with the first one's entries; those for names it does not
  have had no row to show them, and Apply sent them all the same.  An
  entry for a name the config on the page has no row for is now left
  out, and the footer says how many were.  (They are then no longer
  kept: see the known limitations.)
- **The footer's line outlived what it was about.**  It stayed until
  the next line was written: a refusal of a member number that had
  since been corrected, "4 decisions recorded — Apply to confirm"
  beside devices that had since changed, "All overrides cleared."
  beside two new overrides.  Changing anything in the modal now
  clears it; looking at another pane does not.
- **"drop" could not be reached from the keyboard.**  In every pane it
  was a piece of text with a click handler, and Tab passed it by.  It
  is a button, drawn as the link it was: Tab reaches it, and Enter or
  Space presses it.  So are the two links a ports row has while the
  job's port names are not settled, "keep this name" and the second
  "drop"; each is gone once it is pressed, and the focus is then on
  the row's own link and not at the top of the page.  And Apply
  pressed from the keyboard has the
  focus again when its answer is in: the button is disabled while the
  request is out, which left the focus at the top of the page.
- **A port's name typed on a closed list chose another port.**  A
  closed list takes a name key by key, and the table was rebuilt at
  each key: the list was a new one and the name began again, so `47`
  typed chose port 7.  The table is now rebuilt when the typing has
  stopped or the list is left.
- **Reading the source device from the config had no end.**  The
  request had no time limit, the modal said nothing while it was out
  — the source read "(not declared)" and then filled itself in —
  and a text that was never answered for was never asked about again.
  The line under *Source device* now says "Reading the source device
  from the config …", gives up after twenty seconds and says so, and
  the config is asked about again the next time the modal opens.
  Model families that fail to load under an open modal are said at
  once, not when it is next opened.
- **The strip above the table was announced again at every key.**  It
  is a polite live region, and it was emptied and refilled with every
  summary — one for each key typed in a row — though it said
  what it had said.  It is now replaced only when what it says
  changes; *Accept as shown* keeps the focus through a redraw that
  leaves it alone.  A strip that cannot be drawn is taken away, not
  left saying what the last one said.
- **More small things in the rename modal.**  A long unbroken name
  under the strip or in a device note wraps: it used to slide the
  device rows, the notes and the strip out of sight to the left.  A
  closed list of target ports is wide enough to read
  (`sfp-sfpplus11` and `sfp-sfpplus12` were both `sfp-sfpplu` beside
  a remark).  Target profiles that arrive after a family model was
  chosen no longer leave the vendor list reading "(none)" over it,
  and they reach the source list of a modal that is already open.  A
  port kept under its own name reads "(kept as it is, by your own
  entry)", not "needs override".  A space typed just before the
  table is redrawn is still there (`my port` came out `myport`).  A
  bay named like `constructor` in a family file of your own no longer
  stops the device note and leaves the strip on "Checking the device
  …".
- **`detect-deployment` repeated a port name at any length.**  The
  detector's own notes are capped.  The note added afterwards, about
  port names the proposed device does not have, repeated the first
  eight of them whole, and the names in `missing_ports` had no bound
  either: a name of a hundred thousand characters was a note of eight
  hundred thousand.  A name is now cut to 128 characters in
  `missing_ports` and to 32 in the note, and ends `…` where it was
  cut.
- **The ports fit-check banner reappeared on the VLAN and user panes.**
  Editing an override on another pane refreshed the summary, which
  re-rendered the ports banner there.  It is ports-pane only again.
- **A module SKU reached the fit-check banner unescaped.**  The SKU is a
  profile-YAML dict key and profile YAML is operator-authorable; it is now
  escaped like every other profile string the modal renders.

### Added

- **Source and target device pickers in the rename modal.**  The
  ports pane of the Interface rename modal now has a *Source device*
  row and a *Target device* row.  Choose a model — from a model
  family, with its deployment mode, the module in each bay and its
  stack members, or a flat profile where no family describes the
  device — and **Apply** pairs the two port lists by position.
  - The source device is read from the config where the config
    states it, and the modal shows the lines it was read from, each as
    far as its part number.  A device you choose or edit yourself is
    said not to have been checked against the port names the config
    uses.
  - Under the source device, and under a target chosen from a model
    family, a note says what was declared, how many ports it has and
    their first and last name, how well those names are established,
    and every caveat.  A bay nobody stated is counted as empty, and
    said.  A target chosen from a flat profile keeps the profile
    notice it always had, which states no port count.
  - The table becomes the pairing: each source port, the target port
    it was paired with and the position that decided it, a flag where
    the target port is slower or has no PoE, and a row for every
    name that has no place on the target or is not a port of the
    source device.  Names that need a decision are marked and counted
    on the strip above the table.
  - **The strip counts what happened, not what was planned.**  A
    paired port you dropped or sent elsewhere is counted as that, an
    unplaced port you gave a place is counted as placed, and PoE or
    speed lost is counted for the ports that are on the ports that
    lack it.  Its colour is the job's: it stays amber until the job
    that comes back needs no decision.  It also says when a logical
    name was given a port name the target does not have, when an
    entry of yours is a name the target does not list, when a route
    was left naming a port that moved, and when a RouterOS target's
    output has no line that finds a port by its hardware.  A RouterOS
    port the config names says which port of the model it is; a port
    given a name that is not a port of the target says which target
    port its hardware is on.
  - **Accept as shown** records the outcome on screen as your decision
    for every undecided name.  It is a decision about *that pairing*:
    press Apply with other devices declared and it is forgotten, so a
    port that had no place is not kept dropped once it has one; and it
    is not remembered across a page load.  A row you then change by
    hand is your own, and is.
  - A declaration the server would refuse — a member number the mode
    does not have — is said in red under the device, and is still sent
    with Apply: the server refuses the request in words and the output
    is left as it was.  (It used to be left out without a word, and
    Apply then reported success for a translation by name shape.)  A
    preview that could not be fetched at all is said to be unchecked,
    and the server compiles the device itself.
  - Where the name-shape translation put two ports on one target name,
    Apply is no longer held once both devices are declared: the
    pairing by position is what puts each on a port of its own.  A
    collision made by your own entries still holds it, and says so.
  - A stack can be declared on both sides, a member to a row; the
    rows pair in order, and where that puts a member on a member of
    another number the strip and each port's row say so.  More than
    four members fold under their count; a stack set aside by
    choosing a mode in which a device stands alone comes back with a
    stacking mode, and choosing another model for the first member
    keeps the rest.
  - Everything above the table scrolls by itself, so a stack of ten on
    each side leaves the table and the Apply button where they were.
  - A target device belongs to the target codec it was chosen for; a
    translation to another codec starts with none.
  - A same-vendor translation (Aruba to Aruba, say) renames no name
    by itself, and the table listed only the names a rename or a
    warning mentioned — none at all for a clean config, which read
    "No port names recognised in the translated output".  It now also
    lists every hardware port the config uses, and after them the
    names that are no port (a LAG, a VLAN interface, a loopback).
- **Model-to-model port mapping (API).**  Declare the device a config
  came from and the device it is going to, and ports are paired by
  *position* instead of being guessed from the shape of their names.  A
  standalone Aruba 2930F-48G onto a 2930M-48G with an SFP+ module in a
  one-member stack: `1`..`48` become `1/1`..`1/48` and the built-in
  uplinks `49`..`52` become the module's `1/A1`..`1/A4` — 52 of 52, on
  the committed real capture.  Before this a same-vendor translation
  renamed a port only where the request spelled it out in
  `port_rename_map`; nothing was derived.
  - `POST /api/v1/migration/plan` (and every per-pane endpoint) accepts
    `source_deployment` / `target_deployment`: a model, its fitted
    modules, and the deployment mode that decides its port names.  A
    device no family describes yet can be declared by a target-profile
    key instead (`source_profile` / `source_module`, with the existing
    `target_profile` / `target_module`).
  - A stack can be declared on both sides.  A member states its
    number with `id`.  Members pair in the order the two declarations
    list them, not by member number, and the plan says in a line
    where that put a member on a member of another number — in one
    line for a renumbering (1, 3 onto 1, 2), in another, with what to
    do about it, for a crossing (2, 1 onto 1, 2), which holds no job
    either.  A port never changes member to find a place, and a source
    member with no target member in its position is dropped port by
    port and reported.
  - The pairing comes back as data on `MigrationJob.port_mapping_plan`:
    every pair, every source port with no place on the target, every
    name in the config that is not a port of the declared source, what
    each declaration resolved to, and how the run came out
    (`unresolved_ports`, `displaced`, `fused`, `off_target`,
    `landed_off_target`, `stale_next_hops`, `emptied_lags`).
  - A source access or uplink port with no place on the target is
    **dropped and reported** — never moved onto a spare port of another
    kind, and never left in the output under its old name, where on a
    same-vendor pair it could be the name another port was just mapped
    to.  A management port with no management port in the target model
    is the exception: it is left to the ordinary port translation,
    which keeps it where the target has a form for out-of-band
    management (the `oobm` block on AOS-S).  It still needs the
    operator's decision — netcanon does not know whether the target
    device has a management interface at all.
  - **No hardware port shares a target name with another interface
    unless the operator asks for it.**  A name the pairing does not
    decide — that management port, a name that is not a port of the
    declared source, or a logical interface such as an aggregate —
    can come back from the ordinary translation as a port the pairing
    already assigned.  The finished run is checked for that over
    every name the config references, and such a name is dropped and
    reported (`displaced`) instead of being merged into another port.
    A logical interface that is given a port-shaped name the target
    does NOT list — a data port's or a management port's (`em1`,
    `oobm`) — collides with nothing and is not dropped; it is
    listed (`landed_off_target`) and asks for a decision, since its
    config is on a port the device does not have.
    Two logical interfaces the ordinary translation puts on one name
    (two loopbacks, on a target with one loopback form) are still
    only warned about, as before.
  - Names are compared as each platform tells interfaces apart.  On
    AOS-S or IOS `1/a1` is the port `1/A1`.  On FortiOS and RouterOS,
    where an operator chooses interface names as free text, `DMZ` and
    `dmz` are two interfaces.  On a platform that names every
    interface itself in lower case (Junos, OPNsense — and VyOS, which
    cannot be declared yet) another case is the same port misspelt,
    and is treated as that port.  Each codec states which its
    platform is.
  - Between two configs of the same codec a sub-interface
    (`ge-0/0/0.54`) follows its parent port.
  - RouterOS keeps a port's factory name beside the name an operator
    gives it, and finds a port on the device by the first.  With both
    devices declared, every port the mapping places on a RouterOS
    target that the config has an interface for is looked up by the
    port of that device it is on
    (`set [ find default-name=sfp-sfpplus2 ] name=core-a`) — from
    any source vendor, and whether or not the source config stated a
    factory name for the port.  (A port the config names only as a
    LAG member or in a route has no line of its own; under the name
    the mapping gives it, the target port's, it needs none.)  A name
    the operator gave a port in a RouterOS config is kept, unless it
    is itself a port of the target.  An entry of `port_rename_map` whose
    target is a port of the declared target moves the port there; one
    whose target is not gives the port that NAME, changes nothing
    about its hardware, and is said in a line of the plan.  Onto
    another vendor, where a port has one name, a port the operator
    named takes the name of the port it was paired with.  Such a port
    goes by the name the config uses everywhere — in the plan, in the
    job's lists, as the key of a map entry (an entry keyed by its
    factory name is taken for it) — and the plan says which port of
    the model it is (`labelled_ports`) and where its hardware ended
    (`target_hardware`; `source_hardware` for a port nobody placed
    that the output still finds by the factory name it had).  A config
    that looks two
    interfaces up by one factory name is not paired at all.  Without
    devices declared nothing about a factory name changes: an entry
    names the port, as it always has.
  - On a RouterOS target the finished output is read back, and each
    port is judged by its own line.  A port that no line of its own
    looks up by its hardware is listed (`unbound_ports`) and the job
    is `partial`.  Three ways: RouterOS output has no Ethernet line
    for a port whose name reads as a VLAN, a bridge, a LAG or a
    loopback (`bond1`, `bridge-uplink`, `vlan-trunk`, `lo0`), whoever
    chose the name; a placed port the config has no interface for,
    given a name that is no port of the target, is written under that
    name where it is referenced (`slaves=`, `gateway=`) and defined
    nowhere — for most names that hold white space or a comma and
    cannot be read back whole as well; and of two ports of another
    vendor given one name only the first is found.
  - A static route left naming, as next hop, an interface that has
    another name in the output, or is gone, is listed
    (`stale_next_hops`), and the job is `partial`.  No entry rewrites
    the route: correct it in the output, or keep the names it uses —
    on a RouterOS target an entry that gives each such port its old
    name (`{"ether3": "ether3"}`) leaves the route right, since a
    name does not decide a port's hardware there.  A next hop naming a port of
    the declared source that the config has no interface record for
    is listed too; a list of gateways whose members only changed
    places among themselves is not.
  - What a dropped port takes with it is listed: a LAG that lost
    members, a static route or DHCP pool that named the port, a VRRP
    track entry on an interface that stays, and a VXLAN source
    interface.
  - A run that leaves a name dropped, off-inventory or displaced, a
    management port kept, or a logical name on a port the target
    does not list, which the operator has not decided is `partial`
    rather than `completed`; so is one where the operator's own map
    points two ports at one name, one that leaves a route naming a
    port that moved, one where a port is not looked up by its
    hardware in the output, and one where no pairing could be made at
    all.
  - An entry in `port_rename_map` always wins over the pairing, on
    `/plan` and on every per-pane endpoint.  Its target is read as
    the target device spells it (`1/a1` is `1/A1`) where another
    letter case cannot be another interface — the platform has no
    case, or names every interface itself in lower case; on FortiOS
    and RouterOS it is stripped and taken as typed.  A blank target
    is ignored.
  - A declaration is checked: an unknown model, mode, bay, module or
    member id is a 422 that says what was wrong, a member id is an
    integer and nothing else, a profile's module must be one the
    profile lists, and a `target_deployment` without a source is
    refused rather than ignored.
  - `GET /api/v1/migration/model-families` lists the modelled families;
    `POST /api/v1/migration/inventory` shows the ports a declared device
    has, by name, with each port's role, position and evidence grade.
  - `POST /api/v1/migration/detect-deployment` reads the source device
    out of the config itself — the chassis part number, the modules and
    the stacking state an AOS-S config states — and returns a
    `deployment` to confirm and send back as `source_deployment`, with
    the hardware lines it was read from (each as far as its part
    number).  The proposal is checked against the port names the config
    uses, so a module the config does not state shows up as ports the
    proposed device lacks rather than as a silent wrong answer; a text
    that names no port is reported as not checked (`consistent: null`),
    not as consistent.  Every way a config can fail to yield a
    deployment is an answer whose first note is the reason, and what a
    proposal carries is capped whatever the text holds: the members,
    the evidence, the list of missing ports, the notes.  A line that
    sets out to state a member, a module or the chassis and cannot be
    read is counted in a note, and so is a list that was cut.
- **Device-model families.**  A new registry
  (`netcanon/definitions/library/model_families/`) that lists facts
  rather than names: a model's port groups, its module bays, and the
  deployment modes of its family.  A naming rule beside the vendor's
  codec turns those into names for one stated deployment.  Ships with
  the Aruba 2930F (every model HPE has shipped; standalone and VSF) and
  the Aruba 2930M (every model; each of its three uplink modules or an
  empty bay; stacking enabled and disabled).  Each model's values were
  checked against HPE's documents — and, for where the combo and Smart
  Rate ports sit, against the chassis silk-screen in product
  photographs — by a reader briefed to refute them.  One value did not
  survive: the 2930M 40G-8SR's Smart Rate ports are `1`-`8`, not
  `41`-`48`.  An operator can add families of their own under
  `model_families/` in their definitions directory; a file there
  cannot replace a shipped family, and a file that cannot be loaded is
  logged and skipped.
- **Evidence per port, with `capture` granted rather than inherited.**
  A family's naming, a model's panel and a module's port count are
  graded separately, and a port takes the weakest of the facts that
  produced it.  A committed capture grades exactly the deployment it is
  of — that model, that mode, that member id, that module — and
  nothing else: not a sibling with the same port names, not a TAA twin.
  Each claim is re-proven against its fixture on every test run — the
  fixture's ports must equal the compiled inventory — and only the
  claims that test re-proves grant the grade: a claim in an operator's
  own family file is logged and grants nothing.  Each shipped model's
  port names and roles are also pinned by hand, because a capture
  cannot show which ports are uplinks.
- **`MigrationJob.source_ports`.**  The port names a source config
  references, including ports no rename touches.  LAG names are left
  out, and so is anything the source codec marks or classifies as an
  SVI, loopback, tunnel or other logical interface, and a name only a
  route or a DHCP pool mentions unless the codec recognises it as a
  port; a sub-interface, and a pseudo-interface the codec does not
  classify, is still listed.  A RouterOS port the operator named is
  listed by that name — the one the config uses, and the key an entry
  of `port_rename_map` carries.  (A name the codec reads as a LAG or
  a loopback is left out even when it is a port's; a declared device
  pairs such a port all the same, and `port_mapping_plan.pairings`
  lists it.)
  `port_renames` records only names that changed, so for a same-vendor
  translation a client had no way to list the ports at all.
- **Provenance on target profiles.**  Optional fields record what is
  actually known about a profile's port names: `deployment_state` (the one
  state the ids describe -- a port's name depends on how the device is
  deployed, not only on its model), `evidence` (`capture` / `vendor-doc` /
  `inferred`, with `evidence_ref`), and an operator-visible `caveat`.
  `capture` is a checked claim, not a label:
  `tests/unit/migration/test_target_profile_evidence.py` parses the cited
  fixture on every run and fails unless the fixture identifies itself as
  that model, belongs to the profile's vendor, and contains every profile
  port id as a hardware port.  The graded sets are pinned, so a grade can
  neither appear nor vanish unreviewed.  Mutation-checked: fifteen
  deliberate regressions -- the four original errors re-introduced, an SVI
  and a LAG listed as ports, a profile graded against a sibling model's
  capture, a dropped or misspelt grade, a profile flagged with no caveat,
  a missing deployment state, a deleted profile re-added -- each fail.
  Three profiles carry the `capture` grade and eighteen `vendor-doc`; none
  is graded `inferred`.
- **The rename modal says what a profile's port names are worth.**  A
  notice under the fit-check banner shows the deployment state, the
  evidence grade and the caveat for the selected profile, turns amber when
  the names are unverified, and says "not yet graded" for a profile nobody
  has checked.  The definitions page lists the same per profile.  Web and
  desktop alike.
- **Rows whose auto-translated name is not a port on the selected profile
  are marked.**  Selecting a profile does not change auto-translation (see
  Known limitations), so with a standalone 2930F profile a Cisco source's
  `1/1` is a port the chosen device does not have.  Such rows are now
  amber, with "N not on profile" on the section header, until the operator
  picks a real port.
- `test_all_profiles_load` now loads every profile YAML strictly.  The
  runtime loader skips a file that fails validation, so a typo in a
  constrained field used to remove a profile from the product with every
  test green.
- A Hard Rule in `AGENTS.md`: a profile port id comes from a capture of
  that model or the vendor's documentation, never from the formatter, a
  sibling model or recall; when the right name is not established, flag
  the profile rather than swapping one plausible name for another.

### Changed

- **Where a vendor has model families, its flat profiles are under
  their own heading in the target model list.**  Four Aruba 2930F
  switches are both a model of a family and a flat profile, under the
  same words, and the list gave nothing to tell the two apart.  The
  family models now come first, as in the source list, and the
  profiles follow under "Profiles — one fixed port list".  A
  vendor with no family lists its profiles as before.
- **A job with no devices declared is `partial` when the port
  translator left a name unsettled: two names on one name, a name
  dropped because the target has none for it, or a name it could not
  read, left as the source config has it.**  A warning is not a
  status.  Such a job said what had happened in a warning line and
  in `port_renames` / `port_drops`, and said `completed`: its status
  was the validation report's alone, and the check that refuses any
  of this was made only where both devices are declared, and there
  only for hardware ports.  Now every plan request that declares
  none has its finished run read for three things:

  - **two source names on one name of the output** — the config of
    two interfaces written as one.  Any two names, a LAG or a
    loopback as much as a port, compared as each platform tells
    interfaces apart: AOS-S `1/1` and the uplink-module port `1/A1`
    both `Ethernet1`; six interfaces of a Catalyst on `Ethernet1`;
    VyOS `eth0` and `eth1` both `port1` on FortiOS, which numbers
    from 1; Junos `ae0` and `ae1` both `Port-channel1`;
  - **a name dropped** because the target has no name for it.  A
    hardware port — a management port onto a platform with no form
    for one, a breakout lane — and the sub-interfaces that went
    with it; and a logical name just the same — a loopback, a
    tunnel, a `VirtualPortGroup`, a FortiGate hardware switch
    (`internal`) with the LAN address on it.  What was configured
    on the name is not in the output;
  - **a name left as the source config has it**, because the
    translator could not read it as any kind of port (`could not
    classify port name ...; left verbatim`): IOS `GigabitEthernet1`
    (the one-number ports of a virtual router) in a Junos config,
    OPNsense `igc0`, a RouterOS interface an operator named, the
    `VlanN` interface an AOS-S VLAN's address is carried on, where
    the target calls that interface something else (`set
    interfaces Vlan10 ...` on Junos).  Whatever the output has of
    it is under the source vendor's name.  A name the translator
    left that is no foreign name on the target is not listed (see
    "What is not counted").

  The job is `partial`, `job.error` says "Port names are not settled:
  ..." (after the sentence it already had, where it was `partial` for
  the validation report), and three new fields carry the names:
  **`fused_ports`** — each shared name of the output with the source
  names that ended on it; **`unresolved_ports`** — the names that
  were dropped (`source_ports` says which are hardware ports); and
  **`untranslated_ports`** — the names left as the source has them.
  The output is unchanged: nothing is renamed or dropped that was not
  before, and the warnings are the ones the job had.

  Over the committed captures, each onto each codec with no port map,
  219 of the 589 jobs that said `completed` are `partial`.  59 of
  them list a shared name, 67 a hardware port that was dropped, 32 a
  logical name that was dropped and 112 a name left as the source
  has it (99 of those a hardware port); 44 list more than one kind.
  None is a job from a vendor to itself, no job moves the other way,
  and none to or from `failed`; 403 jobs that were already `partial`
  carry the sentence as well.  Each of the 219 is `completed` again,
  with one more request, once every listed name has an entry.

  **To settle such a job**, decide each name with an entry of
  `port_rename_map` — in the Ports pane of the rename modal, or
  through the API.  For two names on one name: a name of its own for
  all but one of them, or `null` to drop it.  For a dropped name: a
  target name, or `null`, which is you saying it is to go; an entry
  that drops a port decides its sub-interfaces with it.  For a name
  left as it was: the name it is to have on the target, or `null` —
  and where it is right on the target as it stands (a RouterOS
  interface you named `WAN`, onto FortiOS, where a name is yours to
  choose), the name ITSELF: `{"WAN": "WAN"}` is how you say so.
  Two entries of your own that point at one name are reported like
  any other two.

  **Declaring both devices settles the hardware ports among these
  names, and no others.**  Ports are then paired by position, each
  with a port of its own.  A pair of devices decides nothing about
  two loopbacks on one loopback, a tunnel that was dropped or a VLAN
  interface left under its source name: with both devices declared
  the output has them the same and the job is not held for them (see
  Known limitations).  So the job's sentence offers the devices only
  where a hardware port is among what it lists, and says so where
  they would decide only some of it.

  **If you gate on the status** (`job.status`, or the
  `X-Netcanon-Job-Status` header): on the captures above more than a
  third of the jobs that passed do not pass until their names are
  decided.  The output of such a job was no safer to apply before.
  `netcanon demo` is not changed, and one of its four scenarios is
  such a job: `opnsense__junos` leaves `igc0` and `igc1`, which are
  no names of Junos.  The demo prints the output and lists the
  names under its advisories; the API calls the same output
  `partial`.  The other three are `completed` on both —
  `aruba__arista` too: the translator leaves its `Vlan10` and
  `Vlan20` as AOS-S names them, and that is what EOS calls those
  interfaces.

  What is not counted.  A Junos reference to unit 0 of an interface
  (`lo0.0` where the interface is `lo0`) is that interface and no
  second one — unless the tree holds unit 0 as a stanza of its own
  beside its port, which is two interfaces.  A VLAN
  interface on a target that writes it from its VLAN (AOS-S) keeps
  its name by design, and is neither dropped nor left for want of a
  name.  Between two configs of one vendor nothing is listed that an
  entry of yours did not cause.

  Nor is every name the translator left a foreign name where it
  lands, and one that is not holds nothing.  Between the two
  IOS-XE codecs (CLI text and NETCONF are one platform) a name the
  CLI classifier does not read is still a name of IOS-XE.  And
  across platforms a logical name — a VLAN's interface, a loopback,
  an aggregate, a tunnel — is not listed where the target itself
  writes exactly that name for the same kind of thing: the
  `Vlan<id>` interface of an AOS-S VLAN's address is `interface
  Vlan10` on EOS, IOS-XE and NX-OS.  Over the captures that is 74
  names in 16 jobs: 56 `Vlan<id>` onto EOS, NX-OS and the two
  IOS-XE codecs, and 18 names of IOS-XE from its CLI codec to its
  NETCONF one.  Never a
  hardware port: which port of another device a port is, is what a
  declared device answers.  Never onto FortiOS or RouterOS, where
  any string is a name, nor from them, where a name is whatever was
  typed (a RouterOS `vlan100` may carry VLAN 20).  And not where
  the target only READS the spelling and writes another: OS10
  prints `vlan10`, so an AOS-S `Vlan10` is still listed there.  The
  translator's warning line names every name it left, listed or
  not.

  And one thing is still said only in a warning: a name the config
  only refers to — in a static route, a DHCP pool, a tracking entry
  or a VXLAN source — that the translator cannot read (see Known
  limitations).

  With both devices declared nothing changes: the port plan carries
  what that path found (`port_mapping_plan.fused`,
  `.unresolved_ports`), and the job's three new fields are empty
  there.

  On the migrate page the status banner shows the sentence.  The
  rename modal says above its table how many names share one, how
  many were dropped and how many were left under their source name.
  The rows the job wrote as one interface carry the collision mark; a
  dropped row and a row left under its source name carry the mark of
  a row that needs a decision, with the count on its section.  A
  dropped row has a **drop** link beside *keep verbatim* — the
  decision that it is to go — and **Accept the drops** records it
  for all of them; with a target device chosen the row's list has its
  *Drop* entry.  A row left under its source name says so, and has
  its name field, **keep this name** and **drop** (with a target
  device chosen, *Keep this name* in its list); no button keeps
  several at once.  After Apply the footer says when names are still
  not settled.  The strip sends nobody to the device pickers for
  names a pair of devices would not settle: with one device chosen
  and no hardware port among the names, it says that choosing the
  other pairs hardware ports and settles none of these; and it
  offers no pair, and no target device, for a vendor nobody has
  described a device of.

  New: `tests/unit/migration/test_run_plan_checked_names.py`.  It
  pins the count above by source codec and reason, and for every job
  that is still `completed` it reads the rendered output back with
  the target's parser and finds interfaces by their addresses: none
  may carry the addresses of two source interfaces, no interface
  that has an address may be missing, and no interface of the source
  may be one the translator's warning says it left under a foreign
  name.  Which names left are the target's own the test decides
  for itself, from the text of the output and a table typed by
  hand; how many are not listed is pinned by pair of codecs.
- **A blank target in `port_rename_map` is a 422.**  `{"mgmt0": ""}`
  (or only white space) was written into the output as an interface
  with no name — `interface ` and the port's address under it — in
  a job that said `completed`; and an entry being what settles a
  name, it would also have cleared the `partial` a dropped port now
  holds a job in.  A target that draws nothing is blank too: one
  made only of control or format characters — a zero-width space,
  a NUL, a byte-order mark — wrote an interface whose name nobody
  can see.  A name has at least one character that is neither white
  space nor one of those.  A value is a name, or `null` to drop: the
  refusal names the keys (a few, each cut short) and says so.  On
  every plan endpoint, with devices
  declared or not.  With both declared such an entry used to be set
  aside and listed in `port_mapping_plan.ignored_overrides`; a caller
  of the pipeline in Python still gets that, and one that reaches
  the translator directly has the entry skipped with a warning.
- **Every plan endpoint applies the request's `port_rename_map`.**
  The four category panes — `/plan/vlans`, `/plan/local_users`,
  `/plan/snmp`, `/plan/snmpv3` — set a posted port map aside unless
  both devices were declared, and named every port by its shape.  A
  job on one of them that is `partial` for its port names could then
  not be settled there.  They apply the map now, as `/plan`,
  `/plan/ports` and `/render` always did, so one body gives one
  status and one set of port names whichever URL it is posted to.  A
  client that posted a port map to one of those four panes and
  counted on it being ignored gets the names it asked for.  The
  other maps are as they were: a pane applies its own category and
  no other.
- **A static route whose next hop is the name of an interface follows
  that interface — in every translation, not only one that declares
  devices.**  Some parsers keep such a next hop in the route's
  gateway: RouterOS `gateway=ether1`, Junos `next-hop et-0/0/24.0`.
  When the interface is renamed — by an entry of `port_rename_map`,
  or by the shape of its name, so with no port map at all — the next
  hop is rewritten with it, and when the interface is dropped the
  route is removed.  It used to be left naming an interface the
  output no longer had.  A next hop that is exactly an interface's
  name follows onto any target.  A Junos unit (`et-0/0/24.0`) follows
  only between two Junos configs, since the suffix means nothing
  elsewhere; a RouterOS list of gateways (`gateway=ether1,ether2`) and
  a routing-table suffix (`ether3@main`) are not followed.  No
  committed capture has such a route.
- **A reserved definitions sub-directory is now reserved only at the
  root.**  The device-definition loader skips `target_profiles/` (and
  now `model_families/`) because their YAML belongs to another schema.
  It used to skip a directory of that name at ANY depth, so an
  operator's own `site-a/target_profiles/` holding ordinary backup
  definitions silently did not load.  Only an immediate child of the
  definitions root is skipped now.  The other side of that: target-
  profile or model-family files kept in a directory of that name BELOW
  the root were never loaded, and now log a validation warning each at
  startup.  Move them to the root-level directory.
- **Profile keys and ids that API clients may have hard-coded.**
  `aruba_aoss/6300M-48G-PoE4-SFP56` is now
  `aruba_aoscx/6300M-48G-PoE4-SFP56`.  The 2930F profiles list bare ids
  (`12`, `49`) where they listed `1/12`, `1/A1`.  The 3810M module SKUs are
  `JL083A` / `JL078A`.  `target_profile` on its own remains advisory --
  none of this changes rendered output.
- **`docs/adding-a-target-profile.md` rewritten** around a capture-backed
  worked example and the evidence-first order of work.  The previous
  worked example was the 6300M, which was wrong on five axes.
- The two C9500 profiles state their deployment (`standalone, switch 1`),
  as every stack-capable profile now must.  Their port ids were not
  examined and they remain ungraded.

### Removed

- **`opnsense/DEC600-IGC`.**  It described a 5-port Celeron N5105 Deciso
  appliance that does not exist.  The current DEC600 2.5GbE units (DEC677
  / DEC697; the rack DEC2687 shares the board) are the 4-port Netboard A8,
  which already ships as `opnsense/Netboard-A8-I225` and now carries those
  model numbers in its display name.
- **`opnsense/Netgate-SG1100` and `opnsense/Netgate-SG3100`.**  Both are
  ARM boards that ship with pfSense Plus.  OPNsense publishes amd64
  images only and has no build for either, so a profile filed under
  OPNsense described a target that cannot exist -- and the SG-3100
  profile also had every port role wrong (`mvneta0` as WAN, no OPT1, four
  invented VLAN children for the LAN jacks).  The x86 `Netgate-SG5100`
  profile is unaffected.  With these gone no shipped profile is graded
  `inferred`; the grade and its amber notice remain, tested on a synthetic
  profile under `tests/fixtures/target_profiles/`.

### Known limitations

- **A sub-interface's number is bounded onto Junos alone.**  On the
  other targets that write a unit's number in its name (IOS-XE, IOS
  XR, NX-OS, EOS and the like) a sub-interface keeps its number from
  any source: what range each numbers is not established here, so a
  number the target does not take is written as it stands.  Read the
  target's own reference for its range before you load such a unit.
- **An IOS-XE or NX-OS sub-interface that states no tag is carried
  with none.**  What either platform does with such a sub-interface
  is not established here (Cisco's IOS-XE guide to Layer 3
  subinterfaces does not say), so the two parsers keep it, and a
  target that names a sub-interface by its tag writes its number for
  one: VyOS `vif <number>`.  Read the source for sub-interfaces with
  no `encapsulation dot1Q` before you load the output.
- **A shut VLAN interface arrives up on AOS-S.**  AOS-S states a
  VLAN's address on the VLAN and holds no admin state for it, so an
  AOS-CX `interface vlan N` that says `shutdown` (or another
  vendor's shut SVI) is written as the VLAN's address, live, in a
  job that says `completed`.  Read the source for shut VLAN
  interfaces before you load the output.
- **An MTU is converted only where the codec reads the interface's
  name.**  A name its classifier does not read -- a Junos `reth0` or
  channelised `xe-0/0/6:2`, a wildcard `interface-range` member, an
  IOS XR `BVI` -- and a loopback or tunnel are copied as they stand,
  since what their number counts is not established here.  Whether
  the media MTU of a Junos trunk in `family ethernet-switching` has to
  hold a tag is not established, and none is counted.  A jumbo value
  near a platform's maximum can pass it once converted (IOS-XE `mtu
  9216` is Junos `mtu 9230`, above the EX range); the device refuses
  the line at commit.  The IOS-XE NETCONF codec carries no MTU into
  the tree.
- **A Q-in-Q sub-interface reaches five targets.**  IOS-XE, IOS XR,
  EOS, Junos and RouterOS write a sub-interface's inner tag; onto
  NX-OS, whose sub-interface statement this codec writes is one tag,
  onto FortiOS, and onto the targets with no routed sub-interface of
  their own, the job is `partial` and the validation report lists the
  inner tag.  A FortiOS VLAN interface on a VLAN interface, a VyOS
  `vif-s` block, and an 802.1ad tag from any source, is left out with
  a row.  A RouterOS VLAN interface on a BRIDGE that says
  `use-service-tag=yes` is read as the bridge's VLAN interface, as
  before: the bridge's own tag type (`ether-type`) is not read.
- **The tree has no IPv6 MTU, and some IP MTUs are not carried.**
  IOS-XE and IOS XR `ipv6 mtu` and a Junos unit 0's `family inet6 mtu`
  are not read.  A Junos unit's `family inet6 mtu` above unit 0 is
  read as the unit's MTU, and so is written for IPv4 as well where the
  unit carries IPv4 and states no `family inet mtu`.  A target with
  one MTU (NX-OS, EOS, RouterOS, FortiOS, VyOS, OPNsense) loses an IP
  MTU stated beside a different MTU, and OS10 writes no IP MTU; the
  job's report says so.  The IP MTU an IOS-XE or Junos config leaves
  unstated under a raised `mtu` is taken to be the payload, which no
  vendor page read says.

- **A RADIUS key stored in a platform's own form is not decoded, and
  goes only to its own platform.**  Cisco type 7 is a reversible
  cipher and could be decoded to the secret; Netcanon does not decode
  it, so an IOS-XE `key 7` is refused on every other target, with the
  server kept and a review line.  Whether EOS's type 7 is Cisco's is
  not established, so an IOS-XE `key 7` is not written into EOS, nor
  an EOS one into IOS-XE.  The global AOS-S `radius-server
  encrypted-key` line is read on the strength of the host-line form
  HPE documents; the global form itself is inferred.  A refused key is
  said by the review line in the output alone, and the job still says
  `completed`, as for a FortiOS `ENC` secret.  And a plaintext secret
  that itself begins with one of the envelopes (`iosxe:`, `eos:`,
  `aoss:`, `fortios:`) is read as that stored form: refused on every
  other target, and on its own platform written in the stored form.
- **A config pasted without its indentation is not translated by most
  block parsers: they refuse it in words.**  The IOS XR parser
  refuses it for the router's reason: IOS XR places a line by its
  indentation when it loads a file (inferred from Cisco's CLI model
  and a Cisco engineer's router output; Fixed, above).  The EOS,
  AOS-CX, IOS-XE CLI, NX-OS and OS10 parsers refuse it for their own
  reason, not the device's: each reads a stanza by its indentation,
  and reading such a text by the mode each command leaves open (as
  EOS is inferred to; what the other four platforms do with it is not
  established here) would need every mode's words, which no vendor
  page lists (Fixed, above).  The AOS-S parser reads it as the
  indented config.  The Junos (set form), FortiOS, RouterOS, OPNsense
  and IOS-XE NETCONF parsers do not depend on indentation.  VyOS keeps
  its tree but loses a Tier-3 row for BGP or OSPF, and the job does
  not say so.
- **A line typed inside an EOS interface's submode is read as the
  interface's, and an EOS `router bgp` block's header has to stand at
  the section's own depth.**  EOS places a line by the mode it is
  typed in, not by its indentation, and no depth inside an interface
  tells a submode's line (`tx-queue`, `evpn ethernet-segment`) from
  the interface's own: a line the parser reads (`shutdown`,
  `description`, ...) typed inside such a submode is read as the
  interface's.  No Arista printout shows one there.  In `router bgp`
  the section's own lines are at the shallowest indentation of any of
  them: a `vrf` or `vlan` header indented deeper than another line of
  the section's own (a hand edit) opens no block, and its route
  distinguisher and route targets are not read, in a job that does
  not say so.  As printed, every header stands at the section's own
  depth.
- **An AOS-CX banner whose text holds its delimiter at the end of a
  line ends there.**  The switch prints a banner's text with the
  delimiter after it, alone on a line or at the end of the last line,
  and nothing in the printout tells a text line that ends with that
  character (`WARNING!` alone, under the usual `!`) from the end -- nor,
  since `!` is also the comment mark, the line the switch printed after
  the text; the switch itself, loading the printout again, would end
  the banner there too (inferred from HPE's input rule; HPE says
  nothing of a banner in a loaded CLI file).  The lines after it are
  then read as configuration (measured: an account line there is an
  account on the target).
- **A banner whose text holds the end the device prints after it is
  refused only where that end is left outside every banner.**  On
  IOS-XE (`^C`), OS10 (a line of the delimiter alone) and AOS-S (a
  quote), the banner ends early, and the device's own end is left on a
  later line, which is refused.  Not seen: such a text whose part after
  its own end opens another banner, which takes the device's end for
  its own, or, on AOS-S, whose quotes are paired so that no later line
  has an odd number; nor, on OS10, a banner delimited by `!`, OS10's
  comment mark.  The lines between are read as configuration
  (measured: an account line there is an account on the target).
- **An IOS `macro auto execute` body is read as configuration.**  No
  printed form of it was found (Cisco shows it typed, ended by `}`);
  `macro name`, which ends at `@`, is read as text.  Nor is an Easy VPN
  server group's indented `banner` (under `crypto isakmp client
  configuration group`) passed over: no Cisco page that shows its form
  was found.
- **An IOS XR banner set through NETCONF can be printed with no end of
  its own**: Cisco's xrdocs.io shows `banner login ! <text>` with no
  second `!`.  Its text then runs on to the next occurrence of its
  first character, and the lines of the configuration between are
  taken for its text: none of them is read, and none is translated, in
  a job that says nothing else of it.  The banner's row counts its
  lines.  Nor is the value of `crypto key generate rsa ... pubkey`
  passed over: no source shows how it is printed.  (FortiOS reads a
  quoted value of several lines whole; Junos, VyOS and RouterOS are
  the next bullet.)
- **The Junos and VyOS parsers read a set-form text a line at a
  time**: a line after a quote that no later quote on its line ends is
  read as a statement of its own.  Whether either device prints a
  value of several lines so is not established.  RouterOS prints a
  line break in a quoted value as `\n`, and its parser reads that as
  the letter `n`: the value is written with an `n` where the break
  was.
- **A value of several lines loses its layout on every target**, the
  ones that could hold it included (OPNsense and IOS-XE over NETCONF,
  in an element's text, and FortiOS between its quotes): it is written
  on one line, each run of breaks as a space, and the job says where.
- **AOS-S `banner exec` is read as `banner motd` is**, though no HPE
  page shows the type; and whether an OS10 banner ends at its
  delimiter in the middle of a line is not established (Dell names "a
  line that contains only the delimiter character"; the parser reads
  the rest as text, the safe side, and a banner that never ends so is
  refused).
- **An EOS account with `nopassword` is written to Junos as a login
  user with no authentication statement**, in a job that says
  `completed`; what Junos then allows such a user is not established
  here.
- **A whole IOS XR `show running-config formal` config is refused,
  not read.**  No capture of it is committed, and Cisco states its
  printed shape for class and policy maps only.  Paste `show
  running-config` without `formal`.  The form is recognised by its
  `interface` lines: a formal excerpt that holds no `interface` line
  with a setting (`show running-config formal router static`, or
  formal output filtered by `| include`) is not recognised, and is
  read as almost nothing, in a job that can say `completed`.
- **The AOS-S probe needs the indentation, or the banner.**  An AOS-S
  config with its `;` banner cut off and its indentation lost is
  detected as no codec; with its banner it is detected whatever its
  indentation.  Choose the source codec by hand.
- **An indented AOS-S stanza header is no header.**  The top of the
  config is read from column 0 only, so a paste that put white space
  in front of every line (` vlan 10`) is read as nothing.
- **A line of the top inside an AOS-S stanza that lost its indentation
  ends the stanza.**  `ip route ...` between two lines of a flat VLAN
  stanza is read as the route, and the VLAN's lines after it are read
  at the top, where none of them is a line of its own.  Whether the
  switch stays in the VLAN's context after such a command is not
  established.  HPE's examples and every committed capture a switch
  printed indent their body lines and close each stanza with `exit`,
  and so do not have this shape; whether any release prints otherwise
  is not established.
- **An AOS-S port tagged and untagged in one VLAN keeps both.**  HPE
  gives a port one participation in each VLAN (tagged, untagged, no
  or forbid), but the parser keeps a `tagged` and an `untagged`
  membership side by side, from the VLAN's lines as from the port's;
  which one the switch keeps is not read.  HPE's own one-line example, `interface 1,6,7-10
  tagged vlan 1,3,5`, does this on a config whose VLAN 1 lists those
  ports untagged.  Older than this release for the `vlan N` form.
- **Dell OS10 cannot be told "every VLAN".**  It has no word for it,
  its VLAN ids end at 4093, and a VLAN must exist before a port is put
  in it.  A trunk of every VLAN is written `switchport trunk allowed
  vlan 1-4094`, as it always was, now under a `! review:` line that
  says so — and for more trunks than before, since a Cisco, Arista or
  AOS-CX trunk that states no list is every VLAN (28 trunks of the
  committed captures, where it was 5).  The line has to be replaced
  with the VLANs the switch has.  The job does not report it.  Pinned
  by a test, and not mended yet.  A list that is NOT every VLAN is
  written as it stands with no such line, and can have the same two
  faults: `2-4094` names an id OS10 does not have, and a list can
  name VLANs the output does not declare, which OS10 wants made
  first.  In the outputs the committed captures make, two lines are
  `2-4094` and 39 name a VLAN the output has no `interface vlan` for
  (those two among them).  Older than this release, and unchanged.
- **Aruba AOS-CX cannot be told "no VLAN".**  A trunk left with no
  allowed VLAN carries every VLAN there, so a trunk that allows none
  has no AOS-CX form.  Neither `vlan trunk` line is written, and a
  `! review:` line in the stanza says what the source said and names
  its native VLAN: list the VLANs the port is to carry, or shut it
  down.  The job does not report it.  What IS written is a switched
  port (`no routing`) with no `vlan` line.  That is taken here to be
  an access port in VLAN 1, by the platform's default — one untagged
  VLAN more than the source's none, on a port that is up — but that
  default is not established here from a vendor's page or from a
  switch.
- **What becomes of a trunk's untagged VLAN is one convention now,
  and these parts of it are not mended.**  A trunk's allowed list is
  what it carries, its native VLAN among them; a native VLAN the
  list leaves out is stated and not carried.  How well that matches
  a switch differs by platform, and is as good as the vendor's own
  page: for AOS-CX it is HPE's sentence; for IOS-XE and NX-OS it is
  Cisco's sentence when the native VLAN is 1, and an inference from
  Cisco's rule for any other, with two phrases of Cisco's command
  reference reading the other way; for the Junos ELS grammar it is a
  requirement Juniper states for receiving, with the send direction
  not established; for EOS it is not established at all; OS10 and
  AOS-S state the untagged VLAN apart and carry it.  Each vendor's
  sentence is in
  `docs/vendor-references/cisco_iosxe_cli_to_juniper_junos/vlans.md`.
  What remains:

  - *A port that carries no VLAN untagged, on IOS-XE or NX-OS
    beside a trunk that carries one.*  Both halves of this are
    mended for IOS-XE, NX-OS, EOS and AOS-CX (the first two entries
    under Fixed), but for one case.  The one form those two document
    for such a trunk on the Catalyst 9300 and the Nexus 9000, `vlan
    dot1q tag native`, tags the native VLAN of every trunk of the
    switch.  Where another trunk of the output carries a VLAN
    untagged -- or a port is in a mode no mode line is written for
    (dynamic, private-vlan, dot1q-tunnel, fex-fabric and the like),
    or holds trunk lines in no mode -- the line is not written: the
    port is written no native line under a `! review:` line that
    says so, and the switch carries VLAN 1 untagged on it by its
    own default.  A port written with no mode and no trunk line is
    not counted: on a Catalyst such a port is in dynamic auto by
    default, and should it become a trunk the line tags its native
    VLAN as well.  Over the committed captures that is one AOS-CX LAG
